decision_maker: Registration of Town and Village Greens Panel
content:
Chris Parry (Head of Corporate,
Property & Information Governance Team), presented the report
which recommended that a non-statutory public inquiry be set up so
that the evidence related to Land off Canberra Crescent could be
properly examined and tested and that further legal arguments could
be made by the various parties, in order to assist the Panel in
determining whether to register the land off Canberra Crescent
(Meir) as a Town or Village Green.

On 16 October 2025 the Council received an application to register
a parcel of land off Canberra Crescent in Meir (shown edged red in
Appendix A of the submitted report) as a Town or Village
Green.

From a land ownership perspective, the site could be divided into
two parts.  The
majority of the Site was privately owned by two individuals and a smaller strip of land belonged to
the Council.

An objection was received from the owners of the privately owned
land raising a range of issues (as outlined in Appendix C of the
submitted report). Amongst other things, the objectors contended
that a Trigger Event had occurred, which would preclude
registration of the site as a Town or Village Green.

Given that an objection had been received, and also taking into
account the Council’s interest in the site as landowner, a
Preliminary Report was commissioned in order to determine whether
there were any clear “knock out blows” that would
permit an expedited determination of the application without a full
inquiry.

Ahead of the independent inspector writing their Preliminary
Report, all interested parties had been invited to submit any
further representations on whether they considered a trigger event
applied or not, and the appropriate procedure for determination of
the application, so that the independent inspector was fully
appraised of all relevant matters. Further submissions were
received from the applicant and objectors (as outlined in Appendix
D of the submitted report). A submission was also received from the
Council’s Property Services Department expressing the view
that the Council owned strip is held as public open space (see also
Appendix D of the submitted report). This is something that would
impact on whether the requirements for a Town or Village Green
pursuant to the Commons Act 2006 are capable of being met. All
submissions were provided to the independent inspector.

The appointed Inspector issued their Preliminary Report in June
2026 and did not consider that there were any clear “knock
out blows” which would justify rejection of the application
without further investigation, and has
recommended that a public inquiry be set up. The independent
inspector’s report was attached at Appendix E of the
submitted report.

Given that it had not been possible to determine this application
by reference to preliminary issues (i.e. there had been no
“knock out blows”), the report recommended that an
independent inspector be appointed to carry out a public inquiry
and to make recommendations to the Panel.

To ensure that the application was determined lawfully, fairly and
robustly, it was considered necessary to appoint an independent
inspector because they would provide:
- expertise in the relevant law;
- independence and impartiality in assessing evidence;
- a structured and transparent process for examining
witnesses.

The associated financial and legal implications were outlined
within the submitted report.

Panel Members confirmed their understanding, in that it was felt
not enough information was available to make a decision at this
point, and questioned the form in which an inquiry might
take.

Officers confirmed the inquiry could either be paper-based,
including additional documents to those provided to the Panel at
the meeting, or could include oral submissions. It was noted best
practice in a case like this, would be to include the submission of
oral evidence. Papers for the inquiry would likely include
additional documents, which would be supplementary to those
included in the agenda pack for the Panel meeting. It was also
possible that a pre-conference could be held beforehand,
in order to discuss protocols and
procedures.

Panel Members also questioned the associated timescales for
progress to be made in relation to this matter. Officers confirmed
they were hopeful of progress within a matter of weeks, and that if
recommendations be approved, they would look to set up the relevant
conference to discuss procedure within this timeframe,
acknowledging the details of this could be impacted by availability
of individuals.
topline: The Registration of Town and Village Greens Panel has decided to appoint an independent inspector to conduct a public inquiry on the registration of land off Canberra Crescent in Meir.

purpose:

nursery.

purpose:
This policy sets out the council’s
approach to issuing civil penalties under housing
legislation.
It reflects mandatory changes introduced through the Renters Reform
framework.
The policy replaces previous enforcement guidance and updates
penalty levels and criteria.
It ensures consistency, transparency, and proportionality in
enforcement decisions.
Civil penalties will be used as an alternative to prosecution where
appropriate.
The policy outlines factors considered when determining penalty
amounts.
It supports stronger action against non-compliant landlords and
letting agents.
Overall, it aims to improve housing standards and protect
tenants’ rights.
content:

the adoption of a new Civil Penalties Policy for Private Sector
Housing.
Agreed (ii) - That delegated authority is granted to the
Director of Housing, Regeneration and Operations, in consultation
with the Cabinet Member for Safe and Resilient Communities and
Housing, to update the policy in response to future legislative,
statutory guidance or case law changes.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to adopt a new Civil Penalties Policy for Private Sector Housing.

content:
In conjunction with other
councils in Staffordshire, to seek approval to progress planning
and undertake work to prepare for:
1. The establishment of new unitary local authorities in
Staffordshire in line with the Government’s chosen model of
Local Government Reorganisation (LGR).
2. The creation of a Foundation Strategic Authority (FSA) for the
whole of the county to enable the transfer of devolved powers and
funding from central government


Agreed - That
Cabinet delegates all necessary Executive powers and
functions to the Chief Executive (in consultation with
the Cabinet Member for Strategy, Economic Development,
Culture, Sport and Homelessness) as
follows:  
·      
Upon receipt of a decision from Ministry of
Housing, Communities and Local (MHCLG) regarding LGR in
Staffordshire to; 
o  
Formulate
proposals and any ancillary information/documentation
required for the creation of a voluntary joint committee, to
be subsequently submitted to Cabinet and Council for
consideration and establishment.  

o  
Negotiate, finalise and approve the
wording of the Structural Changes Order and any supplementary
Orders required to give effect to
or facilitate Local Government
Reorganisation.  

o  
Make operational decisions regarding resourcing,
prioritisation and other tasks required to progress the
implementation of Local Government
Reorganisation.  
·      
In the circumstances where the Ministry of
Housing, Communities and Local Government approves the creation of
a Foundation Strategic Authority for Stoke-on-Trent and
Staffordshire, to finalise a proposal for an FSA
model for submission to Cabinet and Council for
approval.   

·      
Procure any information
or documents that
maybe required to facilitate the subsequent establishment
of a Strategic Planning Board including in a shadow
form.  

·      
Comply with any requirements and carry out
any actions required by a Structural Changes Order or any other
supplementary order relating to the LGR of Stoke-on-Trent and
Staffordshire. 

·      
Accept any Government funding that is provided
for the purpose of FSA, LGR and Spatial Planning and to agree how
the funding should be allocated and spent, in
consultation with the Section 151 Officer. 

·      
Procure any external support or advice which the
Chief Executive, in consultation with
the Section 151 Officer, considers necessary to carry out the
functions delegated under this report.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to delegate powers to the Chief Executive to progress planning for the establishment of new local authorities and a Foundation Strategic Authority in Staffordshire.

content:
To note the feedback from the recent
Masterplan consultation, approval of the preferred Masterplan
option and, should one of the four development options be approved,
approval to procure a Master Developer.

Agreed (i) -
That the feedback from the recent Masterplan
consultation as set out in the report be noted.
Agreed (ii) – That consideration be given to other
relevant factors such as housing need, the number of people on the
Council Housing Register and Local Plan housing supply requirements
to 2040.
Agreed (iii) - That the officer advice relating to Ridge and
Furrow land which recommends that option 1 and Option 3 be excluded
be agreed.
Agreed (iv) – Cabinet notes that Kidsgrove Athletic
Football Club has confirmed in writing that it is open to
engagement on possible relocation.
Agreed (v) – Cabinet determines that the preferred option
is Option 4 - to exclude the Ridge and Furrow Plough land and the
Kidsgrove Athletic Football Club land (at this stage) which would
result in a developable area of 24ha and up to 816 new homes of
which 25% would be affordable rented homes.
Agreed (vi) – Cabinet approves Option 4 to (a) progress to
the procurement of a Master Developer through an appropriate
procurement route (b) commission further surveys and technical due
diligence on the site and (c) progress the submission of funding
bids to Homes England for Social and Affordable Homes Programme
(SAHP) and/or National Housing Delivery Fund (NHDF) and /or any
other relevant funding streams as required.
Agreed (vii) – Cabinet delegates authority to the Director
of Investment, Delivery & Growth to procure a suitable master
developer: to submit grant funding bids; enter into all relevant
legal and other agreements and to take all appropriate steps to
implement the above recommendations in consultation with the
Cabinet Member for Transport, Infrastructure and
Regeneration.
(N.B.
The above recommendations reflect the amendments
and revised numbering required to the recommendations listed in the
report following Cabinet’s decision on this
item).

The Corporate Director of
Resources (S151 Officer) apprised the committee of the outcome of a
light touch review of the financial regulations, including detailed
amendments to the Virement procedure, prior to submission to the
Constitution Working Group on 30 June 2026, and ultimately City
Council.
The Financial Regulations
formed part of the Council’s Constitution and provided the
framework for financial management, control and accountability
across the organisation. They were a key element of the
Council’s governance arrangements, supporting the effective
stewardship of public resources and ensured compliance with
statutory and regulatory requirements.
The Corporate Director
confirmed that a targeted review had been undertaken to ensure they
remained current, clear and operationally effective.  He confirmed that the review had been
intentionally limited in scope and focused on essential amendments
only.  He added that this approach
recognised the forthcoming implementation of the Council’s
new Enterprise Resources Planning (ERP)
system, and that it was considered appropriate to undertake a more
comprehensive review once the new system was in place.

content:
The Pre-Audit Statement of
Accounts 2025/26 was submitted to the Audit and Standards Committee
for information.
The Committee was informed that
it was the intention to publish the Pre-Audit Statement of Accounts
for year ended 31 March 2026 on 30 June 2026 and commence the
period of exercise of public rights on 1 July 2026 through until 12
August 2026, in line with statutory requirements.
The Committee was also informed
that the draft accounts appended to the report set out the main
elements of the narrative and primary statements. It was explained
that the supporting notes to the Pre-Audit Statement of Accounts
were in the process of being finalised along with the consolidation
of the Group accounts (for Unitas).  It
was confirmed that any required adjustments would be made prior to
the publication of the final draft accounts on 30 June
2026. 
Furthermore, the pre-Audited
Statement of Accounts 2025/26 would be certified by the S151
Officer as presenting a true and fair view of the Council’s
Financial position as the 31 March 2026, once any revisions were
completed.
It was also confirmed that the
Draft Annual Governance Statement would be published alongside the
Statement of Accounts.
The
Corporate Director of Resources (S151 Officer),
reported that the City Council’s accounts were
presented on a basis that complied with International Financial
Reporting Standards (IRFS) and Code of Practice on Local Authority
Accounting (the Code) issued by the Chartered Institute of Public
Finance and Accountancy (CIPFA).
Concluding, it was reported
that the Pre-Audit Statement of Accounts would also be subject to
independent review by external auditors, Forvis Mazars LLP, who would issue an audit opinion
which would be reported to a future meeting of this
Committee. 
The Auditors were required to
consider whether the time constraints imposed by the
Government’s backstop date of 31 January 2027 would prevent
them from completing all necessary procedures to obtain sufficient
evidence to issue an opinion on the statement of accounts and
instead issue a disclaimed audit opinion.
The final audited version of
the accounts would be presented to this Committee following
conclusion of the audit.
topline: The Audit and Standards Committee has decided to publish the Pre-Audit Statement of Accounts for the year 2025/26.

content:
The draft Annual Governance
Statement (AGS) 2025/26 was submitted to the Audit and Standards
Committee for consideration and comment.
The Annual Governance Statement
(AGS) explained what the governance framework was and gave a brief
explanation of the component parts. It summarised the key processes
for delivering good systems of control, governance and stewardship
and indicated who was responsible for what. It also addressed how
Stoke-on-Trent City Council intended to monitor, develop and
improve its governance arrangements for the future.
It was explained that the AGS
was a public document and would be published alongside the signed
Statement of Accounts for 2025/26, which would be available to all
customers / partners.
Concluding, the Committee was
advised that the draft Annual Governance Statement would be
considered by the council’s External Auditors as part of the
value for money review for 2025/26. 
Should any changes be required these would be reflected in the
final version which would be submitted to the next meeting of the
Committee.

The Committee was also advised

content:
The Head of Audit and Fraud
submitted a report on the progress and outcomes for the Corporate
Fraud Team (CFT) for the financial year 1 April 2025 to 31 March
2026. The report provided an overview of fraud type which included:
Housing Tenancy (HT) Fraud, Right to Buy (RT) Fraud, Council Tax
– Single Person Discount (SPD) Fraud, Council Tax Reduction
Scheme (CTRS) Fraud, Business Rates, Blue Badge Fraud, Employee
Fraud and Insurance Fraud. 
The Committee was invited to
consider the effectiveness of the Council’s risk management
arrangements, the control environment and associated anti-fraud and
corruption arrangements and to seek assurance that action had been
taken where necessary.
It was recognised that a strong
and effective counter fraud function was a key element of good
corporate governance and evidence of the ongoing activity provided
the Committee with a source of assurance which in turn assisted
them when considering the Authority’s governance
arrangements. 
Concluding, the Committee was
advised that the value of fraud for the year overall amounted to
£2.7m.
topline: The Audit and Standards Committee has reviewed the Corporate Fraud Team's progress and outcomes, highlighting various types of fraud and emphasizing the importance of a strong counter fraud function for good governance.

content:
The Corporate Director of
Housing, Regeneration and Operations submitted a report requesting
the Licensing and Registration Panel (the Panel) to determine an
application for exemption from displaying plates, signage and door
signs for a Private Hire Vehicle, in accordance with the
authorities’ responsibilities for public safety.
The Local Government
(Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1976 required that a licensed
private hire vehicle exhibit a licence plate in such a manner as
the City Council specified by a condition attached to that licence.
The Act also required the City Council, when issuing a
driver’s licence, to issue a driver’s badge in such a
form as may from time to time be prescribed by them. A driver
must at all times, when acting in
accordance with a driver’s licence, wear their badge in a
position and manner such as to be plainly and distinctly
visible.
Section 75 of the Act allowed
the City Council, upon application, to specify either certain
occasions when the plate need not be displayed or issue a notice to
be carried in lieu of the plate being displayed. In these
circumstances the requirement that the driver had to wear a badge
was also waived.
Section 75 was often used in
relation to vehicles that provided ‘chauffeur services’
and ‘executive hire’. The Panel was informed that it
was a matter for them to be satisfied that the character of the
business operation and the vehicle warranted the issue of such
exemptions.
The applicant’s
representatives attended the meeting and confirmed that they had
received a copy of the report and had read and understood it. The
report was outlined at the meeting and
the applicant’s representative was interviewed by the
Panel.
topline: The Licensing and Registration Panel has decided to grant an exemption for a Private Hire Vehicle from displaying plates, signage, and door signs for public safety.

application of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) the provisional

Agreed (ii) - That it be noted, that without the use

resilience, and £5.5 million of capital receipts have been
used to support transformation costs.

relate almost entirely to demand in Children and Family Services and Adult Social Care.

mitigating actions. Expenditure continues to be closely managed and
tightly controlled, with ongoing efforts to identify further
mitigations, some of which are non-recurring in nature.

Agreed (iv) - That it be noted, that all
directorates will continue to maintain strict control over
expenditure in order to address ongoing challenges and
uncertainties within the current financial climate, and to manage
any emerging budgetary pressures.

contingency and the transformation budget be noted.

content:
Helen Slater (Staffordshire and
Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care Board) and Thomas Bailey
(Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care Board) presented
the further update on the wheelchair service.
The report outlined progress
made in response to the Joint Scrutiny Review (August 2024) and the
Wheelchair Service User Representation Group report presented in
January 2026. Ongoing performance issues under the current
provider, AJM, were acknowledged, particularly in relation to
delays, communication and user engagement. Following the issuing of
a Contract Performance Notice, a Remedial Action Plan was agreed
and was confirmed as fully achieved by the end of March 2026. As a
result, 96% of service users were reported to have received
equipment within 18 weeks, all long waits were eliminated, the open
caseload was reduced from 487 to 28, and no service users were
waiting longer than 31 weeks. A corresponding reduction in
complaints, including those raised through MPs, was also
noted.
The outcome of the wheelchair
service procurement was confirmed, with Ross Care appointed as the
new provider from 1 October 2026 for a three-year period.
Mobilisation arrangements were reported to be underway, with
revised performance measures and service user feedback mechanisms
embedded to support improved future delivery and a smooth
transition of services.
In
response to members’ questions and comments, the following
matters were discussed:

·      
The Committee welcomed the report and asked what
mitigations were in place to address legacy issues reported by AJM,
and how similar issues would be prevented for Ross Care.

·      
Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent ICB (ICB) explained
that improved oversight of AJM’s overall caseload had been
established, including identification of an undeclared backlog
which had compounded earlier issues. A stronger working
relationship and clearer visibility of caseload data had been
developed, and this information would be shared with Ross Care to
mitigate legacy risks.

·      
The Committee queried what assurances existed beyond
Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) to prevent a future decline in
performance and how Ross Care would be held to account.

·      
ICB stated that lessons had been learned from the
AJM contract, with stronger contractual levers now in place. More
proactive and regular KPI monitoring would be undertaken, enabled
by revised parameters in the new contract, including clearer
visibility of waits over 18 weeks, to prevent any drop in
performance.

·      
The Chair asked whether the Wheelchair Service User
Representation Group had been engaged in relation to the new
contract.

·      
ICB confirmed that the group had been informed of
the procurement outcome but had not yet been formally engaged, and
that engagement would take place.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to appoint Ross Care as the new provider for the wheelchair service in Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent.

It was reported that the
Integrated Care Board (ICB) and the provider, Opcare, had presented regularly to the Committee
and that assurance had been given that actions against all
recommendations were being addressed. It was outlined that
engagement with service user support groups had been strengthened.
Attendance at PEGiS and MS Mondays had
been undertaken, where information was shared, feedback was
gathered, and concerns were addressed. Ongoing attendance at
regular intervals had been agreed, with flexibility to respond to
emerging issues. Arrangements with Disability Solutions had also
been confirmed, enabling engagement upon request.
It was acknowledged that
continued implementation of these actions was essential to mitigate
risks associated with service user dissatisfaction and reduced
quality of life. The Committee was advised that commissioners
remained assured of progress, with monitoring continuing through
contract review processes. Ther report concluded that improvements
had been made and consideration was invited as to whether this
element of the review could now be closed.

content:
Stephen Gunther (Corporate
Director of Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing) and Shelley
Brough (Director of All Age Commissioning) on behalf of Alison
Elliott (Interim Corporate Director of Adult Social Care and All
Age Commissioning) presented Q3 2025/26 of the corporate
performance measures report.
The report provided an update
on performance against key indicators aligned to the Our City, Our
Wellbeing strategy.
Within the Adult Social Care
and All Age Commissioning directorate, 6 measures were assessed,
with performance described as broadly stable but with ongoing
demand pressures. Backlogs in Care Act assessments increased
slightly, while Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards applications
continued to reduce, albeit remaining above target. Improvements
were noted in the timeliness of safeguarding enquiries and
reductions in outstanding annual reviews, demonstrating positive
impact from management actions. Carer assessments exceeded the
annual target, and satisfaction levels remained high, although
marginally below target.
Within the Public Health,
Protection and Wellbeing directorate, 5 measures were assessed,
with improvements achieved in smoking cessation outcomes following
the introduction of a new service, supported by expanded outreach.
However, a decline in NHS Health Check uptake was observed despite
increased invitations. Public Protection enforcement activity
resulted in £3.1 million of unsafe goods being removed from
circulation.
In
response to members’ questions and comments, the following
matters were discussed:

·      
The Committee commented that fantastic progress had
been made regarding the Adult Social Care and All Age Commissioning
measures.

·      
The Committee commended the recent Trading Standards
seizures, noting several establishments had ceased operating, which
was welcomed.

·      
Cabinet Member for Public Health, Protection and
Wellbeing expressed a strong satisfaction regarding progress made,
particularly in Trading Standards activity. Officers were commended
and encouraged to continue their hard work and positive
performance.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has reviewed performance measures aligned to the Our City, Our Wellbeing strategy.

decision_maker: Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Donna Brayford (Staffordshire
and Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care Board), Rachel Clorley
(Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care Board) and Sharon
Fletcher (Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care Board)
presented the further update on maternity and neonatal (perinatal)
services.
The report outlined progress,
governance arrangements and ongoing challenges within maternity
services. An overview of local service provision was provided,
alongside national developments, including the Independent National
Maternity and Neonatal Investigation, whose interim findings
highlighted safety concerns, inequalities and system pressures.
Local infant mortality trends were reported, showing improvement in
Stoke-on-Trent rates to the lowest level in 15 years, although
rates remained above the England average and inequalities
persisted. A strengthened, system-wide response led by the
Integrated Care Board was described, supported by a refreshed
Infant Mortality Action Plan focusing on prevention, data,
inequalities and engagement.
Assurance was provided on
governance through the revised Perinatal Quality Oversight Model,
strengthened quality surveillance and collaborative learning.
Workforce improvements were reported, particularly at University
Hospitals of North Midlands, with significant midwifery recruitment
and improved retention. Compliance with national safety programmes,
including the Maternity Incentive Scheme and Saving Babies’
Lives Care Bundle, was confirmed.
Engagement with service users
through the Maternity and Neonatal Voices Partnership was
highlighted, with progress noted alongside the need to improve
representation. Overall, it was reported that services had
continued to improve, while recognising ongoing risks and the need
for sustained system-wide action.
In
response to members’ questions and comments, the following
matters were discussed:

·      
The Committee welcomed reductions in smoking rates
but raised concern that infant mortality remained high, asking why
rates were particularly elevated in Staffordshire.

·      
Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care
Board (ICB) responded that health inequalities were a significant
factor. University Hospitals of North Midlands (UHNM) had been
identified as an infant mortality outlier and was undergoing
review, with findings to be reported back. It was explained that
UHNM’s status as a level 3 neonatal unit, higher clinical
complexity, deprivation and pre-term labour all contributed.
Workforce development increased obstetric input and ensuring births
occurred in the right setting were described as key
mitigations.

·      
The Chair expressed longstanding frustration that
clear causes for high infant mortality in Stoke-on-Trent had not
been identified, reflecting on personal experience.

·      
ICB stated that preconception care was pivotal and
that many opportunities were missed before women entered maternity
services. A prevention-led approach was emphasised, addressing
deprivation, education and neighbourhood-level factors. Improved
data integration over the past 12 months and an upcoming infant
mortality meeting on modifiable risks were noted.

·      
Cabinet Member for Public Health, Protection and
Wellbeing queried why a high proportion of women were at increased
risk and what actions were being taken.

·      
ICB referred to ongoing work, including equality,
diversity and inclusion initiatives and specialist midwifery
roles.

·      
Corporate Director of Public Health, Protection and
Wellbeing advised that infant mortality rates were the lowest since
2001 but remained above the national average. A system-wide
approach and a future formal report were offered.

·      
Healthwatch highlighted the complexity of infant
mortality data, noting around 20 infant deaths annually and
requesting a detailed review of contributory factors.

·      
Corporate Director of Public Health, Protection and
Wellbeing confirmed that the Child Death Overview Panel reviewed
every death, including modifiable factors, and offered to share
granular data. It was noted that the panel was being
refreshed.

·      
The Committee sort clarification on whether the 20
deaths included neonatal deaths.

·      
ICB confirmed this covered all deaths within the
first 12 months of life.

·      
The Committee queried how many deaths occurred in
hospital.

·      
Corporate Director of Public Health, Protection and
Wellbeing advised that the Child Death Overview Panel would be best
placed to provide that information.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to further update on maternity and neonatal services, highlighting progress, challenges, and ongoing improvements.

content:
Paul Parkinson
(Director of Housing Management) gave a presentation to the
Committee, explaining that the presentation was a part of the
preparatory work ahead of the housing inspection. The presentation
covered the period up to December 2025, reflecting the position
prior to inspection notification, and that outcomes and a formal
improvement plan would follow within approximately two
months.
The Committee were then
provided with an overview of the regulatory framework, noting that
the Council had not previously been regulated and had developed a
self-assessment plan in 2024. Performance was strong in most areas,
with less-strong areas indicating that while properties were safe,
further development was still needed.
The Committee was
informed that improvements were ongoing in data collection to
better understand tenant demographics, with officers now visiting
tenants at home and telephoning them to gather better
data.
Challenges however,
remained in repairs performance, partly due to the ongoing
implementation of a new IT system, which was expected to improve
appointment scheduling, communication and reporting once fully
embedded. However statutory compliance in areas including fire,
asbestos, and legionella remained fully compliant, with investment
in tower block safety and consideration of service charges also
reported.
In relation to
neighbourhoods, policies were largely compliant though suggestions
were welcomed from the relevant Committees. A satisfaction survey
was also in place, and improvements had been made to ASB by
embedding ASB officers into housing to ensure issues were resolved,
which should raise compliance scoring.
It was then clarified
to the Committee that the regulator had undertaken site visits in
April 2026 and had now requested final information before the
reports would be written and confirmed by a moderator. The service
would then receive a formal grading of C1–C4.
The Committee agreed
that the final inspection report and subsequent improvement plan
would be brought back for scrutiny at a future meeting.
As the presentation was
provided to the Committee after the statutory deadline, Committee
members emphasised the importance of reports being provided to
members on time to allow members sufficient time for
scrutiny.
topline: The Director of Housing Management has decided to approve recommendations for housing improvements.

content:
Councillor Chris Robinson
(Cabinet Member for Housing, Planning, Improvement and Governance)
provided the Committee with an update on previously agreed
recommendations made by the Committee. It was noted that
performance was marginally above target for damp and mould,
however, there had been a decline in emergency repairs completed
within target timescales, attributed in part to performance
pressures during cold and wet weather. It was further reported that
responsive repairs had strengthened and that the number of repair
claims received had remained consistent.
Paul Parkinson (Director of
Housing Management) and Mark Freeth (Director of Repairs and
Maintenance Services) then gave a presentation to the Committee to
update them on the performance of the repairs and maintenance
service. The highlights of the presentation reported that the
Responsive Maintenance Service (RMS) position had improved since
services were brought back in-house, though there were seasonal
issues, particularly during winter months.
Performance reporting had also
been streamlined to better demonstrate outcomes, with key
performance areas including damp and mould, disrepair, anti-social
behaviour (ASB), complaints monitoring, and void property
turnaround times, with these having a financial impact on the City
Council.
It was then noted that routine
repairs had reduced and there had been an increased focus on
capital works to further lower long-term demand. The increase in
emergency works during the winter period had also been consistent
with issues such as heating failures and leaks, though these were
now returning to normal levels. Roof leaks had also reduced
compared to the previous year and a dedicated disrepair team had
been established to work proactively with legal services to address
and prevent claims.
While emergency repairs had
also attended within 24 hours, performance had seemingly decreased
as emergency repairs could not always be completed on the first
visit. Otherwise with changes to resource planning, a dedicated
damp and mould team and a disrepair team had been
established.
The Committee were also advised
that overall anti-social behaviour as a city-wide service was
performing well, with collaborative working arrangements with
Housing Officers now in place to support affected
residents
When considering the complaints
data, it was explained that detailed monitoring had shown that
heating engineers generated the highest number of complaints, with
mis-repair as the most common complaint category. The cause of
these were due to delays in boiler repairs and the use of temporary
heating solutions during the winter months when complaint volumes
were generally much higher because of higher demand. To counter
this, a learning log was maintained to support service
improvement.
It was also explained to the
Committee that the void time between completion of repairs and
letting a property was also monitored due to the loss of rental
income in this period. It was then noted that there had been a
spike in void time due to the opening of the Chatterley Court
sheltered accommodation, in which the delivery of 113 units in a
single phase had temporarily increased void figures due to the
scale of allocations required.
In response to questions from
the Committee, it was confirmed that since repair maintenance
services had returned in-house, the service had shown signs of
improvement.
When asked for clarification on
the removal of secondary heating systems in council properties
however, it was confirmed that since 2023 if secondary heat sources
could not be repaired economically, they were removed from the
property. Repairing secondary heat sources could also be difficult
due to the to their age making it more difficult to source the
required parts to complete repairs.
It was also told to the
Committee that legislation required properties to meet Energy
Performance Certificate standards, which were more difficult to
achieve if a secondary heat source was in the property.
It was acknowledged by the
Committee that there was a cost implication to residents of
removing the secondary heat source, however the Committee were
assured that residents were referred to support agencies such as
Beat the Cold if needed.
At the request of the
Committee, further information on the number of secondary heating
sources removed from the property would be provided, and the data
would be included in the performance reports moving
forward.
On further request from the
Committee, it was also agreed that Committee members would be
provided with data confirming the number of upheld dis-repair
complaints. While this would be provided. it was explained to the
Committee that there would be a lag in the data due to the time
between receiving the complaint letter and the outcome of the
letter being confirmed.
When considering how the City
Council’s performance was benchmarked against other
organisations, the Committee were informed that comparisons were
made against equivalent organisations such as other local
authorities and housing associations, though direct comparisons
were challenging as there were few other organisations the City
Council who could be benchmarked against.
In response to a question from
the Committee about complaints related to damp and mould cases, it
was confirmed that a significant team was now dedicated to
resolving the issue and would respond to reports within 24 hours.
When attending, the operatives would then triage cases to determine
the work required to complete the repair. However, often the damp
and mould were caused by lack of ventilation and so advice would be
given to the property resident.
The Committee also raised
concerns about poor quality properties being let to new tenants.
The Committee were assured that properties had a letting standard,
however there had been incidents, particularly during winter, where
damage had occurred to the property between the final void
inspection and letting the property, requiring repairs to the
tenanted property.
When considering the report,
the Committee also agreed that the topic of empty private
properties in the city would be added to the Work Programme for
further consideration. In conjunction, as the presented data
regarding voids did not include further detail beyond void
durations, the Committee agreed that future reports would contain
information on the amount of time between void completion and the
property being let.
To further explore community
safety in both private and council properties, the Committee also
agreed that a thematic meeting involving relevant ASB officers
would be added to the Work Programme to further explore the ASB
issues raised in the report.
Committee members then advised
that they had receive reports from residents of their ASB cases
being referred the relevant services and then passed between
different services without resolution. The Committee was informed
of the statutory case review process, which allowed tenants to
request multi-agency reviews of ASB cases. The Chair agreed of the
need for improved awareness of this process and reiterated the
importance of bringing relevant officers to the meeting. The
improvements to the repairs and maintenance service since the
service had been returned to in-house was also noted.
Following these discussions,
the Committee members formally voted and agreed to establish a Task
and Finish Group to explore ASB with all the relevant Committees.
Committee members agreed to meet again to scope out the
requirements of the Task and Finish Group.

decision_maker: Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Neil Macdonald (Corporate
Director of Children and Families) and Iain Robinson (Policy
Manager) presented the Family Matters Stoke-on-Trent Children,
Young People and Families Strategy (2026-30) to the
Committee.
The Family Matters:
Stoke-on-Trent Children, Young People and Families Strategy
2026–30 was presented as the city’s new partnership
framework, replacing the previous Room to Grow strategy and setting
out a whole-system approach to improving outcomes for children,
young people and families. Progress since 2020 was highlighted,
including improvements to early help, safeguarding, SEND provision
and education services, although significant challenges were
recognised, including high levels of child poverty, poor health
outcomes, lower educational attainment and the highest rate of
children in care in England.
It was reported that the
strategy was to be informed by extensive engagement with young
people and by national policy promoting prevention, early
intervention and family-centred support. Four whole-city missions
were identified: protecting children from harm, improving skills
and education, improving health and wellbeing, and making
Stoke-on-Trent a more child- and family-friendly city. Seven
strategic priorities were established, focusing on family
stability, community safety, early years, poverty reduction, health
and wellbeing, participation in decision-making, and education,
training and employment opportunities. Delivery was proposed
through existing partnership strategies, Family Hubs and other
multi-agency initiatives, with oversight to be provided by the
Children, Young People and Families Strategic Partnership Board and
progress monitored through agreed outcome measures.
In response to members’
questions and comments, the following matters were
discussed:

The
Committee welcomed the report, commenting that it was well written,
set out the scale of the challenges facing families and clearly
identified the factors contributing to those issues.
The
Chair stated that the final strategy was much stronger, more
coherent and supported by a broader evidence base. However, concern
was raised that accountability, delivery timescales, resources and
arrangements for addressing underperformance were not clearly
defined, making the document appear more aspirational than
operational.
The
Chair also praised the reconvened Strategic Partnership Board and
the leadership shown by the Board Chair, Cabinet Member for
Children’s Services.
CAFS
advised that accountability arrangements were contained within the
Partnership Board’s Terms of Reference and that the Board
would play a key role in delivery and performance
monitoring.
Corporate Director of Children and Families (C&F) agreed
that the strategy was intentionally strategic rather than
operational. It was explained that an implementation plan,
including milestones and accountability arrangements, would be
developed through co-production and led by the Partnership
Board.
The
Committee asked whether greater emphasis could be placed on social
cohesion within the strategy.
Corporate Director C&F agreed that social cohesion was
integral to creating a child-friendly city and confirmed there was
scope to strengthen this area.
The
Chair asked how the strategy would respond to future changes in
national policy.
CAFS
explained that while the strategy reflected the current national
policy direction, the operational plans beneath it would be
adaptable. It was noted that the greatest uncertainty related to
Local Government Reorganisation.
The
Committee queried how issues such as austerity and poverty would be
addressed.
CAFS
advised that a separate anti-poverty strategy was being developed
beneath the overarching framework.
Cabinet Member for Finance, Anti-Poverty, Governance and
Corporate Services confirmed work on the anti-poverty strategy and
Crisis Resilience Fund was underway and acknowledged the
significant impact of poverty on children and families.
The
Committee highlighted the absence of workforce considerations,
stressing the importance of both Council and partner workforces in
delivering the strategy.
Corporate Director C&F agreed that workforce development and
consistency across the system were essential considerations and
should be strengthened within supporting documentation.
The
Committee suggested that employers and the Chamber of Commerce
should be recognised as key stakeholders.
Corporate Director C&F responded that employers were already
included through education, skills, training and apprenticeship
priorities.
The
Chair expressed concern that the governance diagram did not clearly
show accountability arrangements or performance reporting
lines.
The
Corporate Director C&F stated that detail would sit within
implementation arrangements rather than the strategic document
itself.
CAFS
referred members to page 36 of the strategy, noting that the
intention was to connect the Partnership Board to all relevant
boards and forums rather than outsource accountability.
Cabinet Member for Children’s Services noted that work
undertaken through the Strategic Partnership Board may have
addressed some of the concerns raised. They welcomed members’
feedback, emphasised that numerous strategies and datasets had
informed the document, and stated her commitment to ensuring
partners remained engaged and accountable. They agreed that social
cohesion was embedded throughout the strategy, although not always
explicitly referenced.
The
Chair concluded by thanking officers and partners for what was
described as a substantial and greatly improved piece of work that
did not shy away from the challenges facing the city.
topline: The Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve the Family Matters Stoke-on-Trent Children, Young People and Families Strategy 2026-30 to address challenges and improve outcomes for children and families in the city.

content:
Anthony Wild (Director of
Children’s Social: Children in Care & Quality) presented
the update on the local offer for care leavers to the
Committee.
It was reported that
significant enhancements to the Care Leavers Local Offer had been
implemented following Cabinet approval in 2025, in response to
inspection findings and feedback from care leavers. Council tax
exemption support had been extended to care leavers aged
18–25 living outside the city, ensuring greater equity and
financial stability. A flexible public transport support scheme had
been introduced, offering digital and paper bus passes tailored to
individual needs. Progress had been made towards a funded broadband
scheme, while digital inclusion had been supported through
partnership work providing laptops to care leavers. Development of
a dedicated partnership and fundraising post had been explored to
strengthen sustainability and attract external funding. Care
leavers had been recognised within the Council’s Equality
Impact Assessment process, and a wider corporate parenting
commitment had been embedded across Council services. Risks
associated with a weak local offer, including poorer outcomes and
organisational challenges, had been highlighted, alongside emerging
budget pressures linked to increasing numbers of care
leavers.
In response to members’
questions and comments, the following matters were
discussed:

·      
CAFS advised that the forthcoming Children and
Social Work reforms will strengthen requirements around local
offers, transition to adulthood, financial literacy and financial
support information, whilst extending corporate parenting
responsibilities to partner organisations such as the NHS, Police
and education providers. A survey of around 300 children in care
has been completed, with findings being presented to the Corporate
Parenting Board and informing the next delivery plan.

·      
Chair welcomed the report and commented that it was
encouraging to read.

·      
The Committee noted that many elements of the
enhanced offer are now live and asked how the Council reaches care
leavers who are no longer in contact with services.

·      
CAFS explained that support remains available to
care leavers aged 18–25 if they choose to access it. Around
170 care leavers aged over 21 and under 25 remain eligible for
support. Newsletters are distributed regularly and the service
actively promotes the message that young people can return for
support. Survey feedback highlighted a desire for a dedicated app,
which is being explored to improve communication and
engagement.

·      
The Committee asked how former care leavers who have
said they no longer want contact are informed of available
support.

·      
CAFS confirmed that newsletters continue to be sent
unless an individual specifically opts out.

·      
The Committee asked whether data is available on
uptake of the enhanced offer.

·      
Corporate Director C&F confirmed that uptake
figures are available.

·      
The Committee welcomed continued support for care
leavers but raised concerns about the financial implications
outlined in the report, suggesting that funding appeared to be
being redirected from one vulnerable group to another through use
of the Housing Support Grant/Crisis funding
arrangements.

·      
Cabinet Member for Children’s Services
responded that the Household Support Fund has been replaced by the
Crisis Resilience Fund, which is intended to build resilience in
families and communities. They did not consider the funding to
represent taking resources from one vulnerable group to support
another.

·      
The Committee asked for an update on proposals for a
fundraising and partnership post to attract additional external
funding.

·      
CAFS advised that discussions had taken place with
the voluntary, community and social enterprise (VCSE) sector and
further work was progressing before a further report is
presented.

·      
The Committee asked whether similar posts exist in
other local authorities.

·      
CAFS advised not in exactly the
same format, although authorities work with VCSE partners
and there could be dual benefits in supporting children and young
people whilst attracting additional funding.

·      
Corporate Director C&F added that some local
authorities do have comparable roles. They emphasised that the
opportunity extends beyond public sector funding to include private
sector and social value contributions, potentially creating
sustainable revenue streams. They noted that expectations around
care leaver support have increased significantly since 2022,
requiring the Council to adapt and strengthen its offer.

·      
Cabinet Member for Finance, Anti-Poverty, Governance
and Corporate Services acknowledged the validity of concerns raised
regarding funding pressures and highlighted the need to consider
statutory and corporate parenting responsibilities towards care
leavers.

·      
Chair observed that the £200,000 budget
allocation appears sufficient only to maintain the current offer
and not the proposed enhanced package.

·      
CAFS explained that some costs, particularly
transport and broadband support, depend on take-up levels, although
financial modelling assumes high participation. He also highlighted
opportunities to maximise social value contributions from employers
and partners.

·      
Cabinet Member for Finance, Anti-Poverty, Governance
and Corporate Services stated that future workforce strategies need
to support young people to develop skills for changing employment
markets. They suggested care leavers should be supported to develop
digital skills, including being “AI-curious”, whilst
also pursuing trades and vocational careers.

·      
CAFS acknowledged the need to improve employment
outcomes for care leavers aged over 18. Referring to the
partnership working case study, they highlighted the importance of
joint working between Council services and partners to create
employment opportunities and ensure young people leave education
with appropriate qualifications. They noted that care leaver
champions often move on through career progression, creating a need
to continually strengthen the network.

·      
CAFS reported that GCSE results for Year 11 children
in care had outperformed those of other West Midlands authorities,
although a significant attainment gap remains compared with
children who are not in care. They stressed the importance of
ensuring all children in care take core qualifications in English,
maths, science and IT, and said that work is underway to raise
aspirations and narrow the attainment gap.

·      
Chair suggested inviting aspirational speakers,
including members of the judiciary, to engage with young people and
broaden awareness of career opportunities.

·      
Corporate Director C&F said previous attempts to
recruit volunteers for similar opportunities had generated little
interest, potentially because some young people had negative
experiences of the court system. However, they agreed to revisit
the proposal and consider promoting opportunities through the Year
11 newsletter.

·      
Chair emphasised the value of showcasing judges from
non-traditional, working-class backgrounds and encouraging young
people to consider a wider range of career pathways.

·      
Corporate Director C&F agreed to revisit the
idea and explore how such role models could be introduced through
future communications and engagement activities.
topline: The Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to enhance the Care Leavers Local Offer to provide better support for care leavers, including council tax exemption, public transport schemes, and digital inclusion initiatives.

decision_maker: Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Florah Shiringo (Interim
Director of Children’s Social Care: Safeguarding) presented
the Families First Partnership Programme update to the
Committee.
It was reported that the
Families First Partnership Programme (FFPP) had made significant
progress since November 2025, moving from high-level service design
into implementation planning and preparation for early delivery.
Strong and increasingly mature partnership engagement was reported
across children’s social care, health, police, education,
housing and voluntary sector organisations, with shared ownership
of the programme continuing to develop.
It was noted that governance,
programme management and risk arrangements had been strengthened to
support delivery, while service models for the Integrated Front
Door, Family Help, Family Group Decision Making and Multi-Agency
Child Protection Teams had become more clearly defined. A phased
implementation approach was outlined, including the introduction of
a pilot Family Help team and forthcoming workforce
consultation.
Emerging challenges were
identified around securing formal partner commitments, maintaining
consistent representation across agencies and progressing
co-location arrangements. However, these issues were reported as
typical for a programme at this stage and were being actively
managed through established governance and risk processes. Overall,
the programme was reported to be well positioned to move into
consultation and early implementation in a controlled and phased
manner.
In response to members’
questions and comments, the following matters were
discussed:

·      
CAFS advised that any risks identified through the
FFPP are discussed through the Programme Board, which is well
attended and has strong partner representation. This reflects the
programme’s emphasis on multi-agency governance and risk
management.

·      
The Committee highlighted the importance of securing
the long-term commitment of partner organisations, noting that
sustaining partner involvement has historically been challenging
and that the programme must be seen as a collective effort to
improve outcomes across the city.

·      
CAFS responded that partner attendance and
engagement at meetings remains strong, with organisations
continuing to participate actively in programme
discussions.

·      
The Committee asked whether partner organisations
are held accountable for their involvement through inspections or
oversight by their own regulatory bodies.

·      
Corporate Director C&F explained that future
inspections of children’s services will consider partnership
working, and that there are areas of overlap with inspections of
partner agencies. Recent inspection activity involving
Staffordshire Police had identified shared priorities, and police
engagement in the programme was described as positive. Challenges
within health partners were attributed to wider national
restructuring and workforce changes rather than any lack of
commitment from partners.

·      
The Chair asked how the success of the planned
Family Help pilot team would be measured.

·      
CAFS explained that the pilot would test systems,
processes, forms and reporting arrangements ahead of wider
implementation. Learning from the pilot would be used to refine
delivery, while workforce feedback on confidence, training needs
and expectations would form part of the evaluation process. The
wider staffing changes are expected to be implemented towards the
end of the summer.

·      
CAFS added that learning from national pathfinder
authorities is being incorporated into the programme and that close
collaboration is taking place across the West Midlands and
Staffordshire to support consistency of approach.
topline: The Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee has reviewed the progress of the Families First Partnership Programme, highlighting significant advancements in implementation planning and partnership engagement.

decision_maker: Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Neil Macdonald (Corporate
Director of Children and Families), Wendy Fairman (Interim Director
of Education), Florah Shiringo (Interim Director of
Children’s Social Care: Safeguarding) and Anthony Wild
(Director of Children’s Social Care: Children in Care &
Quality) presented the Quarter 3 2025/26 Corporate Measures
performance report for Children and Family Services.
The report presented
performance across 8 key measures of which 4 were rated green, 1
red and 3 without a Red-Amber-Green (RAG) rating. The number of
children in care was reported to have reduced to 1,097, reflecting
fewer care entries and increased discharges through adoption,
special guardianship orders and reunifications. Social worker
caseloads were reported to have increased slightly to 18.2 but
remained below the target of 20. Placement stability was maintained
within target levels, while youth re-offending was reported to have
fallen significantly to 12%, outperforming both local and national
comparators. Contacts increased and referrals decreased, reflecting
the continued impact of early help and triage arrangements.
Persistent absenteeism remained below target at 19.1%. Education,
Health and Care Plan timeliness was reported to have fallen to
42.4%, primarily due to staffing pressures and seasonal service
closures, and remained the only measure rated red.
In response to members’
questions and comments, the following matters were
discussed:

·      
The Committee noted that performance was moving in
the right direction.

·      
The Chair noted that contacts had increased while
referrals had decreased and commented that this indicated children
and families were being directed towards more appropriate early
help and support services, reducing the need for statutory
referrals. This was considered to reflect the positive impact of
early help provision and triage arrangements.
topline: The Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee has reviewed the Quarter 3 performance report, showing improvements in key measures for children and families.

The Corporate Director of
Housing, Regeneration and Operations submitted a report requesting
the Licensing and Registration Panel (the Panel) to determine an
application for exemption from displaying plates, signage and door
signs for a Private Hire Vehicle, in accordance with the
authorities’ responsibilities for public safety.
The Local Government
(Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1976 required that a licensed
private hire vehicle exhibit a licence plate in such a manner as
the City Council specified by a condition attached to that licence.
The Act also required the City Council, when issuing a
driver’s licence, to issue a driver’s badge in such a
form as may from time to time be prescribed by them.  A driver must at all times, when acting in
accordance with a driver’s licence, wear their badge in a
position and manner such as to be plainly and distinctly
visible.
Section 75 of the Act allowed
the City Council, upon application, to specify either certain
occasions when the plate need not be displayed or issue a notice to
be carried in lieu of the plate being displayed.  In these circumstances the requirement that the
driver had to wear a badge was also waived.
Section 75 was often used in
relation to vehicles that provided ‘chauffeur services’
and ‘executive hire’.  The
Panel was informed that it was a matter for them to be satisfied
that the character of the business operation and the vehicle
warranted the issue of such exemptions.
The applicant attended the
meeting and confirmed that they had received a copy of the report
and had read and understood it. The report was outlined at the
meeting and the applicant was interviewed by the Panel.
topline: The Licensing and Registration Panel has decided to grant an exemption for a Private Hire Vehicle from displaying plates, signage, and door signs for public safety.

content:
Lazarus Mafuko (Chief
Accountancy Officer) presented the item to the Committee, advising
that on an annual basis, the Committee was
required to approve the Council’s accounting policies
used in the preparation of the Statement of Accounts, in accordance
with CIPFA guidance.
It was
noted that accounting standards were
usually updated every year and the Committee was therefore required to review and adopt any
necessary changes within its policies, which were subsequently used
by external auditors to assess the City Council’s financial
statements.
Members were informed that, for the 2025/26 financial year, one substantive change introduced
was the measurement and valuation of plant, property and equipment. Previously, asset valuations
had been undertaken over a rolling
five-year programme. Under the revised approach, assets would
continue to be fully revalued at least
every five years; however, where a full valuation had not
been undertaken, indexation would
be applied. In addition, a desktop
valuation would be carried out in the
third year, using a prescribed and agreed indexation methodology to
ensure asset values remained appropriate.
Other changes included minor
wording updates to ensure alignment with current standards and to
improve overall clarity. The Committee was
advised that these changes would not impact service delivery
but might result in movements within the City Council’s
balance sheet.
Committee members were asked to approve the 2025/26 accounting
policies and to delegate authority to the Section 151 Officer to
make any further amendments required to ensure compliance with the
updated standards.
The Committee noted that the
City Council held debts which it was
required to repay in due course
and queried whether land and other assets were
assessed for their potential value under alternative uses.
In response, it was confirmed that the
values of land, assets, capital receipts
and the different uses of land were
reviewed constantly to remain up to date.
topline: The Audit and Standards Committee has decided to approve the Council's accounting policies for the 2025/26 financial year.

content:

(Corporate Director Resources and S151 Officer), the Committee

delegated authority had been granted to finalise any outstanding
adjustments, and to note and present the final report.
There had not been any major
changes to the transactions within the accounts; however, there
were some challenges in relation to group consolidation. The
actions to address these were noted in the report and therefore
might have required additional sign-off.
The Committee was also advised
that there had been challenges due to instability within the team;
however, since a permanent team had been put in place, the team
were working to ensure issues were resolved moving
forward.
When asked by the Committee, it
was confirmed that the City Council was now up to date with its
2024/25 accounts as part of the build-back process, with continued
discussions taking place with the external auditors on how to
return to normality. However, due to the volume of work required,
this would take time to fully resolve.
Members were advised that,
although the accounts were now up to date from the City
Council’s perspective, it continued to receive disclaimed
audit opinions as a result of historic
challenges. It was therefore anticipated that it might take
a number of years before the Council was
able to achieve a fully completed audit. Nonetheless, progress had
been made.
The Committee commented on the
length of time it had taken to reach the current position, although
it was noted that this was a national audit issue and that the
situation had improved.
topline: The Audit and Standards Committee has decided to review the City Council's Statement of Accounts, highlighting challenges in achieving a fully completed audit.

content:
Clare Potts (Head of Audit and
Fraud) presented the report to the Committee, providing the
standard quarterly update on the Council’s corporate risk
register against the City Council’s strategic
objectives.
In summary, the report outlined
key changes to both identified risks and associated mitigating
actions. The Committee was informed that two risks had increased
since the previous update.
The first of these was the risk
of market failure, which had increased due to ongoing global
pressures impacting supply chains and costs. Specifically, areas
affected included IT equipment, laptops, medication, servers, road
maintenance, and potential increases in fuel costs. To mitigate
these risks, the team had continued to engage with the City
Council’s Emergency Planning Team.
The second increased risk was
the implementation of Financial and HR Systems. As there had been
some contractual issues encountered during the implementation
process, mitigation measures included working in partnership with
other organisations to deliver the system. It was noted, however,
that the implementation of new systems was inherently risky and
therefore had to be reflected in the risk assessment.
When questioned by the
Committee, it was confirmed that Nick Edmonds (Corporate Director
Resources and S151 Officer) was monitoring the project. Nick
explained to the Committee that these types of projects were highly
complex and challenging, with rapidly advancing technology, and
therefore it was essential that system modules were implemented
correctly, as the solution was expected to last for at least a
decade.
In conversations with senior
officers in other local authorities, it was reported that they had
faced similar challenges; however, regular meetings had been held
with the contractor and periodic external reviews had been
commissioned to ensure that the right decisions were made to avoid
creating long-term legacy problems. Nonetheless, progress had been
made and work had been underway to
identify efficiency savings where possible. Due to these factors,
the project risk had been escalated.
The Committee then confirmed
the importance of getting the new system implemented correctly the
first time and not rushing the project.
When asked about the timeline
of the project, it was explained that this would depend on two key
decisions to be made in the following two weeks, as these decisions
would significantly change how work was carried out and therefore
strong change management for staff was essential.
It was noted that, once
implemented, the system would improve staff access to information
and enable on-demand analytics, potentially creating cost savings.
One key decision, however, was how to integrate revenues and
benefits, and when the decisions had been made, the Committee would
be updated on the timeline for completion.
topline: The Audit and Standards Committee has decided to prioritize the correct implementation of Financial and HR Systems to mitigate increased risks.

content:
Presented by Clare Potts (Head
of Audit and Fraud), the Committee was informed that the internal
audit plan for the current financial year aligned with new global
internal audit standards. Further information on this would be
provided in the outturn report due in June 2026.
The plan had been produced to
align with the new standards and was risk-based to provide broad
coverage of key risks instead of focusing on whole services. The
plan was prepared by approaching Corporate Directors to understand
their concerns, as well as horizon scanning to understand what
risks other authorities were facing. 
The plan included reviews of leadership and culture.
Work would also cover grants
assurance (to ensure the City Council could still receive grant
funding), monitoring recommendations, and identifying controls to
prevent fraud. Audits would also include targeted visits to
facilities such as schools and small group homes to identify good
practice that could be rolled out to all facilities where
possible.
There would also be close
collaboration with IT colleagues, with the audit plan particularly
focusing on cyber security, adding value alongside external
reviews. Appendix 2 outlined updates to the Audit Charter, noting
that under the new standards, any non-audit duties (e.g.
involvement in accounts) had to be declared to maintain
independence.
In response to questions from
the Committee, it was confirmed that the Internal Audit Strategy
and Plan was a continuation of what had previously been agreed and
was a sound plan based on the principles outlined at the previous
meetings.
It was also advised that, when
completing individual reviews and updating the audit programme, the
team would look at key risks in each area by consulting officers on
their concerns. The Committee was also informed that, despite the
audit team being small, it had undertaken a number of effective
reviews and had proactively identified appropriate recommendations
for improvement.
topline: The Audit and Standards Committee has approved an internal audit plan aligned with new global standards to focus on key risks and controls to prevent fraud.

purpose:
The Pride in Place Programme is a long-term,
community-led regeneration initiative announced by Government in
2025 and updated in 2026. Stoke-on-Trent has been selected as a
participating authority, as eligible neighbourhoods identified
based on deprivation and community need. This report seeks Cabinet
approval for the proposed governance model and arrangements for
delivery of the Pride in Place Programme in Stoke-on-Trent,
including the establishment of Neighbourhood Boards (one per area)
and the associated delegations required to enable programme
delivery.
content:
Agreed (i) – That
Cabinet delegate authority to the Director of Public Health,
Protection and Wellbeing, in consultation with the Leader of the
Council and the Cabinet member for Safe and Resilient Communities,
to establish three Pride in Place Neighbourhood Boards, working
closely with the respective Members of Parliament. This includes
undertaking the necessary appointment and selection processes for
Board members and Independent Chairs.

Agreed (ii) – That Cabinet delegate authority
to the Director of Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing, working
with the relevant local Member of Parliament and the Independent
Chairs (once appointed), to finalise Neighbourhood Board membership
and Terms of Reference, and to make any amendments required in
response to further Government guidance.

Agreed (iii) – That Cabinet delegate authority
to each newly constituted Neighbourhood Board (supported by
Stoke-on-Trent City Council) to develop a 10?year Regeneration Plan
for their respective neighbourhood, including public consultation,
which will be submitted by Stoke-on-Trent City Council to
Government, subject to Section 151 officer approval.

Agreed (iv) – That Cabinet agree that
Stoke?on?Trent City Council will act as
the Accountable Body for Pride in Place neighbourhoods and adopt
the programme governance arrangements as required by
Government.

Agreed (v) – That Cabinet approve the
undertaking of public and/or stakeholder consultation in relation
to the Pride in Place Programmes in the identified
areas.

Agreed (vi) – That Cabinet delegate authority
to the Director of Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing, in
consultation with the Section 151 Officer, to formally accept the
Pride in Place offer and grant conditions, including capacity
funding.

Agreed (vii) – That Cabinet delegate authority
to the Director of Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing to
authorise expenditure of programme funding in accordance with
Government guidance and available expenditure, including
neighbourhood board establishment, community engagement, planning
and programme management.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to establish three Pride in Place Neighbourhood Boards for long-term regeneration plans and community engagement.

content:
Committee Members received the
Authority Monitoring Report 2025, as required by Section 35 of the
Planning and Compulsory Act 2004 and Part 8 of the Town and Country
Planning (Local Planning) (England) Regulations 2012. The Authority
Monitoring Report 2025 also included the Stoke-on-Trent Five Year
Housing Supply Statement 2025.

The report presented up-to-date information on the current five
year housing land supply position, which demonstrated that
Stoke-on-Trent does not have a five year supply of housing when
calculated against the Local Housing Need (LHN) figure, in
accordance with requirements set out within the National Planning
Policy Framework (as amended).

Local planning authorities are required to publish information, at
least annually, providing data and information on the delivery of
development. The Authority Monitoring Report 2025 covered the
period of 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025 and broadly covered the
themes of Housing (including the Five Year Housing Supply),
Economy, Transport, Health & Wellbeing, Heritage & Natural
Environment, Environmental Resources, Planning Obligations and
Local Plan Progress.

In terms of development, the report covered the themes of Housing,
Employment, Office, Retail, Leisure and Other Development.

The council had been successful in securing £694,066 of
specific monetary contributions through Section 106 agreements,
which would support a range of infrastructure requirements across
the city. The contributions have been negotiated as part of key
developments.

The Stoke-on-Trent Regulation 18 Draft Local Plan stage was
consulted in September/October 2025 including proposed policies and
site allocations. Representations were being assessed and a
response will be made in preparing the Regulation 19 Publication
Local Plan along with the updating of a number of evidence bases.
The Regulation 19 Publication Local Plan will be consulted on in
August/September 2026. The Local Plan timetable had been reviewed
and updated within the monitoring year, and can be seen in full in
section 10.1 of the AMR.

The Planning Committee were asked to note the contents of the
Authority Monitoring Report 2025.
