decision_maker: Housing, Regeneration & Operations Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Councillor Finlay
Gordon-McCusker (Cabinet Member for Transport, Infrastructure and
Regeneration) introduced the briefing note to the Committee,
explaining that the briefing note had been prepared by the Head of
Highways at the request of the Committee. It was also explained
that the flooding which occurred on the 31st of October
2025 was the result of an unusually high amount of rainfall and the
52 reports of surface water and flooding had been investigated. As
eleven properties had also been confirmed to have been affected by
internal flooding, plans to prevent this reoccurring were also
being considered. These included a further £500,000 dedicated
to drain clearance, among other flood prevention plans explained in
the briefing note. The Chair confirmed their satisfaction with the
increase in budget to prevent flooding, especially if climate
change were to result in further incidents.
When asked by the Committee if
the City Council were working with the Environment Agency to
prevent flooding, it was confirmed that a new officer dedicated to
local flooding was now in place to resolve the issues. Severn Trent
had also been invited to this Committee meeting, however a response
to the invite had not been received. 
The Committee also asked about
the timescales for gullies to be cleaned and the potential dredging
of brooks to prevent flooding in high-risk areas. Officers
explained that timescales were dependent on the area of the
problem, as areas considered to be at high risk of flooding would
be prioritised. It was also hoped that the dredging of brooks would
begin next year. As the Committee advised there had been
conflicting information provided in regard to the timescales for
clearing gullies and the dredging of brooks, a private meeting was
offered by officers to discuss these concerns in further
detail.
The Committee then voted and
agreed to allow Councillor Andy Platt to speak as an observer.
Councillor Platt requested that the flooding issue be revisited at
a future Committee meeting with a full report for the Committee to
consider, as he was concerned that a petition in regard to flooding
on London Road in 2020 had still not been responded to. The
Committee were told that 52 priority locations had been identified
by the new flooding officer, however it was agreed that a new,
detailed report would be provided to the Committee in July. In the
meantime, officers agreed to provide Councillor Platt with a
response to his petition. The Committee also requested that Severn
Trent Water be asked to attend the meeting in July, as the
Committee also raised concerns about recent sewage leaks on the
roads, as well as concerns about how Severn Trent Water would
resolve any flooding issues.
topline: The Housing, Regeneration & Operations Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to allocate an additional £500,000 for flood prevention measures following recent flooding incidents.

decision_maker: Housing, Regeneration & Operations Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Presented by Councillor Finlay
Gordon-McCusker (Cabinet Member for Transport, Infrastructure and
Regeneration), the Committee were told that due to funding and
grants, the number of bus routes and passengers had increased
whilst the cost had been lowered, and the number of evening and
night services had increased. An issue had occurred however with
pensioner and disabled bus users being unable to use their bus
passes before 9:30am, however a trial scheme to allow this was
underway.
As part of the bus service
improvement plan, further improvements made to the service also
included the ongoing roll out of real time bus updates with screens
on bus stops and the reconstructing of bus stop kerbs to increase
bus accessibility for disabled and pram users. The Committee were
also told that these real time information screens contained CCTV
to improve public safety. The Chair welcomed these
developments.
Zoe Jones (Bus Service
Improvement Plan Programme Manager) then gave a presentation to the
Committee summarising the completed and planned improvements to the
city’s bus services. Alongside bus service improvements, new
parking enforcement cars had also been purchased to enforce parking
restrictions on the new red routes to ease traffic for buses and a
new Customer Charter had been introduced to support customers in
resolving any of their issues.
In response to questions from
the Committee, it was advised that contact had been made with the
bus companies to discuss the introduction of new buses to improve
service reliability. So far, several new buses had been introduced
and due to approved local transport funding, it was hoped that new
buses, including electric buses and their required infrastructure,
would be added soon. The Committed were also told that while a
significant amount of bus stop kerbs had been altered and a further
audit was due to prioritise the remaining kerbs, not all could be
altered due to roadsides or pavements being unsuitable for
changes.
As the Chair asked about the
installation of bus shelters in their Ward, the Committee were
informed that a programme to refurbish and reinstall bus shelters
was being considered. The Chair would be updated on this outside of
the meeting.
As the Committee then noted
that the journey planner on the new bus stop information website
was not working and then enquired about the costs of the flags on
new bus stops, it was agreed these updates would be provided to the
Committee.
The Committee then asked about
the parking enforcement camera cars. It was confirmed there were
currently four, with one car about to be decommissioned and due to
be replaced. When asked about the cost of the camera cars and the
number of fines each car had issued, it was agreed this information
would be provided to the Committee. The Committee were then
reassured that the cars had the required staffing to be used at
full capacity.
In response to a query about
the resilience of the new bus services if funding were to finish,
the Committee were told that reviews were underway on the financial
viability of these services. The Committee confirmed they wished to
see the results of this survey once completed, however it was also
noted that as long as the buses continued to be used, there was a
greater chance of the services being retained.
topline: The Housing, Regeneration & Operations Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for improvements to bus services in the city.

decision_maker: Housing, Regeneration & Operations Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Carol Gibbs (Corporate Director
Housing Development and Growth) summarised the report to the
Committee, noting improvements to the format to improve
readability. Also highlighted was the high demand for temporary
accommodation due to high levels of homelessness. It was suggested
and agreed by the Committee to review city homelessness at a later
Committee meeting.
The Committee then asked about
the lack of measures displayed in regard to the private housing
sector. As there had been significant investment into empty homes,
it was agreed private sector housing would be included in future
reports.
The Committee were then advised
that void turnaround times were also slightly over target, largely
due to the staged approach of moving residents into the latest
sheltered accommodation at Chatterley Whitfield, however this would
reduce the likelihood of meeting the Q4 target.
The percentage of housing
repairs completed right first time had also reduced slightly,
largely due to the Christmas holiday period, however the trajectory
of this was starting to improve, though further improvements were
required. The Committee were reassured that emergency responsive
repairs completed within 24 hours were at their highest.
It was then explained to the
Committee that the delivery time for major adaptations to resident
homes had also increased, due to higher demand for adaptations and
some works requiring residents to be temporarily relocated from
their homes while work was completed. Nonetheless, the importance
of reacting quickly to keep people in their homes was recognised,
and so improvements to these services were being
considered.
When informing the Committee of
Highways reactive maintenance, there had been a drop in the number
of repairs completed due to adverse weather and staff holidays.
Also, Highways policy was to repair any reported issue within 90
days, which had spread resources much more widely. However
following approval for further funding, additional crews were now
available to repair any road defects.
topline: The Housing, Regeneration & Operations Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to review city homelessness, private sector housing, and housing services to address high demand and improve outcomes.

content:
The Chair outlined the process
to be followed in considering the petition ‘Parking
Permit’ in accordance with the procedure set out within the
report provided. The Chair confirmed that the Lead Petitioner was
not in attendance at the meeting and so invited Councillor Finlay
Gordon-McCusker (Cabinet Member for Transport, Infrastructure and
Regeneration) to discuss the petition.
Councillor Finlay
Gordon-McCusker confirmed that he had visited the affected area and
had reviewed the petition, noting that the scheme was proposed at
the request of the local residents who lived on the relevant
street. The Committee were asked to note the report, however it was
explained that when drawing up proposals for the permit, an option
to include a timed phase for parking at different locations on the
street could be considered. If the scheme were also to proceed as a
traffic regulation order, there would be a period of consultation
with the residents and visitors to provide feedback. Councillor
Finlay Gordon-McCusker also confirmed he would be happy to speak to
the Lead Petitioner or Ward Councillor.
The Committee then discussed
the item, noting it would be difficult to discuss the petition
without the Lead Petitioner present, though further feedback would
be provided during the public consultation if the Traffic
Regulation Order were to proceed. Committee members also indicated
concerns that a parking permit scheme could risk moving the parking
issues elsewhere and could affect the number of customers to local
businesses.

professionals and communities. It is intended to enable the local
authority to discharge it's statutory duty under s507B of the
Education Act 2006 'to secure, so far as reasonably practicable,
sufficient educational and recreational leisure-time activities for
young people aged 13–19 (up to 24 for those with learning
disabilities). This duty requires ensuring access to positive
activities, facilities, and a voice for youth in the local offer,
based on identified needs.'

leaders to ensure broad participation. Although initiatives like
the Priority Education Investment area and the Education Challenge
Board have led to progress, continued collaboration is needed to
further improve outcomes for young people.
We have identified four key areas within the city’s schools
that require significant improvement, and we will collaborate with
our Multi Academy Trusts and schools to implement the necessary
changes. Additionally, we have noted several other areas—such
as school transition—that would benefit from closer
examination and increased focus.

Board to oversee the work brought forward within this strategy,

accountability.

content:
Xanthe Townend (Staffordshire and
Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care Board) presented the Integrated Care
System (ICS) Children & Young People’s (CYP) Programme
Update.
The Integrated Care System Children and Young
People’s Programme Board priorities report was presented,
outlining progress across five strategic areas. Reductions in
infant mortality were reported, supported by improved data,
surveillance, and partnership working. Progress on healthy weight
was described, with a whole-system approach and plans for a
localised delivery framework. Developments in emotional health and
wellbeing were highlighted, including early years activity, suicide
prevention work with schools, and a strengthened focus on
prevention and early help, alongside plans to improve access to
services, with a refreshed approach expected by May 2026.
Advances in complex needs provision were
noted, including the development of a new crisis support service
for children presenting with distressing behaviours, with
sustainable funding identified as a key risk and improvements
needed in transition to adult services. Progress in managing
long-term conditions was also outlined. Overall, good progress
across priorities was reported, demonstrating effective system-wide
collaboration, while recognising ongoing workforce and transition
challenges.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

·       
Corporate Director Adult Social Care and All Age Commissioning
raised queries regarding the complex needs workstream, referencing
the West Midlands initiative and recent workshop in Stafford, and
asked what the specific offer would be for Stoke-on-Trent.

·       
Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care Board (ICB)
representative responded this was outside their immediate
remit.

·       
Combined Healthcare representative clarified that funding covered
both Stoke-on-Trent and Staffordshire, with both services fully
engaged in the initiative.

·       
Corporate Director Adult Social Care and All Age Commissioning
highlighted transition challenges to adult services, noting that
while a strong model existed for disabilities, future demand from
CYP with complex mental health needs would be harder to predict and
would require better engagement with schools and colleges.

·       
Chair acknowledged transition as a recognised issue and noted
potential disruption due to changes in ICB portfolios, including
ongoing discussions about the future of the CYP mental health
board.

·       
ICB representative added that internal structural changes were
taking place.

·       
Healthwatch outlined ongoing work on CYP waiting times (including
autism and ADHD assessments) and asked whether this had been
prioritised.

·       
ICB representative confirmed this had been identified within wider
business cases.

·       
Cabinet Member for Children’s Services questioned how
Priority 5 was being delivered and how success would be measured,
emphasising the importance of incorporating feedback from CYP and
families.

·       
ICB representative agreed that this could be strengthened in future
reporting.
topline: The Health and Wellbeing Board has approved recommendations for the Integrated Care System Children and Young People's Programme Update, addressing priorities in infant mortality, healthy weight, emotional health, and complex needs provision.

Angela Aitken (Senior Public Health Portfolio
Lead) presented the Stoke-on-Trent Health Protection Multi-Agency
Strategic Review 2025–2028 was presented to the Board, and
assurance was provided regarding effective, collaborative health
protection arrangements aligned to national standards. Progress
over the past year had been reviewed across key themes including
screening, immunisation, winter preparedness, tuberculosis,
infection prevention, and air quality. Key inequalities affecting
the population, including deprivation, reduced healthy life
expectancy, and variable service uptake, were highlighted as
drivers of increased health protection risks. Strategic priorities
and action plans for 2026–2027 had been outlined, focusing on
multi-agency collaboration, improved governance, data sharing,
workforce development, and targeted interventions. Risks relating
to partnership capacity, system change, and inequalities had been
identified and mitigation measures described.
In response to
members’ questions and comments, the following matters were
discussed:

·       
Healthwatch queried outstanding actions (p.132), specifically those
past their due dates, and asked whether they had been
completed.

·       
Report Author responded that the document had been in transit since
December 2025, and that completion status of actions still required
review; an update would be provided.

·       
Corporate Director Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing advised
that oversight would be managed through the Health Protection
Strategic Forum (HPSF), and that progress reports could be
shared.

·       
Healthwatch noted that while elements of the actions were nearing
completion, they had not yet been fully finalised.
topline: The Health and Wellbeing Board has decided to approve recommendations for the Stoke-on-Trent Health Protection Multi-Agency Strategic Review, focusing on health protection risks and inequalities.

content:
Helen Slater (Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent
Integrated Care Board), Lucy Marquis (Midlands Partnership NHS
Foundation Trust) and Ruth Luscombe (Impower) presented the report
on neighbourhood health planning.
National policy requirements were outlined,
emphasising a shift from hospital-based care to community
provision, from treatment to prevention, and towards integrated,
data-enabled neighbourhood teams delivering personalised care
closer to home. Local progress was presented, including pilot
approaches to frailty in North Stoke (Ageing Well in Whitfield) and
a children and young people multidisciplinary model in Bentilee, both using test-and-learn methods and
strong community engagement. It was highlighted that further work
was required to develop a coherent framework, strengthen data
sharing, and address workforce and funding challenges. The critical
leadership role of the Board was emphasised in aligning partners,
driving integration, and ensuring accountability. Overall, the
approach was positioned as a major opportunity to improve outcomes,
reduce inequalities, and embed prevention through place-based,
community-led models.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

·       
Corporate Director Adult Social Care and All Age Commissioning
stressed that the scale of the challenge should not be
underestimated, with current models considered unsustainable.
Integrated, place-based approaches were identified as essential,
with governance arrangements needing to align around the Health and
Wellbeing Board (HWB).

·       
Cabinet Member for Children’s Services highlighted that
children’s needs must not be overlooked within the model,
noting forthcoming changes and longer-term transition
timelines.

·       
Impower representative emphasised that the HWB should ensure system
alignment, focus on local priorities, and connect neighbourhood
health to wider public service reform.

·       
Corporate Director Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing noted
that the report was welcomed, with the need for stronger system
alignment, community engagement, and opportunities linked to wider
structural reform noted.

·       
Corporate Director Adult Social Care and All Age Commissioning
emphasised that a consistent methodology was required, while
maintaining flexibility to reflect differing neighbourhood needs
and ensuring meaningful community engagement.

·       
Impower representative noted that pilot approaches should inform
mainstream delivery, with a focus on long-term conditions for
success rather than short-term initiatives.

·       
Chair noted that progress had been made, learning would continue
iteratively, and appreciation was expressed to all involved.
topline: The Health and Wellbeing Board has decided to shift towards community-led healthcare models to improve outcomes and reduce inequalities.

content:
Adrian Green (Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent
Adult Safeguarding Partnership Board), Gina Grimes (Principal
Social Worker & Head of Safeguarding) presented the 2024/25
annual report for the Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Adult
Safeguarding Partnership Board (SSASPB).
The SSASPB Annual Report 2024–25 was
presented, and the Board’s statutory duties under the Care
Act 2014 were reaffirmed, including oversight of multi?agency
safeguarding arrangements and the publication of strategic
priorities and Safeguarding Adult Reviews (SARs). During the
reporting period, significant partnership activity was undertaken
to deliver priorities including Making Safeguarding Personal,
mental capacity practice, safe transitions, addressing
self?neglect, and improving engagement with seldom?heard groups. A
new three?year strategic plan (2025–2028) was developed, and
additional focus was placed on rough sleeping and the rising demand
for SARs, particularly linked to self?neglect.
Safeguarding activity trends were reported:
concerns decreased in Stoke?on?Trent but increased in
Staffordshire, with neglect remaining the most prevalent form of
abuse. Duties of enquiry were met more frequently, and most adults
reported that their desired safeguarding outcomes had been fully or
partially achieved. Eight SARs were progressed during the year,
with learning used to strengthen policy, training, and multi?agency
practice. Subgroups delivered audit, assurance, engagement, and
policy improvements, supporting continuous development and
accountability across partners. Overall, safeguarding arrangements
were deemed effective, with strong partnership working evidenced,
though ongoing challenges relating to demand, system pressures, and
consistent implementation of person?centred practice were
highlighted for further improvement.
In response to
members’ questions and comments, the following matters were
discussed:

·       
Corporate Director Adult Social Care and All Age Commissioning
reported that key changes in 2024/25 had included increased
responsibility for homelessness and rough sleeping within
Stoke?on?Trent City Council, with particular focus on vulnerable
individuals, including younger adults and those sofa surfing, and
noted joint working with the police. It was highlighted that,
whilst responses were effective, challenges remained in
understanding the full at?risk population.

·       
Cabinet Member for Children’s Services welcomed the inclusion
of rough sleeping and asked how many such cases had progressed to
Safeguarding Adult Reviews (SARs), suggesting that greater learning
could be drawn from individuals who had engaged with multiple
services, particularly in relation to deaths and service gaps.

·       
Corporate Director Adult Social Care and All Age Commissioning
advised that numbers progressing to SARs were low, referencing
domestic homicide reviews and reiterating that safeguarding duties
applied to those with care and support needs. It was acknowledged
that further work was required to review deaths and service contact
histories.

·       
SSASPB Chair reported that no SARs relating to rough sleeping had
been undertaken locally in 2024/25, although learning had been
considered from other areas. It was noted that the most complex
cases involved individuals who had undergone care and mental
capacity assessments, requiring improved case management and
escalation processes. The work of the Rough Sleeping Working Group
and the appointment of a Board Champion, in line with ministerial
direction, were highlighted.

·       
Staffordshire Police representative advised that the coroner had a
key role in reviewing such deaths and determining findings.
topline: The Health and Wellbeing Board has decided to approve recommendations in the 2024/25 annual report for the Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Adult Safeguarding Partnership Board.

content:
Assurance Report: Reduce Infant Mortality
Stephen Gunther
(Corporate Director Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing)
presented the assurance report regarding the Health and Wellbeing
Strategy’s ‘Reduce Infant Mortality’ Priority,
covering four Aspirations, and progress to date.
 
Aspirations:

·       
Reduce infant mortality rate to be in line with the England
average.

·       
Reduce under-18 conception rates in line with the England
average.

·       
Reduce smoking in pregnancy (at time of delivery) in line with the
England average.

·       
Reduce pre-term births and low birth weight rates in line with the
England average.
 
It was reported that
an updated action plan structured around five priority themes
(preconception, antenatal and interpregnancy health; data,
intelligence and infrastructure; neonatal and maternal care;
inequalities, wider determinants and disparities; and engagement,
co-production, families’ voice and communication) had been
developed, supported by re-established governance and stakeholder
engagement. Infant mortality rates were noted to remain above the
England average and among the highest nationally and regionally,
driven by modifiable risks and wider social and environmental
factors. However, are trending downwards.
A broad,
multi-agency approach had been implemented, including housing
improvements (e.g. damp and mould), strengthened maternity pathways
from preconception to post-discharge into family hubs and targeted
interventions such as smoking cessation, teenage pregnancy
reduction and pre-term birth prevention. Progress had been
supported by partnership work, data analysis and service
developments, including collaboration with University Hospitals
North Midlands. Key risks included system complexity, capacity
constraints and inequalities. Although rates were trending
downward, this was considered multifactorial and further actions
were planned to include case reviews, enhanced engagement and
targeted interventions to sustain improvement.
In response to
members’ questions and comments, the following matters were
discussed:

·       
Healthwatch representative recommended the report be rated
partially assured, noting that although subgroups were reported to
meet monthly, the priority group had not met since December 2025.
Concerns were raised regarding coordination delays, data sharing,
caseloads, and how member engagement had informed the approach.

·       
Corporate Director Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing
acknowledged the feedback and confirmed they would review meeting
arrangements and ensure invitations had been issued to all
members.

·       
Interim Corporate Director Adult Social Care and All Age
Commissioning sought clarification on whether concerns related to
lack of engagement from adult commissioning and Stoke-on-Trent City
Council.

·       
Integrated Care Board (ICB) representative noted that
organisational transitions can create challenges and committed to
follow up with the report author.

·       
Cabinet Member for Children’s Services queried data on
under-18s smoking, noting anecdotal evidence of vaping rather than
smoking, and asked about education on breastfeeding for young
mothers.

·       
Corporate Director Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing advised
that smoking prevalence among under-18s was low based on school
surveys, with patterns shifting towards vaping; highlighted
expanded stop smoking support (including vaping cessation), and
outlined breastfeeding support through family hubs, maternity
services and post-discharge pathways, noting further improvement
was needed.

·       
Cabinet Member for Children’s Services asked about
differences in low birth weight between under-18s and over-18s.

·       
Corporate Director Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing
confirmed under-18s were at higher risk, noted teenage pregnancy
rates were rising again, and described targeted campaigns on sexual
health, contraception, and wider wellbeing; agreed to provide
further detail on low birth weight.

·       
Cabinet Member for Children’s Services asked whether
engagement with educational establishments on sexual health would
be broadened.

·       
Corporate Director Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing
confirmed a Sexual Health Strategy progressing through Cabinet,
including work on contraception, STIs, and related outcomes.

·       
Cabinet Member for Health Integration and Wellbeing welcomed
progress but emphasised the need for further improvement,
requesting feedback from partners on the effectiveness, uptake and
quality assurance of interventions such as smoking cessation in
pregnancy and breastfeeding support. Concerns were raised regarding
trends in teenage pregnancy and when changes had occurred,
alongside questions about who provides support to young mothers.
The importance of strengthening collaboration across partners and
stakeholders to ensure consistent messaging and maximise impact was
highlighted.

 

Assurance Report: Family Led Decision Making
Patrick Myers
(Family Matters Programme Director) presented the assurance report
regarding the Health and Wellbeing Strategy’s ‘Family
Led Decision Making’ Priority, covering one Aspiration, and
progress to date.
 
Aspiration:

·       
Reduce the number of children coming into care to close the gap
against the statistical neighbour average.
 
It was reported that
the Family Led Decision Making programme had been implemented to
reduce children entering care through earlier, family-centred
support, with over 1,300 families engaged through Voluntary,
Community and Social Enterprise partners and family coordinator
services. It had been recognised that support had previously been
provided too late, and a shift towards earlier statutory engagement
had been made. Relational practice principles had been embedded,
and parents had been identified as key agents of change. Progress
had included enhanced mental health support in schools, strong
engagement in Family Learning Matters, and play strategy
development. Further actions, risks around sustainability and
escalation, and secured funding for continued delivery had been
noted.
In response to
members’ questions and comments, the following matters were
discussed:

·       
Cabinet Member for Children’s Services highlighted the role
of the food partnership and queried what work had been undertaken
with schools to support healthy weight, referencing Department for
Education guidance encouraging governors to work with senior
leadership on food provision, education, and initiatives such as
allotments, and emphasised the importance of early education.

·       
Midlands Partnership NHS Foundation Trust representative responded
that close links had been established with education settings, and
a pilot approach had been introduced to test and learn how
effectively this work operated in schools. It was noted that a
collaborative approach had been adopted to assess available
resources and inform future development.

 

Assurance Report: Children and Young People Achieve a Healthy
Weight
Mark Lambourne (Head
of Leisure, Wellbeing and Bereavement Care) and Neal Morrell
(Facilities and Strategic Business Manager) presented the assurance
report regarding the Health and Wellbeing Strategy’s
‘Children and Young People Achieve a Healthy Weight’
Priority, covering one Aspiration, and progress to date.
 
Aspiration: Reduce
the prevalence of children that are overweight (including obesity)
in line with the England average.
 
It was reported that
the in-house National Child Measurement Programme (NCMP) service
was delivered, with underspend utilised to develop a pilot
programme, supported by extensive research and a proposed direct
award to Time for Sport. A multi-agency Food Partnership was
established to improve access to affordable, nutritious food. A
Sport England funded Place Expansion bid (£1.3m) was
submitted to address health inequalities through physical activity.
Key risks, metrics, and next steps were identified, with a
coordinated, system-wide approach emphasised.
 

Assurance Report: Manage Long-term Conditions of Children
Xanthe Townend
(Associate Director Mental Health, Learning Disability and Autism
and Children and Young People – Staffordshire and
Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care Board) presented the assurance
report regarding the Health and Wellbeing Strategy’s
‘Manage Long-term Conditions of Children’ Priority,
covering one Aspiration, and progress to date.
 
Aspiration: Reduce
the number of under 19s with common conditions that are admitted to
hospital in line with England averages (Asthma, Epilepsy &
Diabetes).
 
It was reported that
progress had been made in managing children’s long-term
conditions, with a focus on reducing avoidable hospital admissions
for asthma, epilepsy and diabetes. Local asthma resources had been
developed, training access increased, and engagement with
environmental factors initiated. A business case to expand epilepsy
specialist nursing provision had been progressed, alongside
approved psychological support alignment. Diabetes services had
been reviewed, identifying no gaps for ages 0-18 years, with
improved access to technology underway. Key risks had been
identified, including limited epilepsy nursing capacity and
insufficient engagement for the 19-25 years age group, with further
actions planned to address these issues.
 
In response to
members’ questions and comments, the following matters were
discussed regarding the assurance reporting process:

·       
Chair sought assurance based on available feedback; noted the
evidence provided within the report was not sufficient. Highlighted
multiple priorities and questioned whether there is sufficient
evidence to confirm outcomes have been achieved or progressed.

·       
Healthwatch advised the Board it should consider utilising
workshops to insure robust assurance. Reflected that the current
approach does not fit the operating environment.

·       
Chair stated the process is not unusual given their background;
emphasised the Board needs to be clearer about what it
requires.

·       
Corporate Director Adult Social Care and All Age Commissioning
suggested further work is needed outside the Board. Questioned the
aim of reaching the England average, noting potential difficulty
due to deprivation; proposed statistical neighbours may be a more
appropriate comparator.

·       
Chair warned of the risk in benchmarking only against peers;
stressed the importance of ambition beyond “average”,
identifying barriers, and working towards higher performance.

·       
Corporate Director Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing agreed
ambition should be higher, as residents deserve the best. Noted
significant preparatory work already takes place regarding
assurance reporting; recommended reviewing the framework and
process to strengthen assurance.

·       
Chair suggested partially assured rating be given to all Target
Outcomes and associated Aspirations.

·       
Chair directed Board members to indicate if they disagreed with
this assurance rating; no members indicated.
topline: The Health and Wellbeing Board has decided to focus on reducing infant mortality, family-led decision making, achieving a healthy weight in children, and managing long-term conditions of children to improve overall health outcomes.

Patrick Myers (Programme Director, Family
Matters Family Matters) presented the report on Local Trusted
Organisations (LTOs) Activity and Outcomes to the Committee.
The Committee was advised that the Family
Matters Programme delivers early, community?based family support
through LTOs, with the aim of preventing escalation to statutory
intervention. LTOs provide locality?based coordination, school and
community support, micro?grants and early help via Family
Coordinators.
By January 2026, 643 families were being
supported, with emotional wellbeing, family and children’s
issues and education identified as the most common needs. Outcomes
data indicated that many families experienced improvement or
resolution of presenting issues, with appropriate safeguarding
escalation where required. Specialist support for families with
children with additional needs had been reported as effective and
well?integrated with universal services.
Performance data showed fluctuating referral
levels, a general reduction in referrals from Children and Families
assessments during late 2025, and progress recorded through
Outcomes STAR measures, particularly over time. Wider system
indicators showed a reduction in cared?for children and
stabilisation in Child in Need and Child Protection plans.
It was reported that funding for 2026/27 was
expected to be approximately £1.87 million, with around
£1.1 million allocated to LTO activity. The committee was
informed that LTO arrangements would be extended for a further
year, with future delivery moving towards grant?funded models and a
clearer distinction between universal and targeted early help.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

·       
Director of Public Health stated that Family Matters had been
designed to support families in the community, build trust and
adapt to fluctuating needs. The evolving relationship?based
approach and importance of LTOs’ community presence were
highlighted.

·       
Programme Director, Family Matters reported that families often
felt judged by statutory services and that the programme aimed to
build resilience and relational practice. Additional ICB funding,
food voucher schemes and next?year contracts were confirmed.
Engagement with harder?to?reach families was ongoing, and
multi?agency working was emphasised.

·       
Cabinet Member for Health Integration and Wellbeing thanked
officers and noted that 645 families had been supported in
January.

·       
LTOs reported rising needs relating to exploitation risks, mental
health and educational pressures.

·       
The Committee noted that the report metrics were unclear,
specifically referring to page 24 of the agenda pack.

·       
Programme Director, Family Matters explained that families had
completed STAR self?assessments using ten indicators to measure
progress.

·       
The Committee queried what was being assessed; LTO stated that
questions covered mental health, wellbeing and safety plotted on a
STAR chart.

·       
The Committee noted that residents might not understand the
terminology.

·       
CAFS Officer presented STAR Outcome charts and confirmed STAR as an
established tool.

·       
The Committee queried STAR methodology robustness, long?term
tracking and consistency.

·       
LTO Family Focus explained robust quality processes, Liquid Logic
recording and STAR’s widespread use.

·       
LTO YMCA stated that professional disagreements with family scoring
were recorded without overriding families.

·       
LTOs clarified that future support options were routinely discussed
when cases closed, though long?term tracking was not
undertaken.

·       
The Committee queried why LTOs had used Liquid Logic for less than
a year.

·       
Programme Director, Family Matters acknowledged implementation
delays and noted that case studies and data were recorded prior to
Liquid Logic.

·       
The Committee asked about community engagement and champions.

·       
LTOs reported ex?service?user groups, peer support and strong
community?development links.

·       
The Committee raised concerns about funding sustainability.

·       
Programme Director, Family Matters explained that cost?benefit
modelling was under development.

·       
The Committee sought assurance on ICB funding.

·       
Programme Director, Family Matters confirmed £0.5m had been
approved.

·       
The Committee requested more data?driven reporting and raised
concerns about the use of images of children; Programme Director,
Family Matters agreed to remove them for future reports.

·       
The Committee asked about safeguarding escalation.

·       
LTOs outlined pathways via internal processes, the Integrated Front
Door and weekly multi?agency forums.

·       
The Committee requested the inclusion of service?user voice in
future report.

·       
CAFS offered independent support to Family Matters regarding
this.

·       
Programme Director, Family Matters emphasised that children
supported were the responsibility of the whole city, not solely the
local authority.

·       
LTOs confirmed that duplication had reduced through Liquid Logic
and direct communication.

content:
Peter Tomlin (Corporate Director of Adult
Social Care and All Age Commissioning), Sally Gainsbury (Nuffield
Trust) and Thea Stein (Nuffield Trust) presented the Draft Review
of Staffordshire and Stoke-On-Trent Integrated Care Board's 2025/26
Savings Plans by the Nuffield Trust to the Committee.
This independent report was commissioned due
to concerns raised about the potential impact of the Staffordshire
and Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care Board’s (ICB) savings
plans (2025/26) on local residents and
the Council. The Nuffield Trust is described as an independent
research charity with no affiliation to the Nuffield Hospital
group.
The report examined the ICB’S 2025/26
financial plan, under which exceptionally high system?wide savings
of £277 million were required. These savings were driven by
long?standing pressures, including rising demand, relatively high
acute care costs, reduced post?pandemic funding growth and
dependence on non?recurrent financial support. It was stated that
the financial challenges faced locally were consistent with those
experienced at a national level. It was highlighted that the ICB
had been required both to balance its own budget and ensure
system-wide balance across three National Health Service (NHS)
trusts. It was found that financial balance was likely to be
achieved in 2025/26, but only through extensive one?off measures
that were expected to increase financial risk in 2026/27. Savings
were organised into three main areas: the reduction of some
elective activity, particularly in the independent sector;
efficiency and management cost reductions across the system; and a
narrowing of what was defined by the NHS as healthcare.
Key points:

·       
A £277 million system?wide savings requirement was set for
2025/26, one of the largest in England.

·       
Savings were split almost evenly between £141 million to be
delivered by the ICB and £137 million by three NHS provider
trusts.

·       
The total NHS allocation for the ICB area in 2025/26 was
approximately £3.12 billion, against a “do
nothing” spending pressure of £3.39 billion, leaving an
initial gap of £265 million.

·       
Up to £95 million in non?recurrent deficit support funding
was provided by NHS England in 2025/26.

·       
Around £60 million of ICB savings were planned through
redefining what was funded as healthcare, with £43-44 million
linked to NHS Continuing Healthcare (CHC).

·       
Standard CHC eligibility rates were reduced by around 27-30%
between 2022 and September 2025.

·       
CHC eligibility changes were estimated to generate £37.6
million in annual savings across the system, including up to
£10 million relating to Stoke?on?Trent residents.

·       
The University Hospitals of North Midlands NHS Trust faced a
savings target of approximately £75 million, supported by
over £50 million in non?recurrent funding.

·       
Over £40 million of the ICB’s savings in 2025/26 were
non?recurrent, increasing financial risk for 2026/27.
 
The largest savings were identified within NHS
Continuing Healthcare (CHC), where eligibility rates and care
package intensity were reduced. While these changes were presented
by the ICB as corrections to historic over?provision, risks were
identified of unmet need and cost being transferred to local
authorities and individuals, with disproportionate impacts on more
deprived communities. It was concluded that closer joint working
between the NHS, local authorities and the voluntary sector was
required to manage ongoing financial pressures and protect
vulnerable residents.
Following the report presentation by the
Nuffield Trust, Paul Edmondson-Jones (Staffordshire and
Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care Board) and Claire Finn
(Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care Board) presented
slides to the Committee detailing the ICB’s response.
It was stated that the independent review had
been welcomed and that the need for closer joint working between
the NHS, local authorities and the voluntary sector had been
reinforced. The 2025/26 plan was described as having been
clinically led, evidence?based and aligned with national
frameworks, with assurance provided that
it had been deliverable and that cost?shifting to Councils or
residents had not been evidenced.
National NHS priorities for 2025/26 were
outlined, focusing on living within allocated budgets, improving
productivity, maintaining quality and safety, reducing
inequalities, and improving access, waiting times and mental health
care. Increasing demand, estimated at around 20% growth, was
highlighted alongside population ageing, new conditions and rising
clinical intensity, with sustainability challenges emphasised.
Variation and waste within the system were
identified, including avoidable harm and low?value activity, with
an estimated £640 million of avoidable spend annually across
the system. A value?based healthcare approach was described as
having been adopted to reduce waste, improve outcomes, protect
high?value interventions and support staff morale.
Significant changes were outlined within the
CHC programme, including strengthened governance, reduced
restrictive care, consistent eligibility application, revised
pricing arrangements and improved data and assurance processes.
Performance improvements were reported, including a reduction of
10,000 people on treatment waiting lists, improved
referral?to?treatment times, reduced cancer backlogs, faster
ambulance handovers, delivery of the Mental Health Investment
Standard and mitigation of future financial pressures.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

·       
Elective Care & Independent Sector Activity

o  
Nuffield Trust (NT) explained that the majority
of elective reductions related to NHS?funded activity in the
independent sector.

o  
NT noted that very short waiting times in the private sector had
risked disproportionate expenditure on a narrow set of procedures,
particularly those for cataracts, hips and knees.

§ 
An example of this is seen within NHS?funded private cataract
procedure activity and how it had disproportionately benefited more
affluent residents, with less equitable access for deprived
communities.

§ 
This was primarily due to most private providers only accepting
lower-risk patients for procedures due to a lack of acute provision
within the private sector.

§ 
Lower-risk patients (those without multiple conditions or other
risk-factors to ill-health) were more likely to be from a less
deprived, more affluent socioeconomic background.

o  
NT stated that rebalancing this kind of activity was considered
reasonable, provided it was implemented carefully.
 

·       
Providers & Workforce

o  
NT noted national tariff efficiency requirements placed on
providers included the need to absorb inflationary pressures.

o  
NT raised concerns regarding the implications for staffing levels,
given that staffing represented the majority
of provider costs.

o  
NT reported that illustrative figures previously referenced by the
largest acute provider had not translated into actual workforce
reductions.

o  
NT presented ward-level staffing data as reassurance, indicating
alignment with national patterns and a high proportion of
registered professionals.


·       
Continuing Health Care (CHC) and NHS Responsibility

o  
NT described the largest savings area as involving a firmer
definition of what constituted NHS?funded care.

o  
NT noted distinctions between care that was clinically low value or
unnecessary, and care that may be beneficial but not considered
healthcare.

o  
NT stated historical CHC eligibility rates were described as having
been significantly higher than national averages, though variation
was not explained by age, deprivation or disability alone.

o  
NT stated that it could not be statistically determined what the
“correct” eligibility rate should be.

o  
NT highlighted potential financial impact on the Council was
estimated at £2.6m, with £10m described as a worst?case
scenario.

o  
NT acknowledged that CHC data quality limited the ability to track
outcomes and impacts.
 

·       
Committee Challenge and Questions

o  
The Committee raised concerns regarding the reliance on
non?recurrent savings rather than permanent structural solutions,
including the potential for savings through system reconfiguration,
particularly within mental health provision.

o  
ICB responded that national restructuring options, including group
and integrated care models, were being actively explored. It was
stated that models would continue to be reviewed as part of ongoing
system reform.

o  
The Committee queried payments for unused or under?utilised
buildings, particularly “void space”, and whether these
costs could be addressed.

o  
ICB explained that much of the unused space related to primary care
premises distributed across multiple sites. It was stated that
neighbourhood?based models were being rolled out with the intention
of improving utilisation of such estate over time.

o  
The Committee expressed concerns regarding the potential
safeguarding impact of Continuing Health Care (CHC) savings on
vulnerable residents, including how many individuals had seen
funding reduced or withdrawn, and what governance existed to
prevent financial?driven decision?making.

o  
ICB stated that Quality Impact Assessments had been reviewed
independently by NHS England and found to be robust. It was
emphasised that CHC decisions had been made on assessed care needs
rather than financial considerations, and that appeal routes and
review mechanisms remained in place for patients and families.

o  
The Committee raised concerns that CHC eligibility changes risked
displacing costs onto the Council and residents rather than
reducing need, and that the issue should not be considered purely
through a financial lens.

o  
ICB acknowledged concerns regarding cost displacement were
understood, but it was reiterated that national frameworks were
being applied consistently and were designed to assess health need
rather than fiscal pressure.

o  
The Committee asked how reductions in care packages were clinically
determined, particularly where it had been stated that needs had
diminished.

o  
ICB explained that care packages had been subject to regular
clinical review, with particular focus on reducing overly
restrictive one?to?one care where it was no longer beneficial or
proportionate.

o  
The Committee expressed further concerns about the impact of more
restrictive Personal Health Budget (PHB) rules, particularly where
items such as leisure, travel or nutritional support contributed to
independence, mobility and overall wellbeing.

o  
ICB responded that clinical evidence for some interventions, such
as supplements, was limited, and that alternative support,
including dietetic services, was being prioritised where
appropriate. It was stated that person?centred care remained a core
principle, and that exceptions could be made based on clinical
need.

o  
The Committee raised concerns regarding the lived experience of
residents with complex needs, including those with multiple
morbidities, mental health conditions and neurodiversity, and
whether sufficient safeguarding and independent clinical assurance
was in place.

o  
ICB stated that CHC decisions were clinically led and focused on
improving quality of life, with anecdotal examples cited where
reviews had resulted in improved independence and wellbeing.

o  
The Committee queried the plans to reduce access to support for
individuals with suspected autism or ADHD, where the absence of a
formal diagnosis limited access to adjustments in education,
employment and services.

o  
ICB clarified that plans were reflective of the position at a
specific point in time and had since evolved. It was confirmed that
proposed reductions in private diagnostic services had not been
implemented.

o  
Healthwatch expressed concern about a perceived disconnect between
system?level assurances and patient experience, including confusion
regarding references to workforce reductions.

o  
ICB stated that workforce figures had been illustrative
placeholders within planning assumptions and had not reflected
actual reductions, with delivery of the financial plan having been
achieved through alternative measures.

o  
The Committee Chair thanked all involved for their time and effort
in creating the report.

content:
Nick Edmonds (Corporate
Director of Resources (S151 Officer)) presented a summary of the
report to the Committee. The Committee were advised that the
general fund had a forecast pressure of a £6.3 million
overspend, with the main pressures from the Children and Families
Directorate and due to increase as the year progresses. It was also
noted that the City Council would see emerging pressures within
Adult Social Care that would likely impact on future forecasts.
However, the Housing, Regeneration and Operations Directorate was
forecast to underspend, offsetting some of these
pressures.
The Committee were then advised
of the one-off mitigations in place, including the adjustments
related to the Pension Fund and the Exceptional Financial Support
(ESF). The S151 Officer reiterated that the financial position
remains extremely challenging and would need to continue to be
managed tightly moving forward. It was also stated that the City
Council would continue to face difficult decisions when balancing
future budgets.
The Dedicated Schools Grant
deficit was also forecast to increase to £36.1 million due to
rising numbers of Education Health Care Plans and other pressures,
though the increase is predicted to be less than expected. It was
hoped that the central government would address 90% of this
deficit. The Committee were advised they would be updated on this
when the plans had been finalised and announced.
Councillor Sarah Hill (Cabinet
Member for Finance, Anti-Poverty and Corporate Services) then
explained to the Committee that while the number of children in
care had reduced, the children coming into care with higher needs
and requiring more expensive placements had increased costs. Adult
Social Care had also been affected by rising hospital pressures,
causing higher demand for community care placements and as the need
for placements for younger, disabled residents had increased
nationally, overall costs had significantly increased.
The Chair confirmed that there
were no questions from the Committee members.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to address a £6.3 million overspend and increasing deficits in various directorates.

content:
Peter Tomlin introduced this
report, which provided assurance on the quality of social work
practice, highlighted key achievements and outlined priorities for
strengthening adult social care in the coming year.

Gina Grimes attended to provide further detail for Committee, and
spoke about the team, the CQC assessment summary, practice review,
social work student unit, social work apprenticeship programme,
support for newly qualified social workers, retention &
development, other placement opportunities, feedback from staff,
social care academy, festival of practice 2025, changes made in the
previous year and plans for the next year.

Ian Clarke praised the fantastic work of the team and the approach
to work with staff, coproduce strategies for this area and the
focus on staff development opportunities.

Peter Tomlin echoed the comments made and wished to formally note
how proud he was of the social work teams.

Committee Members also wished to record their thanks to the teams,
noting they do an amazing job and were incredibly professional and
responsive.

decision_maker: Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Peter Tomlin introduced this
item, which provided a response to the Committee’s review and
recommendations into the support available for people with dementia
and their carers in Stoke-on-Trent. The
report also provided an overview of the partnership approach to
develop and improve local services for people with Dementia and
their carers.

Peter confirmed that the associated recommendations had been taken
to, and approved by, Cabinet, and that the purpose of the item at
this meeting was to confirm these would be taken forward, with the
Committee being engaged as appropriate.

Particular areas of focus moving forwards were confirmed as
encouragement of GPs to refer people living with dementia (and
their carers) to Dougie Mac/Approach Dementia Services, the
suggestion for social prescribers to provide follow-up contact
following a diagnosis of dementia to offer guidance and support,
the creation of a hub to support people living with dementia and
their carers and provision of an
advocacy service for people living with dementia.

Ian Clarke spoke in detail about Marrow House, the positive work
done there, and how the Committee recommendations aligned with
priority areas within the Joint Strategy and partnership work with
the Integrated Care Board. The willingness across partners and the
sector as whole to develop this area of work was commended.

Ian Clarke also outlined the pilot of new technology at Marrow
House, which included acoustic monitoring, specific types of
lighting and a new application for the understanding of pain when
people do not have the cognitive ability to communicate the
problem.

Peter Tomlin spoke about the implementation plan, and how the
agreed work would be taken forward longer term. Ultimately, the
ambition is a position whereby all services are working well
together, the appropriate training is in place, there is a good
understanding of the needs of patients and carers and that services
are working together in a joined up way, and not simply in
parallel.

Specific points raised by Committee Members included the need for
improved pathway information, work to address the long wait times
to access a memory clinic and a request that the Council and/or ICB
would commit to the sharing of dementia related data on a quarterly
basis.

Committee Members were joined by a number of students from the
Sixth Form College, who had been invited to attend and talk about
the work they had been undertaking.

The first student noted the coursework they had been completing,
but welcomed hearing this topic discussed and brought to life. They
noted the importance of early diagnosis, and welcomed the comments
regarding collaborative working. The impact on carers and family
was also a key area of consideration. The work completed at College
had identified a number of the same gaps which had been discussed,
and the student was glad these had been picked up and would be
addressed. It was hoped gaps following diagnosis would also be
looked at, to ensure the correct support was available throughout
the whole process.

Another student spoke about a family member who was diagnosed with
dementia, and spoke about the journey their family had been on. It
was noted the time taken to get a formal diagnosis was a long time,
and that this had a significant impact on the individual and the
family. The student felt more memory clinics were needed, as it was
believed there were only a couple of these available locally.

The Chair spoke about her visit to the Sixth Form College, and
thanked staff and students for their warm welcome.

An offer was made for the students to visit Marrow House, should
they wish to, as part of their studies, and both the Chair and
Committee Members thanked them for their interest, attendance and
input to this work.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to confirm recommendations for improving support for people with dementia and their carers in Stoke-on-Trent.

decision_maker: Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Laura Bird, Vicky Oxford and
Andy Hadley, from the Integrated Care Board, attended to present
this item, which provided an update of the programmes of work and
current position for dental services for both information and
assurance.

It was confirmed that local services were delivering higher UDAs at
approximately 90%, outperforming and tracking ahead of the previous
three years.

Urgent Dental appointments continued to be delivered across dental
practices and within the community dental service, and a
communications campaign had been launched in September 2025 to
inform patients of how they could access these services.

Statistics were shared regarding the Oral Health Improvement
programme, which covered elements such as ‘Brilliant
Brushers’, ‘Care to Smile’ and ‘Brushing 4
Life’.

From April 2026, the dental contract was being reformed to make NHS
dentistry more sustainable and rewarding for Dental practices, and
the associated changes were outlined which included a particular
focus on children and also tacking gum disease.

Feedback from Committee Members included noticing an increase in
the taking on of NHS patients which was welcomed.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to update dental services and programmes of work in the local area.

decision_maker: Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Laura Bird, Vicky Oxford and
Andy Hadley, from the Integrated Care Board, attended to present
this item, which gave an update of the work and current position
for access to general practice for both information and
assurance.

Results were outlined from the National GP Patient Survey (patient
experience), which was an annual survey conducted. The most recent
results showed improvements on all metrics with performance above
that of the national average in all areas.

In terms of the number of General Practice (GP) Appointments, the
number delivered had increased. It was felt important to note in
this area the key was effective use of appointments, and not just
to look at the number delivered. 89% of patients had been seen
within the 2 week window, which was measured against the national
target of 85%.

Primary Care Winter Hubs were discussed, with details shared of the
5 Winter Hubs in the wider area (Rugeley, Burton upon Trent,
Newcastle under Lyme, Tamworth and Stafford).

Looking at the digital and care navigation progress, the main focus
was on ‘Modern General Practice’ with access models
such as Cloud Based Telephony, Online Consultation & Care
Navigation.

Progress regarding Pharmacy First and the uptake of the NHS app was
outlined and details of what these services could offer was
confirmed. The positive impact on the amount of hours saved in relation to GP appointments
was also discussed.

A digital inclusion update was provided, noting this was very much
patient focussed with partnership working to support residents to
access and understand how it can help them. The team were clear
this work was not a way of removing access via telephone.

A key element of the work was information sharing, so, as an
example, patients understood what was meant by an online
consultation.
 
Committee Member comments included praise for the number of total
triages, welcoming the NHS app and noting the good work of social
prescribers (dealing with elements such as anxiety, benefits, money
issues & loneliness).
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to update on access to general practice and primary care services, showing improvements in patient experience and progress in digital services.

content:
Mandy Rollins (Disability Solutions –
CEO) presented the report produced by the Stoke-on-Trent Wheelchair
User Representation Group.</AI6>
The report outlined the experiences of 78
wheelchair users and carers across Stoke?on?Trent in 2025, focusing
on service delivery by AJM Healthcare. Wheelchair users emphasised
that appropriate wheelchairs are essential to health, independence
and wellbeing, and reported that unsuitable equipment and long
delays had significant physical, emotional and social consequences.
Although AJM has worked to address an inherited backlog, the
service continues to manage around 1,500 open referrals and
receives approximately 300 new monthly referrals without increased
funding.
The Committee heard that while an 18?week
pathway exists, many wheelchair users had experienced delays far
beyond this, with waits exceeding a year and, in some cases,
stretching to two years. Communication was a major concern, with
wheelchair users citing irregular updates, unclear explanations of
prioritisation and limited transparency around delays. Staff were
repeatedly described as supportive and professional, particularly
at the Tunstall Centre, but the wider service was seen as reactive
rather than proactive.
Concerns were raised about assessments not
always capturing lifestyle needs and about significant delays in
obtaining complex or customised equipment. Instances of incorrect
or unsuitable equipment being supplied were highlighted, sometimes
compromising clinical safety. Repairs, though generally functional,
were described as slow, and wheelchair users wanted clearer
reporting pathways and more reliable access to temporary
replacements.
Three case studies illustrated these wider
themes. They included a breakdown of a newly issued powerchair due
to inadequate pre?delivery checks, a year?long delay affecting a
young person with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, and a two?year wait
coupled with repeated assessment failures despite the family
securing funding themselves. These examples demonstrated systemic
issues in communication, prioritisation and coordination across the
service.
The report set out recommendations including
clearer communication, improved adherence to referral pathways,
enhanced assessments, systematic backlog management and the
introduction of a tiered prioritisation model. It also called for
strengthened repair processes and better capacity planning. A key
theme was the need for commissioners, providers and clinical teams
to revisit their responsibilities under the CECOPS Code of
Practice, each nominating a lead for compliance. The report advised
extending the existing contract rather than retendering, enabling
collaborative improvement with the current provider. While positive
practice was acknowledged, the report concluded that significant
systemic improvements are required to ensure a timely, equitable
and person?centred wheelchair service for Stoke?on?Trent.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

·       
Representative of the Stoke-on-Trent Wheelchair User Representation
Group (WURG) noted the contract is currently out to tender but
stated it would be beneficial to keep the same provider.

·       
WURG Representative highlighted that all service components are
based in Tunstall, enabling efficient repairs and faster access to
parts.

·       
WURG Representative advised that changing provider could create
further backlogs and delays, especially if parts are no longer
stored locally.

·       
WURG Representative stressed the importance of better communication
between providers and commissioners.

·       
Cabinet Member for Adult Social Care acknowledged communication
issues and delays caused by parts not being stored locally and
asked whether repair timescales had improved since the report.

·       
Disability Solutions advised that members of WURG reported little
noticeable improvement, with long delays continuing.

·       
Cabinet Member for Adult Social Care asked how children and young
people, such as those experiencing growth spurts, were being
supported.

·       
Disability Solutions explained that children and young people
remain poorly served as per feedback from parents and carers,
citing a 15?year?old who lost independence due to inappropriate
equipment (the individual was given a self-propelled wheelchair
with no means to self-propel independently).

·       
The Committee asked whether any wheelchair users had reported
improvements in the wheelchair service.

·       
Disability Solutions stated no service improvements had been
reported by wheelchair users, though staff at physical centres were
consistently praised for their professionalism, friendliness and
helpfulness.

·       
Disability Solutions stated that while the feedback system exists,
there has been no obvious improvement in independence or equipment
outcomes.

·       
The Committee clarified that criticism was directed at the service,
not at frontline staff.

·       
Disability Solutions advised that the CEO’s work on the
report had been voluntary, undertaken for free and motivated solely
to give service users a voice.

·       
The Committee asked whether temporary wheelchairs are available for
the instances when an individual’s wheelchair requires repair
or maintenance.

·       
Disability Solutions explained that temporary or
“off?the?peg” wheelchairs are rarely suitable, as
equipment is highly individualised.

·       
Healthwatch asked whether the group had provided feedback on issues
linked to dynamic waiting lists and users being overtaken by higher
priority cases.

·       
Disability Solutions noted confusion around dynamic waiting lists,
with wheelchair users moved up or down without clear communication
to their placement within wait lists.

·       
Disability Solutions noted that when someone of higher priority
entered the system it appeared, no regard was given to how long
others had already waited, and this was not communicated with
wheelchair users on the wait lists.

·       
Healthwatch suggested that recommendations should go further on
transparency around waiting list movement and methodology.

·       
The Committee asked whether any notices or contractual improvement
plans had been issued to AJM and asked if clinical letters from
hospitals were expediting cases.

·       
Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care Board (ICB)
explained that clinical information is passed to AJM, which applies
its own prioritisation process, adding that a robust transition
plan would be put in place if the contract moved to a new provider
after the procurement process completed.

·       
ICB advised that they would be able to answer further questions
regarding any performance notices or improvement plans during their
agenda item (see item 68).

·       
WURG Representative expressed willingness to continue supporting
the ICB to improve the service.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations to address significant delays and communication issues in the wheelchair service in Stoke-on-Trent.

content:
Grame O’Malley (Staffordshire and
Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care Board - Delivery and Improvement
Lead for Planned Care, Cancer and Diagnostics) presented the update
on the Orthotics Service Review report.</AI7>
The Committee were advised that all
orthotics?related recommendations from the Joint Scrutiny Review
have been addressed. It was reported that sustained engagement with
PEGiS, MS Mondays and Disability Solutions has been achieved, with
arrangements now in place for these groups to invite Opcare (the
service provider) to future meetings as required. Oversight of this
engagement will continue through routine contract monitoring.
The report detailed that Opcare had
implemented a range of measures to support service users with
sensory processing needs. These include revised appointment letters
allowing individuals to share their support requirements in
advance, quieter clinical spaces where appropriate, and the
introduction of sensory toys for children. Sensory lighting remains
under consideration, although there are known estate?related
limitations, and further improvements will continue to be guided by
user feedback. In addition, improvements in how feedback on
orthotic footwear is gathered and used was noted. Feedback rates
were reported to have risen significantly, enabling more meaningful
insight into service users’ experiences and driving ongoing
service development.
It was reported that all orthotics?specific
actions have been completed and incorporated into routine contract
monitoring. They expressed confidence that the improvements made
are sustainable and continue to enhance the experience of service
users. The Committee was invited to consider formally closing the
orthotics element of the review.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

The Committee asked
whether the 48% increase in feedback on footwear suitability
reflected negative experiences or whether any particular themes
were emerging.
ICB advised that
this increase represented an improvement, noting that Opcare had
previously struggled to obtain feedback. They confirmed they would
identify and share the specific findings arising from the
feedback.
The Committee
queried what proactive measures commissioners were taking to gather
feedback, beyond attending support groups when invited.
ICB explained that:

They have reached
out to Disability Solutions, and there is a shared understanding
that the group may contact Opcare at any time.
Attendance at MS
Mondays will take place on a bi?monthly basis or when
requested.
Service users now
have the option to submit feedback by email.
PEGiS has offered
an open invitation for attendance at their community lounges, with
Opcare scheduled to attend on 05 March 2026.


ICB stated they are
satisfied with the progress made to date.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to formally close the orthotics element of the service review report, with a focus on improving services for service users with sensory processing needs.

content:
A verbal update on the Wheelchair Service was
provided by Helen Slater (Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent
Integrated Care Board - Director of Community Transformation).
</AI8>
The Committee was advised that AJM’s
(the service provider’s) performance over the lifetime of the
contract had, historically, fallen short of the standards set out
within the contractual agreement. Consequently, a Contract
Performance Notice (CPN) was issued in August 2025.
Following the issue of the CPN, a Joint
Investigation was undertaken, which led to the development of a
Remedial Action Plan (RAP) and an associated performance
trajectory. Performance against both the RAP and the agreed
trajectory has been strong, with progress remaining ahead of
schedule. This has resulted in a marked improvement in outcomes for
service users, alongside a noticeable reduction in negative
feedback and complaints.
To demonstrate the scale of improvement
achieved, the Committee was informed of several key performance
indicators. These included the complete elimination of all service
user waits of 65 weeks or more, and a reduction of more than 300
service users in the overall open caseload awaiting equipment. The
proportion of service users waiting more than 18 weeks for
equipment fell by 9%, equating to over 230 fewer individuals
experiencing such delays. In addition, the number of service users
waiting more than 52 weeks for equipment reduced by 75%.
Performance continues to be monitored on a
weekly basis, with detailed reports submitted to the ICB every
Friday. The improvement trajectory and action plan require the
elimination of waits exceeding 31 weeks by the end of February
2026, and AJM remains on track to deliver this target.
The Committee was advised that the
announcement regarding the outcome of the tender process is now
expected on or around 23 February 2026. It was noted that, as the
ICB representative presenting the report is not part of the
procurement team, no comment could be made in relation to the
ongoing procurement process.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

Staffordshire and
Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care Board (ICB) stated that the points
raised by the Stoke-on-Trent Wheelchair User Representation Group
(WURG) would be taken into consideration in relation to contracts
and the procurement process.
The Committee
queried whether the rigorous contract review described was
different from what had taken place historically.
ICB confirmed that,
due to historic performance issues, all available levers had been
used to ensure improvements with the current provider.
ICB confirmed that
they would share the Stoke-on-Trent Wheelchair User Representation
Group’s report and recommendations with AGM and would lead on
all actioning associated recommendations.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for the improved performance of the Wheelchair Service provider AJM.
