content:
A report on dispensations was
submitted to the Committee for consideration.
The Committee was informed that
under the Localism Act 2011, dispensations allowed councillors to
participate in meetings despite have a disclosable pecuniary
interest (DPI) can be revoked by the decision-maker that granted
it.
On 22 January 2026, Councillor
Diane Williams notified the City Council’s Monitoring Officer
that, due to a change in personal circumstances, she no longer
required a dispensation in relation to the setting of rent for
Council houses, other housing properties and/or land.
Section 33 of Localism Act
2011, particularly when circumstances change, requires a formal
process overseen by the authority’s Monitoring Officer or
Standards Committee. A revocation was generally appropriate if the
circumstances under which the dispensation was granted have
changed, or if the original application omitted information or
contained inaccuracies.
topline: The Audit and Standards Committee has decided to approve the revocation of a dispensation granted to Councillor Diane Williams.

improvement actions to strengthen financial governance, internal
control, and long-term sustainability.
The Government’s
statutory backstop, introduced through the Accounts and Audit
(Amendment) Regulations 2024, requires all outstanding local
authority audits to be concluded by 27 February 2026.  The disclaimed opinion issued for Stoke-on-Trent
City Council’s 2024/25 accounts was a national consequence
and the Committee was advised that the Council submitted its draft
accounts on time, improved the quality of working papers, and
strengthened its closedown processes in line with the Financial
Improvement and Recovery Plan.
The Auditors Completion Report
outlined that the Council continued to rely on Exceptional
Financial Support (EFS) due to historic financial pressures
however, the Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) included a
trajectory to reduce reliance on temporary support and acknowledged
that progress was being made in embedding the Financial Improvement
and Recovery Plan and strengthening budget-setting, forecasting,
and financial controls.
topline: The Audit and Standards Committee has approved the External Auditor's reports for Stoke-on-Trent City Council, highlighting improvements in financial governance and continued reliance on Exceptional Financial Support.

The Corporate Director of
Housing, Regeneration and Operations submitted a report requesting
the Licensing and Registration Panel (the Panel) to determine an
application for exemption from displaying plates, signage and door
signs for a Private Hire Vehicle, in accordance with the
authorities’ responsibilities for public safety.
The Local Government
(Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1976 required that a licensed
private hire vehicle exhibit a licence plate in such a manner as
the City Council specified by a condition attached to that licence.
The Act also required the City Council, when issuing a
driver’s licence, to issue a driver’s badge in such a
form as may from time to time be prescribed by them.  A driver must at all times, when acting in
accordance with a driver’s licence, wear their badge in a
position and manner such as to be plainly and distinctly
visible.
Section 75 of the Act allowed
the City Council, upon application, to specify either certain
occasions when the plate need not be displayed or issue a notice to
be carried in lieu of the plate being displayed.  In these circumstances the requirement that the
driver had to wear a badge was also waived.
Section 75 was often used in
relation to vehicles that provided ‘chauffeur services’
and ‘executive hire’.  The
Panel was informed that it was a matter for them to be satisfied
that the character of the business operation and the vehicle
warranted the issue of such exemptions.
The applicant attended the
meeting and confirmed that they had received a copy of the report
and had read and understood it. The report was outlined at the
meeting and the applicant was interviewed by the Panel.
topline: The Licensing and Registration Panel has decided to grant an exemption for a Private Hire Vehicle from displaying plates, signage, and door signs for public safety.

content:
The following motion was moved
by Councillor Walker and seconded by Councillor Evans:
Supporting Sharlotte’s Law and Responding to the
Government’s Road Safety Strategy Consultation
This
Council notes that:

Sharlotte-Sky Naglis
was just six years old when she was tragically killed in a road
traffic collision in Norton Green in June 2021.
Following the
collision, delays in the testing of blood samples caused
significant additional distress to Sharlotte’s family,
highlighting shortcomings in the current legal and procedural
framework.
Under current law,
while police may take blood samples following a fatal collision,
testing requires the consent of the individual concerned, including
in hospital settings, which can delay
investigations—particularly where suspects are unconscious or
incapacitated.
The
Government’s new Road Safety Strategy has now been published
for consultation and includes consideration of reforms commonly
referred to as Sharlotte’s Law.
The Government has
recognised that the current arrangements for taking and analysing
samples in hospital settings are complex and may impede timely
investigations.
The consultation also
highlights practical challenges, including difficulties in securing
the attendance of an approved medical practitioner to take forensic
samples.

This
Council believes that:

Families affected by
fatal road collisions deserve timely, transparent investigations
and should not face avoidable delays in establishing the
facts.
The current legal
framework does not strike the right balance between protecting
individual rights and ensuring that the criminal justice system can
secure the best available evidence promptly.

This
Council therefore resolves to:

Welcome the inclusion
of Sharlotte’s Law within the Government’s Road Safety
Strategy and recognise the tireless campaigning of
Sharlotte’s family and supporters.
Formally respond to
the Government’s consultation in support of reforming
hospital procedures for drink- and drug-driving investigations, so
that samples can be analysed without unnecessary delay in cases
involving serious injury or death.
Support changes that
ensure timely testing of samples from unconscious or incapacitated
individuals.
Encourage the
Government to explore practical alternatives where the attendance
of an approved medical practitioner cannot be secured, to prevent
investigations from stalling.
Publicise the
consultation locally and encourage residents, stakeholders, and
professionals to submit their views in support of Sharlotte’s
Law.
Request that the
Leader of the Council and Cabinet Member for Transport,
Infrastructure and Regeneration write to the Secretary of State for
Transport to set out the Council’s support for reform and to
underline the importance of delivering a system that works fairly
for victims’ families and the wider community.

On being put to the vote the
motion received the support of the Council and, of those present
and voting, it was unanimously:
topline: The Council has decided to support Sharlotte's Law and respond to the Government's Road Safety Strategy Consultation to improve procedures for drink- and drug-driving investigations.

content:
The following motion was moved
by Councillor Platt and seconded by Councillor Robinson:
Welcoming Government Investment in Bus Services in
Stoke-on-Trent
This
Council notes that:

The Government has
confirmed £33 million of investment in bus services in
Stoke-on-Trent, alongside a further £10 million of Government
funding for the 2025/26 financial year.
For many years, bus
services in Stoke-on-Trent suffered from declining reliability,
reduced routes, limited evening and weekend provision, and rising
costs for passengers, disproportionately affecting working people,
young people, older residents and those without access to a
car.
Between 2010-2024,
bus services in Stoke-on-Trent fell by one of the highest levels in
the country.
Bus services are a
critical part of the city’s transport network, supporting
access to work, education, healthcare, high streets and social
connection, and are essential to economic growth, inclusion and
environmental sustainability.

This
Council believes that:

Sustained public
investment in local bus services is necessary to reverse long-term
decline and to deliver a system that is affordable, reliable, safe
and accessible.
The Government
funding represents a significant opportunity to stabilise and
further improve bus services across the city.
This investment can
support new and enhanced routes, extended operating hours, improved
accessibility, better passenger information, and targeted measures
to keep fares affordable.
Local authorities,
working with operators and communities, are best placed to shape
bus networks around the needs of residents rather than short-term
commercial considerations alone.

This
Council welcomes:

The
Government’s decision to invest in bus services in
Stoke-on-Trent, recognising the city’s transport challenges
and the importance of public transport to everyday
life.
The opportunity this
funding provides to deliver tangible improvements for passengers,
including more frequent services, better coverage, safer journeys
and improved value for money.

This
Council resolves to:

Support the use of
this funding to deliver clear, passenger-focused improvements to
bus services across Stoke-on-Trent, particularly in areas with
historically poor connectivity.
Work with bus
operators, local communities and stakeholders to ensure that
investment decisions reflect local priorities and deliver maximum
public benefit.
Continue to advocate
for long-term, sustainable funding for local public transport so
that improvements delivered through this investment can be
maintained and built upon in future years.

On being put to the vote the
motion received the support of the Council and, of those present
and voting, it was:
topline: The Council has decided to use government investment to improve bus services in Stoke-on-Trent, focusing on affordability, reliability, and accessibility.

Norton and Ball Green
shares similar characteristics from both the index of deprivation
and the community needs index as Meir North and Abbey Hulton
wards. 
Norton and Ball Green
suffer from a lack of civic infrastructure to support residents.
Grant funding currently sits at £13.77 per head of
population, compared to a Stoke-on-Trent average of
£1886.47
Historically
government funding tends to go to areas of the city with both
deprivation, and larger populations to allow results to be
evidenced. This approach is detrimental to Norton and Ball Green
due to their smaller population size.

This
Council calls on:

The Leader of the
Council to write to the Secretary of State for Housing and Local
Government to ask for funding for Ball Green and
Norton.
Stoke North MP to
lobby the government for his constituency to receive the same
funding as Stoke-on-Trent Central and Stoke-on-Trent
South.

On being put to the vote the
motion received the support of the Council and, of those present
and voting, it was:
topline: The Stoke-on-Trent City Council has decided to call for funding for Norton and Ball Green to address infrastructure and funding disparities.

content:
The following motion was moved
by Councillor Aumir and seconded by Councillor Davison:
Celebrating the Passage of Labour’s Workers’ Rights
Bill
       This
Council notes that:

The Employment Rights
Act is the most significant upgrade to workers’ rights in a
generation, and this Council welcomes its passage into
law.
This landmark Labour
legislation is proudly pro-worker and pro-business, finally
dragging Britain’s outdated employment laws into the 21st
century.
An estimated 15
million workers across the UK will directly benefit from new
protections, including:

-    An end to exploitative
zero-hours contracts and the introduction of   
     guaranteed
hours,

-           
An end to unscrupulous fire-and-rehire
practices,
-           
Strengthened statutory sick pay,
-           
New day-one rights to parental leave and bereavement
leave, and
-           
A stronger collective voice for employees through
enhanced workplace rights.
-           
A rise to the National Minimum Wage – as
announced in the most recent Chancellor’s Budget, in
November.

Stoke-on-Trent has a
proud industrial and labour movement history, built on the dignity
of work and the principle that working people deserve fairness,
security, and respect.
Insecure work, low
pay and weak rights hold back productivity, suppress wages, and
damage local economies like ours.

This
Council believes that:

We cannot build a
strong economy on insecure work.
Higher productivity
and rising living standards go hand in hand with stronger rights at
work.
The Employment Rights
Act sets in motion a long-overdue shift towards greater security,
dignity, and fairness for people in work, while providing clarity
and stability for responsible businesses.
This legislation
represents the clear difference between a Labour government that
stands with working people and parties that repeatedly side against
them.

This
Council further notes with concern that:

The Conservative
Party has declared war on workers’ rights:

a. They have pledged to scrap every single measure in
Labour’s landmark boost to worker’s rights.
b. Their party is anti-unions, and over 14 years in government,
they presided over the increase of rampant in-work poverty which
sees working people having to have their wages topped up by the
welfare state.
c. The Conservative Leader Kemi Badenoch has described maternity
pay as “excessive” and has opposed further increases to
the minimum wage.
Reform UK would roll
back hard-won rights at work:

a. They want to make it “easier to hire and
fire”.

b. They – alongside the
Conservatives – voted against this bill to strengthening
workers’ rights in parliament.
c. Their leader Nigel Farage has long opposed increasing the
minimum wage and has even argued for cutting it for younger
workers.
d. He has also claimed that women returning to work after raising
children worth “far less” to employers.
This
Council resolves to:

Celebrate the passage
of the Employment Rights Act as a historic victory for working
people in Stoke-on-Trent and across the country.
Publicly affirm this
Council’s support for strong workers’ rights, fair pay,
secure work, and dignity at work.
Commit to promoting
awareness of new employment rights among residents, workers, and
local businesses.
Call on all political
parties represented locally to commit to defending – not
dismantling – these hard-won rights.
Reaffirm that
Stoke-on-Trent City Council will always stand on the side of
working people, not those who seek to undermine their pay,
protections, and security.

On being put to the vote the
motion received the majority support of the Council and, of those
present and voting, it was:
topline: The Stoke-on-Trent City Council has decided to celebrate the passage of Labour's Workers' Rights Bill and affirm support for strong workers' rights and fair pay.

the Licensing and Registration Panel (the Panel) to determine an
application for exemption from displaying plates, signage and door
signs for a Private Hire Vehicle, in accordance with the
authorities’ responsibilities for public safety.
The Local Government
(Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1976 required that a licensed
private hire vehicle exhibit a licence plate in such a manner as
the City Council specified by a condition attached to that licence.
The Act also required the City Council, when issuing a
driver’s licence, to issue a driver’s badge in such a
form as may from time to time be prescribed by them.  A driver must at all
times, when acting in accordance with a driver’s
licence, wear their badge in a position and manner such as to be
plainly and distinctly visible.
Section 75 of the Act allowed
the City Council, upon application, to specify either certain
occasions when the plate need not be displayed or issue a notice to
be carried in lieu of the plate being displayed.  In these circumstances the requirement that the
driver had to wear a badge was also waived.
Section 75 was often used in
relation to vehicles that provided ‘chauffeur services’
and ‘executive hire’.  The
Panel was informed that it was a matter for them to be satisfied
that the character of the business operation and the vehicle
warranted the issue of such exemptions.

decision_maker: Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Anthony Wild (Director of
Children’s Social Care - Children in Care & Quality)
presented the Social Worker Caseloads Report.
The report outlined the current
position regarding social worker and Personal Adviser caseloads
across Children and Family Services. The Committee were advised
that manageable caseloads are essential in enabling practitioners
to build strong relationships with children and families, respond
effectively to need, and deliver consistent, high?quality support.
Excessive caseloads, conversely, can contribute to stress, reduced
effectiveness and higher turnover, which disrupts continuity for
families.
The Committee was informed that
significant progress had been made over the past year in
stabilising the workforce. Turnover had reduced to 8.6%, permanent
recruitment had increased markedly, and agency use had fallen to
14.5%, with 22 agency workers converting to permanent posts since
May 2024. At the time of reporting, 322 FTE social work posts were
budgeted, of which 251 were filled permanently, 46.5 by agency
staff, and 24.5 remained vacant, representing a vacancy rate of 22%
and continuing a downward trend.
It was noted that the average
social worker caseload as at December 2025 was 17.8, with expected
variation across teams due to the different intensities of work
undertaken. Caseloads in specialist teams such as FAST, Court Teams
and Child Exploitation were appropriately lower, while Assessment
and Duty teams held higher short?term assessment work. Caseloads
for workers undertaking their Assessed and Supported Year in
Employment were capped at 16, with an average of 14.4 across the
cohort.
The Committee also received
data on Personal Adviser caseloads for care?experienced young
people. Fifteen PAs were supporting 351 young people, with
caseloads ranging from 2 to 31 and an average of 23.4. Additional
investment during the year had enabled the creation of four further
PA posts, and caseloads were expected to reduce as new staff took
on more young people. Work continued to ensure all eligible 16? and
17?year?olds were allocated independent PAs.
Early Help caseloads were
reported as averaging 24 children per worker within the Supporting
Families service. Partner?led Early Help caseloads were not yet
reported in a format suitable for inclusion.
It was also noted that the
wider context of the Families First Partnership Programme, which
seeks to strengthen early intervention through Family Hubs, the
Integrated Front Door and new Family Help Teams. This programme
aims to simplify processes for families, ensure a single lead
professional and assessment, and embed multi?agency working to
improve outcomes and reduce demand for statutory
intervention.
In response to members’
questions and comments, the following matters were
discussed:
·      
CAFS reported improvements in workforce efficiency,
including increased permanent starters, fewer leavers and several
agency workers choosing to become permanent. They explained that
caseload data in the report shows average figures across teams,
with lower numbers sometimes due to sickness, new starters, leavers
or case complexity. CAFS added that four additional PAs had been
recruited to help reduce caseloads, with the average now 23, and
that the team structure is being reviewed to support
this.
·      
Cabinet Member for Children’s Services stated
that workforce stability had now been created, acknowledging that
there are many newly qualified workers but this forms part of the
natural regeneration of roles. They confirmed the workforce is
stable.
·      
The Committee welcomed the positive improvements in
turnover and the reduction in agency staff and asked whether the
progress was sustainable.
·      
CAFS replied that improvements have been ongoing for
some time and are particularly positive given the national shortage
of social workers. They noted that an average caseload of 22.3 is
still not the desired position and that the Families First
restructure aims to address this. Recruitment remains more
difficult in some teams than others, but progress is being
made.
·      
The Committee commented that the presentation of
caseload information was much clearer and asked whether the figures
included ASYEs.
·      
CAFS confirmed that ASYEs were included.
·      
The Committee asked how many ASYEs were within the
cohort and noted that three social workers held caseloads in the
30s, requesting the raw caseload data by email.
·      
CAFS advised that the Director share the raw data
with the Committee.
·      
CAFS stated that staff are engaged in fortnightly
discussions about upcoming changes and challenges, ensuring they
remain informed and involved. They emphasised the value of
co?designing changes with staff, particularly given past retention
issues, noting that staff are now more receptive to
change.
·      
The Committee observed the need to balance doing
what is right for the city with ensuring staff feel comfortable, as
this supports retention.
·      
CAFS agreed, adding that staff involvement has
improved acceptance and supported retention.
·      
The Committee praised the significant progress made
in the past two years and thanked officers, cabinet members and
councillors for their work.
The Chair exited at 11:25 and
returned at 11:28.
topline: The Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee has discussed the importance of manageable caseloads for social workers and Personal Advisers to provide consistent, high-quality support to children and families.

decision_maker: Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Neil Macdonald (Corporate
Director of Children and Families) presented the Children’s
Services Improvement Plan.
The report presented the
Children’s Services Improvement Plan which was developed in
response to Ofsted’s May 2025 inspection. The plan focused on
strengthening audit and quality assurance, improving management
oversight and supervision, enhancing the response to homeless 16?
and 17?year?olds, improving transition planning for older children
in care and disabled young people, increasing the participation of
care?experienced young people, and improving the local offer for
care leavers, particularly in relation to employment, education,
and training. These priorities had been supported by clear
milestones, identified leads and success measures, with progress to
be monitored bi?monthly through the Children’s Improvement
Board.
Improving capacity around
practice quality and supervision had been highlighted as a key
element of the improvement journey, supported by targeted training
and expanded practice evaluation activity. The voice of the child
had remained central, reinforced through refreshed participation
work, community?based engagement, and improved performance data to
support oversight by Heads of Service. It was also reported that
work to improve the local offer for care leavers included a
refreshed version with a commitment to further enhance it,
particularly around employment and training opportunities.
Engagement and strategic planning involving young people with lived
experience had also been prioritised to shape
improvements.
The report warned that failure
to deliver the plan could risk poorer outcomes and potential
regulatory intervention, though this had been mitigated through
clear governance and accountability arrangements. Financial
implications had been limited to existing training budgets, aside
from a proposed Fundraising and Partnership role. It was reported
that the plan provided a structured framework for improvement,
demonstrating the Local Authority’s commitment to raising
standards across children’s services.
It was suggested that future
meetings could explore the practice evaluation process in more
depth. This would include understanding what was recorded on case
files, what practitioners, children, and families could contribute,
and how this insight could be used to strengthen practice and
improve line of sight.
In response to members’
questions and comments, the following matters were
discussed:
·      
The Committee noted that the Children’s
Improvement Board remained broadly the same structure as before,
meeting bi?monthly with elected members and senior officers; and
asked about the financial implications of including a fundraising
role.
·      
CAFS confirmed that the Children’s Improvement
Board operated as described. They explained that the proposed
fundraising role aimed to generate additional support for care
leavers, following engagement with voluntary and community
organisations and identification of new funding
opportunities.
·      
The Committee queried the use of Blue Red Amber
Green (B-RAG) ratings in appendix 1 (Children’s Improvement
Plan), expressing concern that actions recently achieved had
already been marked as “sustained” after very little
time, and asked officers to review the approach.
·      
The Committee queried whether quality assurance
activity was being carried out solely internally and asked whether
external assurance or collaboration with other local authorities
had been considered.
·      
CAFS reported that the improvement lead appointed by
the service was external and brought extensive experience in
inspections, providing fresh perspectives.
·      
The Committee asked which of the six priority
improvement areas presented the greatest concern.
·      
CAFS advised that management oversight and
supervision remained the most pressing area. They noted that
achieving this would be challenging given the current financial
climate.
·      
The Cabinet Member for Children’s Services
stated that transitions were the greatest concern due to the high
number of children in care approaching adulthood. They welcomed the
proposed fundraising role as a means of strengthening the care
leavers’ offer. They also noted that improvements in
management, supervision and practice, and changes within the
Families First Partnership, would have significant operational
impact but should ultimately streamline practice.
·      
The Committee stated that the Children’s
Improvement Board had previously felt poorly attended, but
attendance had now improved, with Jon Rouse’s involvement
helping to strengthen the partnerships and stakeholder engagement.
The Committee commented that the Board had become more effective as
a result.
·      
CAFS confirmed that board membership was under
review to ensure it remained relevant and functional.
·      
The Committee expressed satisfaction that the
Children’s Improvement Board continued to operate and
emphasised the need for ongoing improvement, particularly
in light of the MacAllister Review. They
also stressed the importance of workforce stability during
forthcoming local government reorganisation, noting that a stable
workforce was essential for sustained improvement.
·      
CAFS stated that the three foundations for
improvement, workforce, partnership, and practice, were being
strengthened, including a revamped workforce board, regular
discussions within the Families First programme, and ongoing
Q&A sessions with teams and directors to support engagement and
retention.
·      
The Cabinet Member for Children’s Services
reported that the number of agency social workers had halved over
the past year, and staff turnover had also reduced
significantly.
CAFS invited the Committee to
consider future deep?dive sessions into specific elements of the
Improvement Plan.
topline: The Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to implement the Children's Services Improvement Plan to enhance services for vulnerable children and young people.

content:
Delyth Mathieson (Director of
Education) presented the Improving Education Strategy Consultation
Update.
An update on the consultation
undertaken for the Improving Education Strategy 2025–2030 was
provided. The Committee were informed that academic attainment in
the city remains a significant challenge, despite some emerging
positive signs. Although Priority Education Area funding ended in
spring 2025 and no replacement funding has been identified, strong
partnership working has continued, enabling good practice to be
shared and cross?city groups to be developed around leadership,
curriculum, safer schools and SEND.
It was reported that the
Improving Education Strategy has been co?constructed with education
leaders, multi?academy trusts, partners and young people. The
strategy sets out a shared ambition to raise standards, close the
attainment gap, and ensure every child and young person in
Stoke?on?Trent can reach their full potential. Members were advised
that extensive consultation activity has taken place, including two
citywide education forums, working groups, discussions at
established leadership networks, and targeted engagement with young
people through schools, youth organisations and partner agencies.
Their views have been incorporated into the final draft of the
strategy.
The Committee was updated on
the development timeline, noting that informal consultation took
place over summer 2025, followed by a formal public consultation
during October and November. The final draft has since been refined
to reflect consultation feedback and the publication of the 2025
summer results. The strategy is scheduled for Cabinet consideration
in March 2026, with a proposed launch in May 2026 and the
establishment of a governance board in June 2026.
In response to members’
questions and comments, the following matters were
discussed:
·      
CAFS advised that the draft Improving Education
Strategy is scheduled for Cabinet in March and that extensive
consultation with young people has taken place. CYP had expressed a
wish for SEND support to be available in mainstream
schools.
·      
CAFS highlighted the importance of utilising
relationships with trusts, noting that the number of trusts has
reduced from 28 to 25 as they consolidate. They reported strong
discussions with schools, the DfE and trust CEOs, and confirmed
that committee feedback had been incorporated. They added that the
SEND strategy feeds into the work, including the cluster model and
learning from other local authorities, and that an accessible
version for CYP is being created.
·      
The Committee thanked officers for returning with
the updated work so quickly, for incorporating feedback, and
thanked the Cabinet Member for pursuing the matter.
·      
CAFS explained that this forms part of the wider
joint children’s strategy, which focuses on safety and
achieving the best outcomes for children.
·      
The Committee asked when the new children’s
strategy would be brought forward.
·      
Cabinet Member for Children’s Services stated
that they had only just received it and confirmed it would be
returning in due course.
topline: The Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee has approved the Improving Education Strategy 2025-2030 in Stoke-on-Trent.

content:
Neil Macdonald (Corporate
Director of Children and Families) presented the Corporate Measures
Performance Report for Q1 & Q2 of 2025/26.
An update was provided on
performance against the Council’s corporate measures for
Quarters 1 and 2 of 2025/26. Members were reminded that the revised
performance framework, agreed as part of the ‘Our City, Our
Wellbeing’ strategy, continues to provide oversight of key
operational services across all directorates. A total of 53
measures were reported this quarter, with performance broadly
stable.
It was noted that contacts to
Children’s Services had marginally reduced, and referrals had
similarly fallen, reflecting the continued impact of Early Help and
the operation of the Police Protection Notice triage. Average
social worker caseloads had risen slightly to 17.6 but remained
below the target of 20, with recruitment and agency staffing used
to manage pressures in assessment teams.
Placement stability remained
strong. Only 8.4% of children experienced three or more placement
moves, which was below both the previous quarter and the 10%
target. Youth reoffending rose to 19%, but performance continued to
compare favourably with national and YOT family averages due to
sustained targeted interventions.
The Committee was advised a
temporary reduction in EHCP timeliness to 65.5%, attributed to
summer delays in securing statutory advice. However, performance
remained above national levels, with completion times averaging
21–24 weeks. Numbers of cared?for children increased to 1,109
as entries to care outpaced exits. Work was continuing to identify
safe discharge options through reunification, alternative orders and a review of
children placed with parents.
Across the wider Council,
directorate performance showed mixed RAG ratings, with strong
performance in several areas but ongoing challenges in others,
particularly where statutory pressures and demand continued to
rise.
In response to members’
questions and comments, the following matters were
discussed:
·      
The Committee commented that the level of
improvement across the service over the past two years had been
“phenomenal.”
Cabinet Member for
Children’s Services expressed satisfaction with progress in
SEND, stating that Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP)
performance had “vastly improved” compared with the
previous year.
topline: The Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee has reviewed the performance report for Q1 & Q2 of 2025/26, noting stable performance but ongoing challenges in key operational areas.

content:
Nick Edmonds (Corporate
Director of Resources - Section 151 Officer) and Lisa Dale (Head of
Finance – CAFS) presented the Budget Consultation
2026/27.
The Cabinet Member for Finance,
Anti?Poverty and Corporate Services opened discussions by outlining
recent changes to the national fair funding formula and set out how
these adjustments are expected to impact Children’s Services,
particularly in terms of how need and deprivation are assessed and
funded.
It was outlined that there was
continuing financial pressures on the Local Authority, driven by
rising demand for children’s and adult social care and
sustained inflation across staffing, contracts and operational
costs. It also noted that this was the first budget prepared under
the Government’s new Fair Funding Review, which updated the
national funding formula. While the revised formula better
recognised deprivation and relative need, the funding allocated
remained insufficient to offset the long?standing financial
challenges faced by the Council.
Children’s social care
had been identified as the most significant financial pressure
facing the Council, driven by Stoke?on?Trent’s position as
having one of the highest rates of children in care nationally. The
Committee were informed that despite the multi?year Local
Government Finance Settlement improving planning certainty, the
Council still faced an initial budget gap of £31.2 million
for 2026/27. This had been partly reduced through additional
Government funding, a proposed 4.99% council tax rise and
£9.8 million of corporate savings and efficiencies. Temporary
reductions in pension contributions had also helped ease pressures.
However, significant demand in children’s social care meant
the Council still required £10.5 million of Exceptional
Financial Support to maintain resilience, meet statutory duties and
sustain adequate reserves. The report emphasised that this support
formed part of a multi?year recovery plan. Committee Members had
also been advised that delivering the Children’s Improvement
Plan was integral to the Council’s longer?term financial
recovery, reflecting the central role of children’s services
in the authority’s overall budget position.
The Committee was advised that
the Budget Consultation had opened on 5 January and would run until
9 February 2026, with scrutiny feedback contributing to final
proposals for consideration by City Council on 26 February 2026.
The report highlighted that failure to support core elements of the
strategy would necessitate alternative measures to deliver a
balanced and lawful budget by the statutory deadline. The report
concluded that the proposed budget reflected the seriousness of the
financial challenges faced while continuing to prioritise essential
services and longer?term sustainability.
In response to members’
questions and comments, the following matters were
discussed:
•       
The Committee sought clarity on the budget gap,
questioning whether it results from reliance on emergency funding,
increased Council tax for discretionary services, or wider national
funding policy.
•       
The Committee also challenged whether the new Fairer
Funding formula can truly be considered “fairer” while
major gaps remain.
•       
Finance acknowledged that although the revised
formula improves deprivation targeting, it does not resolve the
Council’s financial pressures. They highlighted systemic
national issues affecting all local authorities, including resource
constraints, economic conditions and rising demand. Transformation
of local services and continued lobbying for fairer national
funding remain essential, alongside debates around deprivation
weighting.
•       
The Committee raised concerns that including housing
costs in deprivation calculations disadvantages Stoke?on?Trent,
where much lower housing costs could make the city appear less
deprived than it is.
•       
Finance agreed this risk exists, though income?based
indicators would still show Stoke?on?Trent as deprived.
Nonetheless, the housing-cost element introduces an imbalance that
does not reflect local realities.
•       
The Committee noted that previous budget reductions
had been offset by UK Shared Prosperity Fund (SPF) allocations and
asked about impacts on the voluntary sector now that SPF funding
has reduced or ended.
•       
Finance reported that some externally funded schemes
have naturally concluded, though £1.25m has been set aside to
maintain selected SPF?backed programmes. Despite this, pressure on
the voluntary and community sector continues both locally and
nationally.
•       
The Committee asked what funding the city loses
without a mayor in a potential devolution deal (via Local
Government Reorganisation).
•       
Finance explained that Stoke?on?Trent misses out on certain general grants
and skills?related funding that government intends to route through
mayoral combined authorities, with these funds redistributed
elsewhere.
•       
The Committee noted they support a longer?term move
to a mayoral model but highlighted that the city is currently in a
transition phase that offers no associated funding benefits and
requested a breakdown of mayoral funding – Finance
agreed.
•       
The Committee questioned why Children in Care
(CiC) numbers have not reduced further
and what new approaches are planned.
•       
Children and Family Services (CAFS) emphasised that
safe and sustained reductions rely on improved practice quality,
noting the recent Ofsted “requires improvement” rating.
Learning from successful authorities shows that strengthening
practice is key.
•       
Early improvements were reported, with CiC numbers falling from 1,109 to 1,086, the lowest
in years. Historically, there are longstanding local challenges
– for example, in 2016 117 children per 10,000 were in care,
versus a national average of 70.
•       
CAFS explained that costs can rise even when numbers
fall, due to increasing complexity of children’s needs and
high fees charged by external residential providers. Provider
profits are rising nationally, prompting discussions about
potential profit caps. Complex emotional and mental health needs
have also grown post?COVID.
•       
The Committee acknowledged the long timescales for
improving Children’s Services and called for transparent
financial planning, including national regulation of placements and
placement caps, not only profit caps.
•       
The Cabinet Member for Children’s Services
detailed extensive work to improve practice and flagged the
unsustainable growth in residential placement costs. Residential
care needs have nearly doubled. Foster carer recruitment is a
priority, with 49 enquiries from new digital advertising and a rise
in applicants progressing to panel. Permanency outcomes have
improved, including a 77% increase in Special Guardianship Orders.
Thirteen additional children have been placed with in?house foster
carers this year.
•       
The Cabinet Member for Finance stressed the need for
whole?system change and long?term investment in early years,
parenting and prevention to keep children safely within
families.
•       
The Committee asked how the Council is fostering
collaborative work to reduce CiC
numbers.
•       
CAFS highlighted system?wide approaches, including
Families First, strong multi?agency partnership work and oversight
through the Children’s Improvement Board.
•       
The Committee asked about partner
engagement.
•       
CAFS confirmed strong involvement from schools,
education providers and the voluntary sector, but acknowledged
difficulties with health partners due to major Integrated Care
Board restructuring.
•       
The Committee asked which services would be affected
by the £4m savings target and whether vulnerable children
would be impacted.
•       
CAFS explained that £2.9m relates to moving
children from external residential placements into family?based
care where appropriate, recognising that many children nationally
are in residential settings due to foster carer shortages, not due
to need. Other savings come from reducing emergency placements,
reallocating budgets, lowering legal costs and streamlining
telephony.
•       
The Committee stressed the need for scrutiny of
non?consulted savings, despite the strategy stating no frontline
impact. Members requested further detail – Finance
agreed.
The Committee thanked officers
and members for their contributions to the budget work.
topline: The Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to address the financial challenges faced by the Council, particularly in Children's Services, through a proposed budget for 2026/27.

content:
Lee Calvert (Director of Adult Social Care)
presented the Care Quality Commission (CQC) Adult Social Care
Improvement Plan.
It was outlined that following the CQC’s
June 2025 assessment of Stoke?on?Trent City Council’s adult
social care services, an improvement plan had been developed. The
assessment had reviewed performance across working with people,
providing support, safety, and leadership, and it had acknowledged
the Council’s determination to improve outcomes despite
financial and operational pressures.
The CQC had rated the service
‘Good’ overall, citing strong leadership, effective
governance and clear transformation plans. Inspectors had
highlighted productive partnerships with health and voluntary
sector organisations, positive feedback from service users and
carers, and innovative approaches such as Community Lounges and the
hospital discharge hub. The Council’s commitment to
co?production and continuous improvement had also been
recognised.
Alongside these strengths, the CQC had
identified several priority areas for development. These included
delays in Care Act and Carers assessments and annual reviews,
limited strategic oversight of Equality, Diversity and Inclusion,
and delays in Occupational Therapy assessments and equipment
provision. Improvements were also required in data quality,
performance reporting, respite support for carers and uptake of
direct payments.
The risks highlighted by the CQC had already
been reflected in the Council’s corporate risk register.
Mitigation actions had been progressing, including investment in
review teams, strengthened data systems, improved performance
culture, clearer strategic accountability and enhanced staff
training. Recruitment activity, including establishing the Quality
and Compliance Team, had supported preparation for inspection and
delivery of the improvement plan.
Councillor Kanneganti exited the meeting at
15:50.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

The Committee asked
for clarification on the position regarding the Fair Pay
Agreement.
Adult Social Care
(ASC) responded that it was not appropriate for ASC to comment, as
there was insufficient information available to determine its
impact at that time.
Cabinet Member for
ASC confirmed that all recommendations from the CQC assessment had
been incorporated into the Improvement Plan.
The Committee
praised the report, stating had been a positive conclusion to the
meeting and noted that the CQC rating was an excellent legacy for
the authority.
The Committee
recorded its thanks to Peter Tomlin and Lee Calvert for their
contributions and efforts within Adult Social Care at the City
Council.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has approved recommendations from the Care Quality Commission (CQC) Adult Social Care Improvement Plan.

decision_maker: Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Nick Edmonds (Corporate Director of Resources
- Section 151 Officer), Lisa Dale (Head of Finance for CAFS) and
Tim Baker (Head of Finance for ASCAAC & PHPW) presented the
Budget Consultation for 2026/27 to the Committee.
It was outlined that there was continuing
financial pressures on the Local Authority, driven by rising demand
for children’s and adult social care and sustained inflation
across staffing, contracts and operational costs. It also noted
that this was the first budget prepared under the
Government’s new Fair Funding Review, which updated the
national funding formula. While the revised formula better
recognised deprivation and relative need, the funding allocated
remained insufficient to offset the long?standing financial
challenges faced by the Council.
Members were informed that despite the
multi?year Local Government Finance Settlement improving planning
certainty, the Council still faced an initial budget gap of
£31.2 million for 2026/27. This had been partly reduced
through additional Government funding, a proposed 4.99% council tax
rise and £9.8 million of corporate savings and efficiencies.
Temporary reductions in pension contributions had also helped ease
pressures. However, significant demand in children’s social
care meant the Council still required £10.5 million of
Exceptional Financial Support to maintain resilience, meet
statutory duties and sustain adequate reserves. The report
emphasised that this support formed part of a multi?year recovery
plan.
The Committee was advised that the Budget
Consultation had opened on 5 January and would run until 9 February
2026, with scrutiny feedback contributing to final proposals for
consideration by City Council on 26 February 2026. The report
highlighted that failure to support core elements of the strategy
would necessitate alternative measures to deliver a balanced and
lawful budget by the statutory deadline. The report concluded that
the proposed budget reflected the seriousness of the financial
challenges faced while continuing to prioritise essential services
and longer?term sustainability.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

·       
The Committee highlighted pressures arising from an ageing
population, noting increased numbers of residents with complex
needs and delays in hospital discharge. Members questioned how
these challenges could be managed within existing financial
constraints.

·       
Adult Social Care explained that the budget had been designed to
reflect the anticipated rise in demand and emphasised the need for
an upstream, community?based approach to delay or prevent frailty
and help individuals remain independent for longer.

·       
Finance explained that future projections remained uncertain until
the size and demographics of the reorganised authority were known.
They referred to published information on the potential asset split
under LGR, noting that it remained broad due to reliance on
population proxies.

·       
The Committee raised concerns about the Local Authority’s
heavy reliance on the Voluntary, Community and Social Enterprise
(VCSE) sector and sought clarity on how its future funding would be
secured.

·       
Adult Social Care acknowledged these concerns, noting that specific
funding had been set aside for VCSE organisations and the services
commissioned from them.

·       
Finance added that the Crisis Resilience Fund was designed, in
part, to bolster community?level support. An action was agreed for
an in?depth report on the Crisis Resilience Fund to be presented at
a future meeting.

·       
The Committee questioned whether Adult Social Care’s
infrastructure was sufficient to meet future targets, especially
with imminent changes to leadership.

·       
Adult Social Care reported improvements in governance and delivery,
stating that the Heads of Service structure would remain unchanged
and that transformation work would continue despite Local
Government Reorganisation (LGR). They highlighted that systematic
ways of working were expected to withstand organisational
change.

·       
Healthwatch commended the report and the Equality Impact
Assessments, recommending that the presentation be published online
as it was more accessible and more easily understood than current
information available.

·       
The Committee queried the Local Authority’s repeated reliance
on exceptional financial support, the interest paid and what
alternative uses those funds might otherwise have supported.

·       
Finance responded that borrowing levels were as expected and that
the Local Authority were working to a four?year plan to reduce
reliance on exceptional financial support. They confirmed that the
£8m repayment figure included both interest and principal,
with interest approximately 4.5%.

·       
The Committee queried where Stoke-on-Trent City Council sat in
comparison to other Local Authority’s for Council Tax
rates.

·       
Finance confirmed that, following the proposed rise, Council Tax
would remain the seventh lowest among 99 councils.

·       
The Committee queried what consultation had been conducted with
local residents, especially underrepresented groups.

·       
Finance confirmed there had been no direct consultation with
specific groups, though engagement had taken place with various
partners and stakeholders. They highlighted challenges associated
with exceptional demand and increasing complexity of need and
described extensive modelling undertaken to prepare for different
service scenarios.

·       
The Cabinet Member for Adult Social Care commended the finance
team, acknowledged the significant financial challenges in 2023,
emphasised the importance of maintaining valued services and
continuing transformation work. They noted that uncertainties about
future costs made planning difficult and encouraged members to
remain engaged.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to address significant financial challenges through a proposed budget for 2026/27, including a council tax rise and corporate savings.

decision_maker: Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Adrian Green (Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent
Adult Safeguarding Partnership Board - Independent Chair),
Stephanie Kincaid-Banks (Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Adult
Safeguarding Partnership Board) and Gina Grimes (Head of Adult
Safeguarding and Principal Social Worker) presented the annual
report of the Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Adult Safeguarding
Partnership Board.
The report outlined that the Staffordshire and
Stoke-on-Trent Adult Safeguarding Partnership Board (SSASPB) had
fulfilled its statutory obligations to publish a strategic plan,
produce an Annual Report and undertake Safeguarding Adult Reviews
(SARs). It had confirmed the Board’s role in providing
system?wide oversight of adult safeguarding and in challenging
partners where their actions or omissions placed adults at
risk.
Covering the period from April 2024 to March
2025, the report had summarised work led by the Independent Chair
and outlined progress across key themes, including Making
Safeguarding Personal, mental capacity and Liberty Safeguards
practice, self?neglect, safer service transitions and identifying
adults whose needs fell outside formal eligibility thresholds.
Preparatory work for the new 2025-2028 strategic plan had also been
detailed.
It was noted that significant safeguarding
activity across both Stoke-on-Trent and Staffordshire local
authority areas. Stoke?on?Trent had seen a 12% reduction in
safeguarding concerns, alongside an increased proportion
progressing to formal enquiries. In both areas, neglect, financial
abuse and physical or emotional harm had remained the most
prevalent categories, with self?neglect emerging as a key driver of
rising SAR referrals.
Wider system developments had been
highlighted, including national direction to strengthen
safeguarding responses to rough sleeping, restructuring within NHS
England and the Integrated Care Board, and the Board’s
resulting shift in strategic priorities. These changes had been
identified as placing increasing pressure on safeguarding systems
and review capacity.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

Cabinet Member for
Adult Social Care (ASC) queried why financial and physical abuse
figures were similar for Stoke?on?Trent and whether this pattern
was expected or represented an increase.
SSASPB responded
that variations were common across areas and that familial and
financial abuse had risen nationally.
The Committee
queried the reduction in safeguarding concerns in Stoke?on?Trent
alongside a significant increase in Staffordshire, particularly in
Section 42 enquiries.
Both SSASPB Chair
and ASC explained that revised practice had redirected
inappropriate or non?eligible referrals to alternative support, and
that differing approaches between Councils meant conversion rates
were not directly comparable.
Healthwatch
representative noted that Healthwatch held a seat on the Board but
had not been attending and confirmed their intention to resume
attendance.


The Committee asked
what steps were being taken to better engage underrepresented
groups.
SSASPB stated that
the Council was actively working on this through local campaigns,
improved understanding of community needs and a business?plan
priority on engagement with ethnic minority groups. They reported
ongoing work on accessibility, including sensory needs and language
barriers, supported by a cross?agency scoping exercise.
Cabinet Member for
Health Integration and Wellbeing expressed concern that despite
long?standing commitments, there was little evidence of improvement
over the past 5-10 years. They argued that reliance on digital
engagement excluded many residents and called for more rigorous,
demonstrable action, requesting visible progress before the next
meeting.
SSASPB acknowledged
the concerns and emphasised that the Board had prioritised outreach
and co?production using multiple formats, not solely digital. They
noted that responsibility for implementing change lay with partner
agencies.
ASC indicated that
the forthcoming Improvement Plan would address the issues raised
and respond to the Cabinet Member’s concerns.


Cabinet Member for
ASC observed that community lounges were valuable assets but were
not being accessed by minority ethnic groups, highlighting a gap in
service delivery and accessibility of information.
Cabinet Member for
Health Integration and Wellbeing agreed, stating that outreach
needed to be proactive and community?based, as ethnic minority
groups were not using existing venues. They stressed the importance
of understanding what these communities want and need.
ASC referenced the
CQC report findings on equality, diversity and inclusion, noting
that audits had identified a need for greater cultural sensitivity.
They stated that locating community lounges where people already
gather had not been sufficient, and that further work, particularly
identifying community connectors, was needed.
Cabinet Member for
Health Integration and Wellbeing added that Councillors from ethnic
minority backgrounds were an untapped resource and noted they
personally had never been approached to support engagement
efforts.
ASC confirmed that
while some culturally sensitive work was taking place, staff
confidence varied. They welcomed the offer of councillor support
and stated that the Improvement Plan would incorporate this.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations made by the Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Adult Safeguarding Partnership Board's annual report.

decision_maker: Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Helen Slater (Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent
Integrated Care Board - Director of Community Transformation)
presented the update on the Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent
Community Transformation and Neighbourhood Guidelines 2025/26.
An update was provided on the neighbourhood
health and care programme led by the Staffordshire and
Stoke?on?Trent Integrated Care Board (ICB). The report outlined
recent national publications, including NHS England’s
Neighbourhood Health Guidelines 2025/26, which had set out
expectations for transforming health and care by shifting activity
from hospitals into communities, prioritising prevention, and
expanding digital access.
The Committee heard that further national
direction had been provided through the 10 Year Health Plan for
England published in July 2025. This plan committed to establishing
neighbourhood health centres, increasing multidisciplinary working,
expanding the role of community pharmacy, reforming general
practice and modernising hospital care. It also introduced new
planning expectations, including a five?year rolling planning cycle
and a requirement for Health and Wellbeing Boards to define
neighbourhood footprints, priority outcomes and multi?neighbourhood
delivery arrangements by April 2026. Additional detailed guidance
from the Department of Health and Social Care was still awaited,
including model frameworks and system archetypes to support
neighbourhood health planning.
The ICB and partners had completed the
national Neighbourhood Health Maturity Self?Assessment in July
2025, rating themselves mainly at the “starting” level,
though noting broader strengths. Feedback had since been received,
outlining further development actions. Work was also underway to
establish at least one adult and one children and young
people’s Integrated Neighbourhood Team. Adult
multi-disciplinary team (MDT) work had advanced in North Stoke,
East Staffordshire and Stafford Town, and frailty MDTs were
operating across several Primary Care Networks. A Children and
Young People MDT pilot in Stoke?on?Trent had been initiated, with
data scoping, partner engagement and early cohort design
underway.
It was also noted that next steps, would
include continued work across the core components of the
neighbourhood model, beginning the development of Neighbourhood
Health Plans in collaboration with Health and Wellbeing Boards, and
progressing joint working with Shropshire, Telford and Wrekin ICB
under a new cluster arrangement. This partnership was expected to
support shared learning and benefit from Telford’s
participation in the National Neighbourhood Health Implementation
Programme.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

The ICB reported
that four key pieces of national guidance were still awaited. These
were originally due in October/November 2025 and related to:

Naming conventions
and neighbourhood arrangements
Neighbourhood
health centres
Contracting models
for multi? and single?neighbourhood provision
Development of
neighbourhood health plans through Health and Wellbeing Boards
(HWBs)


The ICB confirmed
that progress had continued in frailty work. Both the Frailty
Integrated Neighbourhood Team and the Children & Young People
(CYP) Integrated Neighbourhood Team could return to the Committee
for future updates.
The ICB emphasised
that an exceptional level of system?wide work was underway across
partners, recognising that neighbourhood health transformation was
a 5-10 year programme.
The ICB noted that
Public Health data in the appendices had not yet been linked to the
Pathfinder tool, but Pathfinder and JSNA data were being used to
inform locality planning.
The ICB advised
guidance on working with HWBs, including nomenclature and
expectations, was still awaited.


The Committee asked
how digital tools would be supported for residents with low digital
literacy.

The ICB responded
that several initiatives were in place, including a health literacy
programme across Staffordshire and Stoke?on?Trent, digital
champions in community teams and the promotion of appropriate
digital apps. They emphasised that clear alternatives were always
offered and communications were designed to be easily
understood.


The Committee asked
how consistency and uniformity across neighbourhood offers would be
achieved, and how forthcoming changes to access would be
communicated to residents.

The ICB stated that
commissioning, partnership arrangements and service provision would
be defined through the forthcoming guidance. They added that the
North Stoke pilot, as an example, had been discussed with PCNs when
it was first established.


Adult Social Care
highlighted the role of co?production in reducing inequalities and
suggested that progress could be driven where Primary Care Networks
were willing to participate.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for the implementation of the Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Community Transformation and Neighbourhood Guidelines 2025/26.

decision_maker: Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Helen Lester (Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent
Integrated Care Board - Associate Director of Planned Care) and
Graeme O'Malley (Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care
Board - Delivery and Improvement Lead for Planned Care, Cancer and
Diagnostics) presented the update on the Orthotics Service
Review.
An update was provided on the actions taken in
response to the Joint Scrutiny Review of Wheelchair and Orthotic
Services (August 2024) and subsequent reports in 2024 and 2025,
focusing solely on the Orthotic Service. Commissioners had
confirmed that all recommendations had been addressed and
incorporated into routine monitoring with the provider, Opcare.
By December 2025, significant progress had
been reported by the ICB: Opcare had strengthened engagement with
support groups including PEGiS, MS Mondays, and Disability
Solutions, ensuring user concerns were heard and acted upon.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

·       
The ICB reported previous difficulties contacting MS Mondays and
Disability Solutions; stated that Opcare had since confirmed
contact had been made.

·       
The Committee advised that MS Mondays reported they had not been
approached since November 2025.

·       
The ICB acknowledged the discrepancy, apologised and agreed to
verify whether incorrect information had been provided.

·       
The ICB further agreed to invite an Opcare representative to attend
the next time this item is addressed.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for the Orthotics Service Review, despite concerns about communication with user support groups.

content:
The Chair outlined the process
to be followed in considering the petition ‘Rejection of
Packmoor Masterplan’ in
accordance with the procedure set out within the report
provided.

The Lead Petitioner, Mr Darren Bamford, was given the opportunity
to briefly outline the details of the petition. Committee Members
had an opportunity to ask questions to verify their understanding
of the information provided.

Mr Bamford outlined residents’ concerns regarding the
proposed Masterplan and the Draft Local Plan, stating that he
believed the two were interlinked and posed long?term impacts on
the area.

A number of key concerns, questions and recommendations were
presented, and it was agreed that where appropriate, these would be
responded to in writing by officers.

Councillor Finley Gordon-McCusker responded as Cabinet Member,
thanking Mr Bamford for his and residents’ feedback. It was
outlined that Cabinet was clear the City needed more good quality
homes, and that in terms of Packmoor it
was felt a masterplan would ensure the area was looked at as a
whole including the required infrastructure.

Tony McGovern, Director of Investment, Delivery & Growth,
confirmed that where possible the City Council promoted building on
brownfield sites first, working with developers as appropriate on
more difficult sites, however it was noted that in order for
development, the land owner needed to be willing for the site to be
developed. Not all brownfield sites in the City had this
endorsement from landowners. It was also acknowledged that there
had been a significant under-delivery of housing in the City over
previous years and therefore work needed to be done to address
this.

Committee Members debated the petition and issues involved, asking
direct questions as necessary.

Councillor Finley Gordon-McCusker was given the opportunity to make
any final remarks, whereby he confirmed the Council welcomed
petitions and recognised they were one way that people can let us
know of their concerns and feedback on proposals for the city. He
confirmed the petition and evidence submitted would be considered
as part of the wider work.
It was the view of Cabinet that
the best way forward was to continue to engage with the community
and continue to develop a Packmoor
Masterplan which would set out more specific proposals for further
public consultation, acknowledging therefore that there would be
plenty more opportunities for people to have their say. Further
detail would also provide people with a clearer view of the
residential, extra-care facilities and highways improvements that
could be delivered alongside new homes and affordable homes.

Mr Darren Bamford was given the opportunity to make any final
remarks, whereby he questioned if this item would be debated again
at this Committee and if the recommendations he had proposed would
be actioned.

It was confirmed there were no proposals for the item to be
re-debated at this Committee, and dependant on the recommendations
from Committee Members it was proposed this work was picked up
alongside the ongoing work related to this matter. In terms of the
recommendations from Mr Bamford, officers did not feel able to
commit to actioning all of these, but had committed to responding
to the questions and proposals as appropriate, in writing.

A motion to note the report was moved by Councillor L Davison and
seconded by Councillor L Carter. An amendment to this was proposed
by Councillor Jellyman, which was accepted as a friendly amendment.
It was therefore:-
topline: The Housing, Regeneration & Operations Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to continue engaging with the community and develop a Packmoor Masterplan for further public consultation.

content:
Councillor S Hill (Cabinet
Member for Finance, Anti-Poverty and Corporate Services) introduced
this report, and supported by Nick Edmonds (Corporate Director for
Resources (Section 151 Officer)) provided an overview of the
Council’s proposed General Fund Revenue Budget and the Budget
Statement and Consultation for 2026/27.

Nick Edmonds outlined the financial context in which the budget had
been developed, noting that the national funding formula now
included updated indicators reflecting local need, albeit the
revised formula did not resolve all challenges.

Members were informed that the 2026/27 budget was the first to be
prepared following the Government’s Fair Funding Review,
which updated the national funding formula used to distribute
resources between councils. Although the multi?year settlement
offered greater certainty, the Council continued to face
significant financial challenges with and an initial budget gap of
£31.2 million for 2026/27.

To support financial sustainability, the proposals included a 4.99%
council tax increase (2% Adult Social Care precept and 2.99%
general increase), a request for Exceptional Financial Support
(EFS) from Government for 2026/27 and a programme of efficiencies,
savings and service transformation, focusing on demand management,
digital modernisation and improved commissioning.

Committee were advised that there were no proposals related to
their remit which required specific consultation.

In terms of the four non-consult proposals, further detail was
clarified as:
- HRO2627-A (NC): A member of the senior management team was due to
retire, and this position would not be replaced.
- HRO2627-B (NC): This proposal related to efficiency savings
related to estate management.
- HRO2627-C (NC): This proposal related to contract savings from
energy from waste.
- HRO2627-D (NC): This proposal related to the realignment of
income and expenditure budgets within operational services, in
particular highways.

Committee Members expressed support for the work undertaken to
develop the budget, noting the absence of reductions to frontline

decision_maker: Strategy and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Introduced by Councillor Jane
Ashworth (Leader of the City Council), the Committee were informed
that the budget was a turning point to stabilise and place
Stoke-on-Trent on the road to recovery, as while there were still
financial challenges to overcome, the budget was an opportunity to
move forward. As the budget did not present any consult proposals,
it was confirmed there would not be any cuts to front line
services.
Nick Edmonds (Corporate
Director of Resources (S151 Officer)) provided further detail on
the budget, explaining that following a Fair Funding review by the
central government, a provisional financial settlement had been
agreed in December 2025, which would increase the funding available
for the City Council for three years. Though the City Council
continued to face significant financial pressures, the stability
provided by the provisional financial settlement allowed the City
Council to update its medium-term financial planning.
It was then explained that
there remained a gap of £41.7 million in the budget, largely
due to pressures such as inflationary costs, wage increases and
social care pressures. To ease these pressures, further Exceptional
Financial Support (EFS) had been requested, and council tax would
be increased by 4.99%. The budget would also offer £9.8
million of non-consult savings, which included a restructure of the
Transformation and Project Management Team and a restructure of the
Benefits Service. Additional income of £2.5 million would
also contribute to the closure of the financial gap.
In response to general
questions from the Committee, it was clarified that the £2.5
million additional income consisted of various grants to be
received by the City Council, as well as income from Silicone Stoke
which was contracted to be received.
The Committee were also
notified that as the UK Shared Prosperity Fund (UKSPF) had ended, a
budget had been set aside to protect a number of schemes which had
been funded by the UKSPF. At the request of the Committee, the
schemes affected by the ending of the UKSPF would be provided to
the Committee members. 
The council tax collection rate
was also confirmed to the Committee as at 95-96%, with it rising to
99% over time as council tax arrears were collected. 
When asked how the EFS would be
repaid, the Committee were informed that capital receipts from the
sale of assets would be used. However, at this point, further
detail could not be provided as to which assets would be used, as
this had not been formalised by the S151 officer. Councillor Sarah
Hill (Cabinet Member for Finance, Anti-Poverty and Corporate
Services) assured the Committee that if the EFS were not required,
it would not be used to reduce the cost of financing the
loan.
When asked if consult savings
had been considered to reduce the need for further ESF, the
Committee were advised that they had, but it was decided that front
line services could not be reduced any further.
Due to the high levels of
deprivation for Stoke-on-Trent and potential long-term savings to
the central government, it was suggested by the Committee that a
request be made to the central government for the EFS debt to be
forgiven. While it was advised that there had been no indication of
debt relief being offered by the central government, the suggestion
would be considered.
When considering the number of
Band D council tax properties in the city and in neighbouring
authorities, the Committee asked if Band D properties in local
Parishes were included? This would be checked and the Committee
would be updated.
In response to Committee member
questions relating to the non-consult proposals, it was clarified
that the Transformation and Project Management Team would be
restructured by creating more lower-level Project Managers and
reducing the number of higher-level Project Managers by
streamlining management responsibilities. As the City Council
managed Housing Benefit also continued to be replaced by the DWP
managed Universal Credit, the Housing Benefit team would be
restructured and staff redeployed to different areas to accommodate
reduced workloads.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve the budget for Stoke-on-Trent City Council, including a council tax increase and non-consult savings.

challenge campaign for children, which encouraged record numbers of
children to attend their local library, and the visitor counter
equipment at Stoke Library having been repaired to allow for more
accurate visitor numbers.
When asked about the measures

the data was collected annually, and so was not available for this
report, or there had been a change in how the data was collected.

layout of the report would be reviewed, to consider alternative
methods to display the data which had been greyed out.
The Committee noted their
satisfaction at the increase in number of children reading due to
the summer reading challenge, with it hoped that library attendees
would increase further in 2026.
