content:
Alison Budd (Lead Midwife for the Local
Maternity and Neonatal System – Staffordshire and
Stoke-on-Trent ICB), Lynn Tolley (Assistant Chief Nursing and
Therapies Officer - Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent ICB), Jenny
Brown (Lead Midwife for Maternity Transformation –
Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent ICB) and Jill Whitaker (Deputy
Director of Midwifery for Workforce – Staffordshire and
Stoke-on-Trent ICB) presented a further update on the maternity and
neonatal (perinatal) services. The purpose of the report was to
inform the Committee of progress, challenges and regulatory
responses within local maternity and neonatal services.
It was noted that services had been provided
across multiple sites, including consultant-led and midwife-led
units, freestanding midwifery birthing units and home birth
services. Governance links with Derbyshire and Black Country
commissioners had been maintained and access to neighbouring
providers had continued.
National initiatives had been outlined
including the Perinatal Equity and Anti-Discrimination Programme,
the implementation of the Submit a Perinatal Event Notification
(SPEN) system, the introduction of a national performance dashboard
and the establishment of an improvement support team. University
Hospitals of North Midlands (UHNM) had launched SPEN and integrated
national metrics into its dashboards, while University Hospitals of
Derby and Burton (UHDB) had progressed training and process
mapping.
A review of infant mortality had been
undertaken and a draft action plan addressing high-impact
priorities such as substance misuse, stillbirth and low birthweight
had been developed. Governance arrangements had been strengthened and a leadership group had been formed
to accelerate progress.
The Local Maternity and Neonatal System (LMNS)
had continued oversight of the national three-year delivery plan,
supported by monthly forums and collaborative learning meetings.
Implementation of the Saving Babies’ Lives Care Bundle
version 3.2 had reached 91%, with outstanding compliance issues in
smoking cessation, foetal growth restriction and diabetes
management being addressed.
The Maternity Incentive Scheme (MIS) year 7
requirements had been reviewed and UHNM had reported being on track
to meet all ten safety actions. Additional resources had been
secured to strengthen service user engagement through the Maternity
and Neonatal Voices Partnership.
Care Quality Commission (CQC) ratings had been
confirmed, with UHNM and RWT rated as Good and Queens Hospital
Burton improving to Requires Improvement. Workforce recruitment had
been highlighted as positive at UHNM, with over 90 midwives
recruited in two years, while UHDB and RWT continued to address
vacancies.
The temporary closure of freestanding
midwifery-led birthing units at County Hospital and Samuel Johnson
Community Hospital had been subject to formal consultation, with
findings under review. Service user engagement had been
strengthened through face-to-face forums and multilingual
surveys.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

·       
The Committee queried impact of neonatal consultant shortages,
implications of birth unit closures and infant mortality trends.
Expressed concern about high-risk birth rates and prevention
potential.

·       
Public Health highlighted poor women’s health in the city,
risk factors for low birthweight and pre-term births and the need
for system-wide approaches including pre-conception work. Stressed
importance of retaining skills and knowledge in the workforce.

·       
Healthwatch asked about opportunities to expand peer support within
the broader workforce.

·       
The ICB reported Baroness Amos’ review was underway, expected
to conclude in spring 2026. Highlighted improved midwifery
retention with 70 new midwives recruited and retained, supported by
engagement events and positive feedback.

·       
The ICB confirmed consultation findings on freestanding birth units
were received, with an action plan expected by March 2026. Assured
neonatal consultant vacancy had not impacted 24-hour service
coverage and recruitment was ongoing.

·       
The ICB explained that closures affected only birthing services,
with other services continuing at both sites. Emphasised
system-wide approach to reducing high-risk births (currently 86%),
noting health inequalities and lifestyle factors. Confirmed
workforce diversification efforts and expansion of peer support,
led by an EDI midwife. Stated some high-risk factors cannot be
prevented due to disengagement and substance misuse, though
interventions are promoted.

·       
The Cabinet Member for Children’s Services questioned how
much of the 86% high-risk births could be prevented.

·       
The ICB stated that there will always be an element of high-risk
births that cannot be prevented due to factors such as
disengagement, substance misuse and smoking. They explained that
interventions and support are promoted during maternity care but
sustaining these changes beyond maternity services remains a
challenge.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for progress in local maternity and neonatal services, addressing concerns about high-risk birth rates and workforce recruitment.

decision_maker: Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Stephen Gunther (Corporate Director of Public
Health, Protection and Wellbeing) and Cynthia Folarin (Public
Health Consultant) presented the update on the Stoke-on-Trent
infant mortality action plan. The purpose of the report was to
provide an update on progress and outline future priorities. The
Committee was informed that infant mortality refers to deaths of
children under one year of age and serves as a sensitive indicator
of population health. Historically, Stoke-on-Trent’s infant
mortality rate had been significantly higher than the national
average, remaining around 7.5–7.6 per 1,000 live births
between 2009 and 2023. However, during 2022–2024, the rate
fell to 5.7 per 1,000 live births, marking the lowest level in 15
years. Despite this improvement the rate exceeds the England
average of 4.2 per 1,000.
The Committee was advised that infant
mortality is complex and influenced by multiple factors, including
socioeconomic deprivation, smoking status, obesity, ethnicity and
quality of care. Local Child Death Overview Panel data confirmed
that prematurity-related conditions, congenital anomalies and
sudden unexpected death in infancy (SUDI) were the leading causes
of infant deaths. Modifiable risk factors such as smoking during
pregnancy, high maternal BMI, unsafe sleeping practices were
highlighted. It was noted that deprivation remained a strong
determinant, with infant mortality rates in the most deprived areas
being nearly three times higher than in the least deprived
areas.
Progress achieved through the Infant Mortality
Steering Group was outlined. A system-wide action plan for
2024–2028 had been developed, supported by regional expertise
and national initiatives such as the Saving Babies’ Lives
Care Bundle. The plan focused on five priority themes:
preconception, antenatal and interpregnancy health; data,
intelligence and infrastructure; neonatal and maternal care;
inequalities and wider determinants; and engagement and
co-production. Collaborative work with the Office for Health
Improvement and Disparities and the Local Maternity and Neonatal
System was emphasised, alongside strengthened governance and
data-sharing arrangements.
The Committee was informed that while
improvements had been made, continued strategic focus and
partnership working were essential to achieve rates below the
national average and reduce health inequalities. Recommendations
included endorsing the action plan, supporting system-wide
collaboration, prioritising tackling modifiable risk factors and
ensuring engagement with families and communities to shape
culturally competent services. The importance of monitoring
progress and maintaining momentum through regular updates was
stressed.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:
·       
Service-user and staff engagement were emphasised as central to the
action plan.
·       
An in-depth study of all babies who died under 28 days was
proposed, reviewing maternal and infant case notes despite
governance challenges.
·       
Infant deaths were noted across Stoke-on-Trent, Staffordshire,
Derby and Wolverhampton hospitals, with targeted interventions
planned for deprived areas.
·       
Wider determinants such as housing, tobacco control, reproductive
health and economic factors were discussed as part of a
population-wide approach.
·       
Healthwatch raised concerns about data-sharing barriers, logic
models and the absence of an Equality Impact Assessment; ethnicity
inclusion and teen pregnancy prevention were discussed.
·       
Questions were raised about high rates of congenital defects in
Stoke, Birmingham and Leicester; further study was proposed to
explore causes and ethnic variations.
·       
The Cabinet Member for Health Integration and Wellbeing called for
further investigation into the causes of high rates of congenital
defects in Stoke-on-Trent, including an analysis of key
demographics to understand any potential variations between
communities and geographics areas.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations to address infant mortality rates in Stoke-on-Trent.

decision_maker: Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Patrick Myers (Programme Director Family
Matters), Lisa Healings (VAST) and Stephen Gunther (Corporate
Director of Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing) presented the
update on the Cabinet’s response to the 2024 scrutiny review
of food poverty and insecurity in Stoke-on-Trent, conducted by the
Committee. The Cabinet’s response focused on promoting local
emergency food providers, supporting foodbank referral systems,
endorsing the Food Partnership’s Theory of Change and
encouraging residents to grow their own produce. The Holiday
Activity Programme was delivered to improve nutrition, physical
activity and wellbeing for children during school holidays.
Foodbanks remained integral to support networks, ensuring tailored
assistance and long-term guidance.
The Food Partnership was formally established
in 2024, marking its first official year of operation under VAST.
Its Theory of Change provided a strategic framework for achieving
outcomes, including reducing hunger, improving cooking skills and
fostering resilience. Membership growth was significant, tripling
from 37 to over 90 organisations within a year, creating a strong
coalition and addressing geographic cold spots. Working groups were
convened to set priorities, including planning the first Food
Partnership Conference for 2026, drafting a city-wide food survey
and shaping a position statement on food and health messaging.
The partnership’s work was linked to
wider strategies such as the Infant Mortality Action Plan,
reinforcing efforts to improve access to nutritious food. Data from
the Trust report highlighted that 31% of children aged 0–5
were growing up in food-insecure households, particularly in areas
of greatest need. It was noted that 30% of foodbank referrals were
from people in work, confirming that food insecurity is an
income-related issue as well as cultural. Additionally, 20% of
those experiencing food insecurity were disabled, underlining the
intersectionality of the problem.
Initiatives funded by the Household Support
Fund included cooking demonstrations and distribution of ingredient
packs, while future plans involved
“grow your own” events to promote self-sufficiency.
Risks were acknowledged regarding sustainability beyond current
funding, with efforts underway to identify alternative sources.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

·       
The Committee noted that many minority-ethnic groups were not
attending and asked how this was being addressed.

·       
VAST confirmed work was underway to identify cultural needs and
include culturally appropriate foods. Cooking demonstrations
featured meals using food bank ingredients and cultural dishes.

·       
The Committee asked about funding arrangements.

·       
VAST explained that the Food Partnership had minimal funding of
£10,000 from the Household Support Fund, with additional
funding expected from the Trust. Grants were being provided to
grassroots organisations.

·       
Family Matters suggested the Community Resilience Fund as another
potential source of funding and emphasised promoting “grow
your own” initiatives.

·       
The Cabinet Member for Children’s Services commended progress
since inception, noting previous fragmentation and lack of clear
support routes. They highlighted the need for work with schools to
educate children and change family cooking habits to break the
cycle of poor nutrition.

·       
VAST acknowledged the need for school engagement but confirmed this
had not yet started.

·       
Public Health stated that food-related ill-health was a key
priority in the Local Improvement Framework. Emphasised integration
with family hubs, preconception support, school provision and home
facilities. Recognised food as an emotional issue tied to stress
and family experiences. Confirmed plans to build on current work as
a priority for next year.

·       
Family Matters highlighted other projects, including Heat
Foundation initiatives, promoting home cooking over convenience
foods and an air fryer project. Confirmed the Food Partnership was
acting as a catalyst for collaboration and shared learning with
other local authorities. Mentioned school projects to provide
healthy meals beyond cost considerations.

·       
Cabinet Member for Children’s Services suggested governors
review food culture in schools and teach children cooking and food
identification skills, noting challenges in engaging all 26
governing bodies.

·       
The Committee referenced Japanese government’s success in
improving nutrition through schools, banning convenience food and
linking better nutrition to improved educational attainment.

·       
The Committee congratulated the Food Partnership on its
achievements.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations to address food poverty and insecurity in Stoke-on-Trent, focusing on promoting local emergency food providers and supporting foodbank referral systems.

decision_maker: Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Peter Tomlin (Corporate Director of Adult
Social Care and All Age Commissioning) presented the report on
health and social care all age approach to supporting people in
local neighbourhoods. The purpose of the report was to provide
information on the role and impact of Community Lounges in
Stoke-on-Trent, along with developments in delivering all-age
support.
It was reported that Community Led Support
(CLS) had been adopted as a strength-based, place-based approach,
underpinned by seven principles focused on co-production, trust,
empowerment and minimal bureaucracy. The importance of
collaboration and early engagement with stakeholders, including
people with lived experience, was emphasised. The initial
implementation began in 2021 with a pilot project at Port Vale
Football Club, which led to the creation of the first Community
Lounge. This model was subsequently replicated across various
communities.
A vision was agreed for vibrant, inclusive
communities where people feel a sense of belonging and have access
to opportunities that improve health and wellbeing. Governance
arrangements were established to ensure oversight by a
multi-stakeholder group rather than statutory bodies alone.
By December 2025, 18 Community Lounges were
operating as hyper-local spaces driven by volunteers and supported
by Locality Connectors. These lounges provided food support, mental
health activities, digital access to NHS services and social
engagement opportunities. Utilisation had increased significantly,
with visits projected to double by April 2026. The main presenting
needs were identified as loneliness, food support and housing
advice.
Recent developments included the allocation of
£250,000 from the Household Support Fund to Community Lounges
for hyper-local distribution, alongside Better Care Fund grants for
multi-generational and out-of-hours support. Plans were outlined to
link lounges with youth hubs and increase support for care
leavers.
Key risks were noted around rising demand and
financial sustainability, with mitigation strategies focusing on
digital innovation and partnership working. It was concluded that
Community Lounges represented a cost-effective model for early
intervention and prevention, reducing pressure on statutory
services and improving health outcomes. Continued investment was
recommended to strengthen local resilience.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

·       
The Committee stated that it was encouraging to hear the progress,
noting that the approach was built on asset-based community
development and was the right way forward.

·       
The Committee suggested that local markets were a good resource
that could be utilised and emphasised the need for a stigma-free,
accessible space.

o  
The Committee asked whether there was any appetite for this idea
and observed that financial constraints often lead to consolidation
of services such as youth hubs.

o  
Adult Social Care explained that the guiding principle for
Community Lounges was to avoid high costs and locate them where
people already gather.

·       
Adult Social Care highlighted that Community Lounges had been
funded through a patchwork of grants and external sources rather
than Council budgets, making further expansion challenging.

·       
Adult Social Care stressed the importance of intergenerational work
and partnerships addressing wider determinants of health, such as
isolation and deprivation.

·       
Adult Social Care reported that they are consulting national
networks to learn from others who had set up in markets or shopping
centres. They added that partners who resource and staff Community
Lounges would be approached for their views.

·       
Healthwatch proposed exploring opportunities for cross-pollination
and shared learning and conducting a mapping exercise of community
support services to prevent duplication.

·       
Public Health agreed to take these suggestions forward and provide
feedback. They confirmed that the Council aimed to strengthen
shared learning, which was already occurring between Community
Lounges and Family Hubs.

·       
Public Health noted that better coordination across the City
Council’s community engagement approach was a priority for
the coming year and mentioned that the Future Stoke Leadership
Programme would commence next week.

·       
Adult Social Care acknowledged that while the Council did not
control all levers, it needed to enable communities to support
residents and reduce dependency on services.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for the expansion of Community Lounges in Stoke-on-Trent to provide hyper-local support for residents' health and wellbeing needs.

decision_maker: Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Peter Tomlin (Corporate Director of Adult
Social Care and All Age Commissioning) and Stephen Gunther
(Corporate Director of Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing)
presented their respective corporate measures for Q2 2025/26. The
purpose of the report had been to provide an update on performance
against the Council’s corporate measures relevant to the
committee, as part of the delivery of the Our City, Our
Wellbeing strategy approved in May 2024.
A total of 53 measures had been reported
across both directorates. Of these, 26 were rated green, 4 amber,
11 red and 12 had no target assigned. For Adult Social Care and All
Age Commissioning, six measures had been updated: two were green,
two amber and two red. Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing had
five measures updated, with one rated red.
Within Adult Social Care, the number of
unallocated Care Act assessments had been reduced from 578 in
Quarter 1 to 500 in Quarter 2, supported by improved throughput and
staffing measures. The backlog of unallocated Deprivation of
Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) applications
had also been reduced from 874 to 777, although it remained above
the annual target. Safeguarding enquiries open for more than 61
days had decreased slightly to 64.5% but continued to exceed the
indicative target of 35%. Outstanding annual reviews for
individuals with commissioned services had fallen from 1,563 to
1,467 and carer assessments had increased significantly from 186 to
271, putting performance on track to meet the annual target.
Service user satisfaction had remained high at 96.6%, close to the
target of 97%.
In Public Health, leisure centre attendance
had reached 316,650, representing a 3% increase compared with the
same period last year, although swimming and gymnastics
participation had declined. Smoking cessation performance had
worsened, with four-week quit rates falling to 61% and quit rates
among pregnant smokers dropping to 35%. NHS Health Check delivery
had reduced due to seasonal fluctuations and plans for
recommissioning were being developed. Trading Standards
interventions had resulted in £3.4 million worth of illegal
and unsafe goods being removed from or prevented from entering the
market, including major product recalls and seizures of tobacco and
vape products.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has approved recommendations based on the performance update for Q2 2025/26.

To seek approval to

staff.


Agreed (i) - That

the development and delivery of the Council’s Digital
Transformation Programme.

Agreed (ii) - That subject to approval of the said
engagement of expert capacity, authority be delegated to the Chief
Executive, in consultation with the Cabinet Member for Finance,
Anti-Poverty and Corporate Services to make relevant appointments
and carry out required procurement processes and to approve
contracts in support of this.

Agreed (iii) - To fund the engagement of additional
strategic capacity from the Transformation Fund in consultation
with the S151 Officer and the Cabinet Member for Finance,
Anti-Poverty and Corporate Services.

Agreed (iv) - To delegate to the Chief Executive, in
consultation with the S151 officer and the Cabinet Member for
Finance, Anti-Poverty and Corporate Services to use the
Transformation Fund to take the initial steps in developing a main
software platform for managing our relationship with residents and
businesses, including acquisitions of licences to allow the
potential of the preferred platform to be fully explored, prior to
a formal Cabinet decision on full adoption and roll-out.

Agreed (v) - To commit to consideration of the
funding requirements of the Council’s Digital Transformation
Programme as part of the Medium-Term Financial Plan 2026/27 –
2030/31, considering the likely impact of local government
reorganisation.

To seek approval for the

Agreed (i) - That the
City Council agree no changes are to be made to the current Local
Council Tax Support scheme (also called Council Tax Reduction
scheme) for working age residents.

Agreed (ii) - That the City Council agree to a
further consultation for the 2027/28 Local Council Tax Support
scheme in relation to the City Council potentially making changes
to the scheme which will be reviewed over the next 12
months.

includes re-examining the purpose and objectives of the scheme and
the option of changing the protected groups in future to further
re-align the scheme with Universal Credit.

content:
Introduced by Vicki Yates (Public
Health Programme Manager), the Board were presented with a summary
of the report. The purpose of the report was to bring support and
awareness of the strategy to make Stoke-on-Trent smoke free, with
it requested that the Board take the strategic lead and approve the
strategy. The report was due to appear before Cabinet for approval,
and it was hoped that annual reports would be brought to the Board
for their consideration moving forward.
It was stated
that the aim of the strategy was to reduce smoking in the city to
5%, from the current figure at 13%. The strategy was developed
following a needs assessment and consultation, with the four
priority areas shaped by evidence on how to limit
smoking.
When discussing
the report, officers confirmed that smoking continued to drive
health inequalities and was still a significant risk to health, and
there had not been a strategy for some time. However, while smoke
free hospitals were important, it was suggested that mental health
awareness be considered for patients undergoing treatment for
mental health, as smoking could be the patient’s coping
mechanism. It was agreed that while vaping would not be recommended
for non-smokers, patients and smokers could still use vaping as a
harm-reduction tool.
The Board
supported the strategy, noting a reduction in children admitted to
hospital with respiratory conditions following the smoking ban and
the impact of smoking as cause of house fires. The smoking strategy
was also a national ambition to achieve and so there were no
sanctions for failing to reach the target.
topline: The Board has decided to approve a strategy to make Stoke-on-Trent smoke free, aiming to reduce smoking rates in the city.

content:

city. As part of the review, the Beth Johnson Foundation were also
commissioned to provide further information on resident’s
hopes and aspirations.
The report also provides

wellbeing, with individuals encouraged to make small improvements
with the support of their communities and services.

while noting the importance of promoting intergenerational
activities.

content:

following a Domestic Abuse Related Death
Review in the city by the Community Safety Partnership, the
resulting report had proposed a recommendation for the Board to act
upon. The recommendation was for the Director of Public Health to
provide a report to the Board on the absence of local strategies to
deal with addiction and the impact on domestic violence, and how
this would be addressed.
The Board were assured that
addiction strategies were being delivered, with a focus on
gambling, substance abuse, tobacco etc. with elements of domestic
violence to be added, as the new domestic violence strategy had
been signed off by the Board in June 2025.
The Board confirmed their
acceptance of the recommended actions, and so following this, a
response would be written to the Community Safety Partnership to
confirm that the Board had considered and would implement the
recommendations.

decision_maker: Strategy and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Presented by Nick Edmonds
(Corporate Director Resources (Section 151)), the Committee heard a
summary of the report to explain the latest financial challenges
for the City Council. Of note, the Q2 overspend had been reduced
with further mitigation work planned, while the Housing Revenue
Account (HRA) budget was balanced, but with significant cost
pressures.
The Dedicated Schools Grant
(DSG) deficit was also forecast to increase by the end of the year
due to high needs pressures, and while overall there had been
positive movement within the General Fund, work was still required
to ease the pressure from the Children and Families Directorate due
to an increase in the number of children in care.
Having noted an underspend in
economic development in the report, the Committee requested further
information on this to be provided.
As there had been an overspend
in Communications and Marketing, it was explained to the Committee
that the majority of the overspend consisted of internal recharges
due to be paid by other City Council directorates. At the
Committee’s request, further information would be provided to
explain how much was spent on the Chief Executive directorate by
Communications and Marketing.
An overspend in Human Resources
was then clarified to the Committee as the result of a reduction of
income in traded services. Meanwhile an overspend in Transformation
and Programme Management was advised to be the result of projects
across the City Council requiring additional funding. The Committee
requested further details in regard to
these projects.
As the Committee noted the high
costs of agency spending in finance, and procurement in particular,
they were told that there had been successes in the recruitment of
permanent staff, but due to changed reporting standards and
continued staff recruitment challenges, temporary agency staff were
still needed while new staff were trained and new procedures
implemented.
High IT costs mentioned in the
report were also noted as the result of contract re-negotiations
for City Council system licenses. The Committee were also assured
that a system rationalisation plan was in place to remove obsolete
licenses, while jointly purchasing systems with other organisations
would lower system costs.
An overspend in Planning and an
underspend in Highways were also queried by the Committee, and so
further information would be provided to the Committee.
The Committee then considered
the implications of AI usage in the City Council, with the
Committee advised that transformation of service work was largely
focussed on the implementation of AI to support staff. While the
possibility of AI replacing staff was discussed, Committee members
contemplated the importance of maintaining the human element and
retraining staff where required, with AI to be used as a staff
support tool. The Committee agreed for this to be added to the Work
Programme for discussion at a future meeting.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to address financial challenges and discuss the implications of AI in the City Council.

content:
Emily Bagnall (Head of Customer
Contact and Libraries) provided a summary of the report to the
Committee, highlighting an increase in Stage 1 and Stage 2
complaints received, but a decrease in the number of MP enquiries
received. The Committee were also advised that housing repairs data
had not been included in the report, however this would be added in
future reports. The Committee were then assured that the data
collected in the report would be used to inform the transformation
of services.
Following
questions from the Committee, it was explained that there had been
a reduction of complaints related to Children’s Social Care,
but an increase in corporate complaints due to the reclassification
of complaints. It was also clarified that Children’s Social
Care had its own statutory process for managing complaints, however
if the complaint was in regard to the
conduct of an officer, it would be considered a corporate
complaint.
When asked about
the reduction of MP enquiries, officers advised that MPs would
often forward their enquiries to Councillors, or enquiries would be
raised when MPs met with the City Council Leader and Chief
Executive. These enquiries were then logged by the Customer
Feedback Team and the data added to the report. It was suggested by
the Committee that Councillor enquiries raised within the casework
system could be provided to the Committee to allow them to review
any changes to the number of enquiries Councillors had received.
However, concerns about the accuracy of the casework system were
raised, as actions were not consistently logged in the
system.
The Committee
also suggested that malicious or repeat complaints be logged
separately in the report, as they could affect the accuracy of
complaint figures.
As the Committee
considered the response times to complaints, they were advised that
if complaints could not be resolved within 10 working days, an
application could be made to extend the deadline, and the
complainant would be notified. The often-cited reason for the
request to extend the deadline was to allow more time to resolve
complaints at Stage 1. The Committee agreed that a further report
to provide more information on the complaint response times would
be made to the Committee at the next meeting.
It was then
noted by the Committee that the complaints data included
Children’s and Adult’s Social Care. The Committee
agreed that a recommendation be made to Cabinet for customer
feedback data to be provided and considered by the relevant
Overview and Scrutiny Committees as part of their performance
monitoring.
As new
legislation related to data protection had also been passed and
would come into effect by mid-2026, it was suggested to the
Committee that they consider the changes and their implementation
by the City Council. The Committee agreed to add this item to the
Work Programme.
topline: The Committee has decided to approve recommendations for improving customer feedback services based on complaints data.

The Chair introduced the item
to the Committee, confirming his satisfaction with the report and
advising that the report was requested as members of the public may
wish to watch webcasts of overview and scrutiny meetings. The
Committee discussed this in further detail, with officers informing
the Committee that further staff would be needed to webcast and
monitor webcasted meetings, and if meetings were to be webcast via
services such as YouTube, this system was not integrated into the
modern.gov system. It was also explained if further resources were
needed to webcast meetings, a request for the necessary budget
would be made to Cabinet or Council.
The Committee also acknowledged
the low viewership of webcasted meetings, with it suggested that
members of the public tended to show the most interest in meetings
where the issues discussed directly related to them. It was
therefore suggested by the Committee that certain items relevant to
the public be promoted to boost public interest in webcast
meetings.
When asked if viewing figures
of webcasts could be confirmed as from the public or from officers
within the City Council, the Committee were told that this had not
been previously monitored, however following a system update,  the figures
could be provided to the Committee in the future.
The Committee noted that
despite the low viewing figures, webcasting meetings still provided
a public record, and so it was proposed and agreed by the Committee
members that the current webcasting arrangements continue, and the
Committee would not recommend to Cabinet that the webcasting of
meetings be expanded to Overview and Scrutiny meetings.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to continue current webcasting arrangements for meetings.

decision_maker: Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Delyth Mathieson (Director of Education) and
Rachel Dodd (Strategic Manager Early Intervention) presented a
report on the Young Carers Service. 1,328 young carers had been
identified in Stoke-on-Trent. The statutory duty under the Children
and Families Act 2014 and Care Act 2014 was highlighted, requiring
local authorities to identify and assess young carers, defined as
anyone under 18 providing practical or emotional care.
Assessments had been carried out by two Local
Authority caseworkers, with North Staffs Carers commissioned to
provide ongoing support under a contract extended to March 2027.
The Joint All Age Carers Strategy (2025–2029), overseen by
the Carers Partnership Board, was referenced as the guiding
framework.
Referral data over seven years showed
fluctuations, with education as the main source: 48.5% from schools
versus 2.91% from health services, potentially indicating a need
for greater awareness among health professionals. Most young carers
lived in southern localities; 29% had SEND needs and 7.4% held an
EHCP. Young carers were disproportionately affected by deprivation:
77.43% received free school meals and 80.5% lived in the most
deprived areas. Attendance concerns were noted, with persistent
absence rates of 32.3% in primary and 43% in secondary schools,
compared to non-carers. National data confirmed similar trends.
North Staffs Carers had provided respite
activities, wellbeing sessions, counselling and transition support.
Governance arrangements included the Young Carers Manager
contributing to strategic planning and retendering. Strategic
priorities focused on early identification, holistic assessments
and smooth transitions to adulthood.
The recent Ofsted inspection was reported as
positive, confirming that young carers’ needs were clearly
identified and addressed. Future plans
were outlined, including professional training, improved referral
processes, promotion of the Young Carers in Schools Award and
bespoke attendance interventions.
Risks were acknowledged, particularly the
potential for insufficient capacity due to rising referrals.
Financial, legal and equality implications were noted as minimal at
this stage, with full assessments planned during retendering. In
conclusion, the service was described as a small but vital part of
wider support for children and families. The need to adapt
provision to meet changing needs and reduce the impact of caring
roles on education and wellbeing was emphasised.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

·       
It was reported by Children and Families Services (CAFS) that a
representative from North Staffs Carers had attended the hub and
that work had been undertaken with a potential young person from
the youth group.

·       
It was asked by the Committee whether two caseworkers were adequate
for resourcing and what actions would be taken if demand
surged.

·       
It was explained by CAFS that the caseworkers only carried out
assessments and did not provide direct support, which helped
mitigate demand on the two assessors.

·       
It was stated that a surge in demand would present a significant
problem due to current overspend and cuts would need to be
identified to increase capacity.

·       
It was noted that Ofsted had observed Stoke-on-Trent as unusual for
the high number of young carers, with a wider cohort identified
compared to most other local authorities, attributed to effective
local identification rather than absence elsewhere.

·       
It was acknowledged that if demand increased, the same challenges
faced in other areas would apply locally.

·       
It was asked by the Committee what joint working existed with Adult
Social Care (ASC), particularly for adults with complex needs.

·       
It was confirmed by CAFS that many referrals originated from ASC
and that close working relationships were maintained, with young
carers aging out being passed to ASC for continued support.
 
For the record – a 5-minute adjournment
of Committee took place from 11:05-11:10am for a short comfort
break.
topline: The Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for the Young Carers Service in Stoke-on-Trent, highlighting the need for ongoing support and strategic planning.

decision_maker: Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Florah Shiringo (Interim Director of Children
& Families Help and Protection) presented the report on the
Families First Partnership Programme (FFPP) update to the
Committee. The programme was described as a national reform
initiative launched by the Department for Education in March 2025.
Its ambition was outlined as rebalancing the system away from
crisis intervention towards earlier, joined-up support for
children, young people and families, ensuring that help was
provided at the right time to keep children safely within their
families wherever possible. Evidence from pathfinder areas was
noted as having informed the approach and substantial investment of
over £500 million for 2025–26 was reported.
Three core components were highlighted:
1.    
Family Help was explained as combining targeted early help and
child-in-need services to reduce handovers and provide support at
the point of need.
2.    
Multi-Agency Child Protection Teams (MACPTs) were described as
required to strengthen safeguarding arrangements through integrated
teams supported by clear protocols.
3.    
Family Group Decision Making (FGDM) was noted as promoting family
involvement in planning and decision-making.
Governance arrangements were reported as
having been overseen by the FFPP Programme Board, which had
embedded learning from regional pathfinders and emphasised robust
communication and co-design with families and partners. Engagement
feedback was summarised, including strong support for co-location
of services, a shift to needs-led assessments through a Single
Assessment and Plan (SAP) and the introduction of a Family Help
Lead Practitioner role to ensure continuity.
Concerns raised during engagement were noted,
such as safeguarding focus in referrals, independence of child
protection chairs and systemic issues like repeated information
sharing and stigma. Workshops on Family Group Decision Making were
reported as having taken place in October 2025 to inform future
design.
Service design proposals were described as
supporting locality-based co-location models for Family Help and
MACPTs, with two options being costed. It was stated that
government anticipated the transformation phase would conclude by
March 2026, with implementation following thereafter. Financial
implications were reported, including £4.7 million allocated
to Stoke-on-Trent City Council, comprising £2.8 million from
the Children’s Social Care Prevention Grant and £1.9
million mainstreamed from the Children & Families Grant.
Funding for 2025–26 was noted as being used to support
existing preventative services and prepare for transformation.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

·       
The Committee praised the great work underway.

·       
It was stated by the Cabinet Member that, following Josh
McAlister’s review into social care, the current system was
not working, with high numbers of children in care and that it was
considered an exciting time to oversee radical changes.

·       
It was asked by the Committee whether flexibility to adapt locally
would be available if the national model underperformed.

·       
It was confirmed by CAFS that flexibility was allowed within the
framework and guidance, following the independent review by central
government.

·       
It was explained that the system had been reoriented to focus on
health rather than risk, while statutory responsibilities remained
unchanged.

·       
It was noted that one of the pathfinders had been inspected to
ensure statutory functions remained robust.

·       
It was highlighted that the biggest challenge would occur if issues
arose at a national level, potentially shifting the model back to a
risk-based approach.

·       
It was emphasised by the Cabinet Member that intervention often
fractured families and impacted communities and that the proposed
shift aimed to build resilience through holistic family support and
families helping families.
topline: The Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for the Families First Partnership Programme update, aiming to provide earlier, joined-up support for children, young people, and families.

content:
Delyth Mathieson (Director of Education) and
Michael Hill (Head of Education, Standards and Partnerships)
presented the Improving Education Strategy which was outlined as
building on the Young People’s Learning and Skills Strategy
and supporting the Corporate Vision – Our City, Our Wellbeing
and the Future 100 initiative. It aimed to create a high
support/high challenge culture, close attainment gaps and
strengthen staff engagement, while promoting economic independence
and resilience among future residents.
Developed through forums, consultations and
partnerships with educational leaders and academy trusts, the
strategy drew on the Priority Education Investment Area and
Education Challenge Board experience. Transparency in school
performance monitoring and early intervention were emphasised.
The local education context was noted: 93
state-funded schools, seven maintained primaries and 28 academy
trusts. The authority’s role in school improvement was
described as limited since the withdrawal of government funding in
2022, with support now provided via the Golden Thread Teaching Hub
and DfE initiatives.
Two Education Forums and working groups shaped
priorities and actions, aligning the draft with national policies
such as the RISE offer, Ofsted changes and the Children’s
Wellbeing and Schools Bill.
Key risks included persistent attainment
challenges and the end of Priority Education Area funding in Spring
2025. Mitigation focused on stakeholder engagement and
adaptability. Financial and legal implications were noted, with
staffing from existing resources required. The committee was asked
to provide feedback for Cabinet consideration.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:

·       
Members were informed that the draft Improving Education Strategy
was open for consultation until 27 November, allowing discussion
and feedback before Cabinet consideration.

·       
Officers explained that the strategy focused on co-production with
schools, academy trusts and stakeholders, using data analysis,
trends and previous investment areas to identify priorities aligned
with government and council objectives.

·       
Questions on timelines were addressed: with the submission date for
Cabinet approval being pushed back to allow further consultation,
with full approval and an action plan expected by March 2026 under
a new Education Partnership Board involving employers, schools,
trusts and young people.

·       
The Cabinet Member confirmed schools’ input had been taken on
board, noting they felt heard and valued and were willing to
collaborate. The importance of aligning education outcomes with
employer expectations was emphasised.

·       
Current performance concerns were highlighted: only 59% of pupils
met KS2 standards in reading, writing and maths, and 53% achieved a
standard pass in English and maths at GCSE. A strong drive for
city-wide improvement was acknowledged.
 

·       
Engagement with High-Performing Trusts

o  
Challenges in attracting more high-performing trusts were noted,
given most high schools were already within trusts. Options
discussed included re-brokerage and strengthening partnership
working.

·       
Skills and Workforce Alignment

o  
Members queried how education outcomes would align with workforce
needs. Officers confirmed collaboration with LSIP, Chambers of
Commerce and youth voice groups to embed vocational and life
skills.

·       
Trusts and Accountability

o  
Concerns were raised about clarity in policy regarding trusts,
whether expansion or partnership is preferred and mechanisms for
democratic accountability given limited Council powers. Officers
outlined statutory monitoring, data sharing and partnership
boards.

·       
Policy Context and Timing:

o  
Members expressed concern about developing strategies while
national policy remained uncertain. Officers acknowledged delays in
government white papers but stressed the need to progress locally
through quality assurance and partnership work.

·       
SEND and Inclusion:

o  
Questions focused on how the strategy addressed SEND and
disadvantaged pupils. Officers confirmed mainstream inclusion as a
priority, supported by cluster models and increased resources, with
parent engagement ongoing.

·       
Performance and Outcomes:

o  
Discussion included disparities in attainment, gender gaps and
learning from high-performing schools in deprived areas. Officers
highlighted improvements for Section 19 children and ongoing work
to raise standards city-wide.

·       
Future Governance and Partnership:

o  
The role of the new Education Partnership Board was discussed,
including its remit to set criteria, share data and drive
collective responsibility for improving outcomes.
topline: The Children and Family Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve the Improving Education Strategy, aiming to close attainment gaps and promote economic independence among future residents.

content:
The Leader referred to item 15
of the agenda, Participating in the West Midlands Safe Centre SPV.
She explained that due to the report containing commercially
sensitive information, it was necessary to consider the report in
the private part of the agenda to protect the integrity of ongoing
legal and financial due diligence. 
However, she wished to highlight the significance of this
proposal.
Councillor Ashworth reported
that the Safe Centre would be the first regionally owned secure
children’s home in the country, designed to meet the complex
needs of vulnerable children aged 10–17 who required secure
welfare placements. It would provide trauma-informed, integrated
care, education, and health services within a purpose-built
facility, addressing a critical gap in regional and national
provision.
Councillor Ashworth confirmed
that the project was fully funded by the Department for Education
through its Children’s Homes Capital Programme, with
£71 million allocated to support construction and delivery.
This national investment reflected the strategic importance of the
Centre in expanding secure welfare capacity and improving outcomes
for children across the region. A Special Purpose Vehicle would be
created to operate and manage the provision on behalf of 14 local
authorities and children’s trusts anticipated to be
involved.
Concluding, Councillor Ashworth
suggested that joining the Special Purpose Vehicle offered
strategic benefits, in that it ensured priority access to places at
preferential rates lower than market costs. Participation also
ensured that children who were struggling the most had access to
the specialist support they required which would improve outcomes
through access to specialist care, whilst supporting priorities
around tackling inequality and improving life chances.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to join the Special Purpose Vehicle for the West Midlands Safe Centre, a secure children's home to provide care for vulnerable children.

content:
Stephen Gunther (Corporate Director of Public
Health, Protection and Wellbeing presented the Director of Public
Health Annual Report 2025.
The Director of Public Health Annual Report
2025 fulfils the statutory duty to review and report on the health
of the local population. This year’s report was framed around
the centenary of Stoke-on-Trent as a city and provided a historical
narrative of health and wellbeing over the past 100 years,
alongside reflections on current challenges and aspirations for the
future.
The Cabinet Member for Adult Social Care and
All Age Commissioning (the Cabinet Member for Health Integration
and Wellbeing at the time this report was created), stated that
they were impressed with the report and the work that went into it,
and noted a wellbeing survey was currently ongoing, and that the
Directorate of Public Health, Protection and Wellbeing was
undertaking significant work to identify population needs. They
expressed support for the report’s recommendations and
highlighted the importance of tackling health inequalities,
improving mental wellbeing, and creating opportunities for
residents to lead healthier lives. They also emphasised the need
for collaborative approaches to address social challenges such as
addiction and isolation, and to ensure that communities feel safe
and supported.
The Corporate Director described the report as
an honour to produce and noted that it had been a fascinating
project to look back over the last century and gave thanks to the
Beth Johnson Foundation and Dr Sarah Suleyman Omran for their
contributions. The report emphasised that while much progress had
been made, some issues present a hundred years ago remain today.
Tuberculosis rates were increasing in the city, violence was
rising, and although infant mortality had reduced significantly,
much more work was needed. The report also highlighted that
Stoke-on-Trent once had a population greater than today, and that
historical context helped inform current priorities. The importance
of increasing physical activity, addressing addictions and
non-communicable diseases, and improving social connectivity was
stressed. Safety and the perception of safety were identified as
key concerns, alongside ensuring that people can live with dignity
and access neighbourhood support services when needed. It was
highlighted that these priorities were linked to the Future 100
plans, which set out Council ambitions for the next century.
The report contained recommendations for
individuals, communities, and the Council. For individuals, the
focus was on improving mental wellbeing and increasing physical
activity. For communities, the emphasis was on fostering
connectedness and reducing harm from alcohol, drugs, and unhealthy
lifestyles. For the Council, priorities included creating jobs,
building affordable homes, and integrating essential services such
as housing, food access, mental health, and substance misuse
support.
Progress on last year’s actions were
also reported, including the establishment of 18 community lounges
offering mental health and other support, the launch of the Family
Matters programme to reduce the number of children in care, and the
expansion of physical activity initiatives. The Council achieved
signatory status for the Prevention Concordat for Better Mental
Health and strengthened partnerships tackling loneliness and
promoting volunteering.
In closing, the report emphasised that while
the health of Stoke-on-Trent today is vastly improved compared to a
century ago, significant challenges remain. It emphasised that
through collaborative working, long-term planning, and community
engagement, the city can continue to build on its progress and
create a healthier, more resilient future.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:
·       
The Committee expressed that the quality of the report was very
good.
·       
The Committee questioned why the report had gone to Full Council
before Overview and Scrutiny and asked about the purpose of
scrutiny at this stage.
o  
Public Health explained that timings had not aligned and apologies
were given; the discussion was considered useful for shaping next
year’s report.
·       
The Committee queried how the investment in physical activity was
being sustained.
o  
It was confirmed that physical activity was a Health and Wellbeing
Board priority, led by Together Active, with a joint bid to Sport
England, six accessible hubs planned, and further funding
sought.
·       
The Committee asked why examples of resilience were not included in
the report.
o  
It was stated that the statutory report was data-driven and
previous reports had not focused on resilience.
·       
The Committee queried the status of the 2024 and 2026 wellbeing
survey results.
o  
It was confirmed that 2024 was complete and 2026 was in
progress.
·       
The Committee asked how ward-level inequality data could be
accessed.
o  
Public Health advised this was available in the Joint Strategic
Needs Assessment and via the Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD)
2025 data.
·       
The Committee raised concerns about sustainability of community
lounges.
o  
Public Health noted reliance on the Public Health grant and
statutory duties, with pressures acknowledged and equity
prioritised.
o  
Adult Social Care added that community lounges were co-designed
locally and aimed to address health inequalities using community
assets and partnerships.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve the recommendations in the Director of Public Health Annual Report 2025, focusing on improving health and wellbeing in Stoke-on-Trent.

decision_maker: Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Hayley Allison (Portfolio Director -
Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care Board), Phil Smith
(Chief Delivery Officer - Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent
Integrated Care Board) and Jack Butler (Head of UEC Delivery and
Improvement - Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care
Board) presented the Staffordshire & Stoke-on-Trent Integrated
Care System Winter Plan 2025/26.
The report was presented to the Committee to
provide assurance of system readiness for winter pressures. The
plan was developed collaboratively with NHS trusts, local
authorities, ambulance services, and voluntary sector partners,
embedding shared ownership and shared risk across the system.
Governance and oversight arrangements were strengthened to ensure a
coordinated approach.
Vaccinations were highlighted as a critical
component of the winter response, with renewed efforts to increase
uptake among patients during routine appointments, on discharge,
and through targeted initiatives for at-risk groups, care homes,
school-aged children, maternal flu and RSV, and older adults.
Workforce vaccination was also prioritised. The plan was confirmed
as dynamic, adapting to UKHSA data and infection trends, which have
already shown an earlier-than-usual rise in illnesses, including
both Flu A and Flu B.
Lessons learned from last winter, which was
marked by critical incidents, informed the approach. The plan was
developed earlier than in previous years and supported by robust
capacity and demand modelling using STAR-level data. Bed modelling
indicated a significantly reduced gap compared to last year, with a
worst-case deficit of 11 beds in January versus 36 previously.
Temporary escalation measures, such as corridor beds and ambulance
waiting areas, were included. Initiatives such as the High Impact
Team were outlined to accelerate discharge during peak periods and
reduce acute occupancy before Christmas.
The plan was structured around thirteen
oversight pillars covering pre-hospital, in-hospital, and
post-hospital services, each with executive and managerial leads.
Key components included the UEC Improvement Plan, which introduced
a 24-hour single point of access to ensure patients are directed to
the right care setting from the outset. Investments in primary care
were reported, including same-day access hubs, additional GP
appointments via NHS 111, modern general practice guidance to
reduce the 8 a.m. rush, online consultations, acute visiting
services, and urgent dental care appointments. Additional acute and
community beds were opened, with further capacity planned in
Cheadle, alongside continued collaboration with Staffordshire Fire
and Rescue for discharge and falls prevention.
System escalation arrangements were described,
including enhanced clinical leadership at the frontline, real-time
decision-making, and daily monitoring of urgent and emergency care
metrics. The Aegis winter exercise was undertaken to test the plan
against the national incident framework, with key learning themes
identified around communication, critical incident response, and
use of supporting documentation.
Financial, legal, and HR implications were
reported as minimal, and equality impact assessments were confirmed
as in progress. Four principal risks were identified: surge
capacity mobilisation, workforce availability, patient safety, and
financial spend, with mitigation measures in place. Workforce
availability was highlighted as the most significant challenge,
with collaborative approaches adopted to secure additional staff
and maintain resilience.
The Committee was informed that the Winter
Plan will remain a live document, subject to continuous review
throughout the winter period, with oversight provided by
established governance structures and escalation mechanisms.
In response to members’ questions and
comments, the following matters were discussed:
·       
The Committee commended the significant amount of work
undertaken.
·       
The Cabinet Member for Adult Social Care and All Age Commissioning
praised early planning compared to last year and noted historic
concerns about community hospital closures and bed
pressures.

·       
Model of Care & Capacity
o  
The Committee queried the 80% target for empty beds.
§ 
ICB explained that the target was 20% empty beds by Christmas Eve
(24/12/25) to prepare for the post-Christmas surge and that High
Impact Teams would accelerate discharge during peak periods.
o  
The ICB noted an additional 46,000 GP appointments available for
the winter period, with unused appointments to be reallocated to
the NHS 111 service.
o  
The Committee asked why more out-patient procedures were not being
done within the community, instead of in hospitals.
§ 
The ICB explained that this was being considered for the future,
including IV (intravenous) antibiotic administration within
community settings to alleviate pressure on hospital
settings.

·       
Learning
o  
The Committee asked what learning the ICB had gained from the
previous winter for this year’s plan.
o  
The ICB noted that capacity and demand modelling was underestimated
last winter and did not account for higher-than-expected infection
rates.
§ 
It was noted that they had included a buffer of additional capacity
to this winter’s predicted need and would be employing
virtual ward utilisation improved through a “pull
practitioner” approach to identify suitable patients for home
monitoring.
o  
They also reported that continuous review of feedback and learning
from other regions (e.g., Portsmouth’s mobile X-ray service)
would be conducted.

·       
Vaccination
o  
The Committee queried COVID-19 jab pricing for the public.
§ 
The ICB clarified JCVI sets age criteria, anyone outside of that
criteria must pay prices dictated by the private sector.
o  
Both the ICB and Local Authority noted vaccination uptake should
remain a priority, with initiatives targeting patients during
routine appointments and discharge, as well as staff.

·       
Financial Planning
o  
The Committee raised concerns about reported £6 million
cuts.
o  
ICB clarified the following:
§ 
There were no budget cuts to winter planning: focus was on value
for money and effectiveness.
§ 
Capacity planned and funded upfront to avoid costly reactive
measures.
§ 
Transparent communication with bank staff regarding additional
staffing needs.
§ 
De-escalation plans in place to close extra capacity when no longer
needed.
o  
Investments in same-day access hubs, online consultations and acute
visiting services and urgent dental care had been made to support
winter planning.

·       
Ambulance Handover & Escalation
o  
The Committee queried current and ongoing handover delays for
ambulances.
o  
The ICB noted the average handover times improved to under 40 mins
in early summer but worsened from September 2025.
§ 
Current tolerance was 45mins; national target was 15mins.
o  
The ICB stated protocols had been put in place for patients waiting
in ambulances, including clinician assessment at the
vehicle.

·       
Patient Experience & Engagement
o  
Healthwatch asked what metrics were being used and collected on
patient experience.
o  
The ICB stated they’re committed to improving communication
and sharing patient experiences.
o  
There is planned engagement and feedback for the end of the winter
period.
topline: The Adult Social Care, Health Integration and Wellbeing Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve the Staffordshire & Stoke-on-Trent Integrated Care System Winter Plan 2025/26 to address winter pressures in the healthcare system.

content:
The City Council’s
Strategic Risk Register was submitted to the Committee for review
and comment.  The Strategic Risk
Register was reviewed on a quarterly basis and advised of the
current position on strategic risks, in terms of potential impact
on the City Council’s ability to deliver its strategic aims
and statutory responsibilities, and outline mitigations in
place.
The Head of Audit and Fraud
highlighted the amendments made which included a change to the
format to indicate new developing mitigations and a review of the
current controls to make the register more manageable.
In relation to Risk 11 -
Corporate Parenting, it was noted that the risk score had risen
from high to very high, which linked to an overall increase in the
number of children in care since May 2025.  Members of the Committee expressed their concerns
and sought assurances about the trajectory and plans to resolve the
situation particularly as high numbers of children in care had a
significant impact on the authority’s financial
position. 
The Committee was also keen to
understand if the Corporate Parenting Board was aware of the
corporate parenting risk level and impact on the city
councils’ financial resources and the Corporate Director of
Resources gave assurances that the matter would be raised with the
Director of Childrens Services.  The
Committee was advised that this was a national problem which was
unfortunately felt more acutely in Stoke-on-Trent
In conclusion of the
discussion, a motion was passed that the Committee writes to the
Education Secretary urging her to accelerate the change that has
already commenced in Children’s Social Care Practice, noting
the current situation was making Stoke-on-Trent City
Council’s financial position worse.
topline: The Audit and Standards Committee has decided to urge the Education Secretary for accelerated changes in Children's Social Care Practice.

content:

During the six months period,

related to planned audits identified within the annual

Appendix 1b and gave rise to 64 recommendations.  Of the 18 reports, four received negative
opinions, one received an unsound opinion, one received an
unsatisfactory opinion and two received marginal
opinions.
The report also detailed the
processes in place to monitor the implementation of agreed audit
recommendations and set out progress made against the 2025/26 Audit
Plan, in addition to highlighting the planned audits that were in
progress. 
In relation to outstanding
recommendations with negative opinions, the Committee was advised
that these related to Direct Payments and NHS Health Checks and the
Chair requested that an update be provided from the Service Leads
at the next meeting of the Committee.
topline: The Audit and Standards Committee has reviewed Internal Audit activities and recommendations, with some audits receiving negative opinions.

content:
The Committee considered the
Treasury Management Annual Report for the 2024/25 financial year
and a performance summary of treasury management activity that had
taken place during quarter one of 2025/26.
The Committee was advised that
the treasury function and responsibility is to manage effectively
all monies held by the City Council, develop and follow the
Treasury Management Strategy and make borrowing investment
decisions.  The activity for this
function sits within the Resources Directorate.  The day-to-day procedures were governed by the
City Council’s Treasury Management Practices (TMPs) that
adhere to the CIPFA Treasury Management Code which provided advice
of best practice.
Key points highlighted
included:

·        
That all investments made during 2024/25 and the
first quarter of 2025/26 complied with the 2024/25 and 2025/26
Treasury Management Strategies.

·        
That interest earned from all investments during
2024/25 was £2.377 million, a surplus against the budget of
£0.150 million, which was incorporated into the final council
outturn position for 2024/25.

·        
That the committee note that prudential indicators
approved by City Council on 5 March 2024 and 30 January 2025
respectively had been monitored throughout 2024/25 and the first
quarter of 2025/26 and there had been no breaches of the policies
or indicators.
Committee questions included
clarification on the levels of the risk rate used for investments
and about who decided on which investment to make.  In response, it was confirmed that the city
council didn’t invest in any rating lower than AA- and that
advice was sought from independent credit agencies such as
Arlingclose.
topline: The Audit and Standards Committee has approved the Treasury Management Annual Report, highlighting compliance with strategies and indicators.

The information presented
outlined the fraud type identified, value, number of cases and
provided a comparison to the previous year’s
figures.
The Committee was advised that
the Corporate Fraud Team had been involved in securing 13 tenancy
terminations so far this year in addition to preventing the
purchase of 9 properties through improved scrutiny and had
identified 22 cases where residents had failed to declare to the
council that they were no longer the lone adult
occupier.
Updates were also provided in
relation to the National Fraud Initiative,  Staffordshire Counter-Fraud Partnership, Fraud
Awareness Training and a legislative change to prevent fraud which
came into force from September 2025.
topline: The Audit and Standards Committee has reviewed the progress of the Corporate Fraud Team in addressing fraudulent activities in the first half of the financial year.

content:
The Committee considered a
summary of the external auditor’s progress report which
highlighted the key developments in the audit of Stoke-on-Trent
City Council’s financial statements and value for money
arrangements.
The Committee was advised that
the statutory timetable required councils to publish financial
statements by prescribed deadlines, even where an audit opinion
cannot be issued.  Stoke-on-Trent City
Council received disclaimed opinions for the year 2020/21 to
2023/24. In addition, the auditors have indicated that they intend
to treat 2024/25 similarly, using a historic testing approach to
rebuild assurance.  This involved a
detailed examination of prior-year transactions and records and was
expected to run across several years (estimated 2025/26 to
2028/29). 
The 2024/25 value for money
assessment (VFM) was in progress. Focus areas included financial
sustainability, governance and efficiency.  A draft VFM report was expected by November
2025.
The 2024/25 audit fee was yet
to be confirmed and would depend on the scope of historic testing
and additional audit procedures. Any significant fee increase would
be reported through regular budget monitoring and to the Audit and
Standards Committee for review and scrutiny.
Members of the Committee
expressed their disappointment and frustration at the likelihood of
receiving another disclaimed opinion and reference was made to the
national shortage of auditors and accountants and the Governments
ongoing Local Audit Reform to address the backlog
concerns.
topline: The Audit and Standards Committee has decided to address the ongoing disclaimed opinions received by Stoke-on-Trent City Council for their financial statements and value for money arrangements.

The Corporate Director of
Housing, Regeneration and Operations submitted a report requesting
the Licensing and Registration Panel (the Panel) to determine an
application for exemption from displaying plates, signage and door
signs for a Private Hire Vehicle, in accordance with the
authorities’ responsibilities for public safety.
The Local Government
(Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1976 required that a licensed
private hire vehicle exhibit a licence plate in such a manner as
the City Council specified by a condition attached to that licence.
The Act also required the City Council, when issuing a
driver’s licence, to issue a driver’s badge in such a
form as may from time to time be prescribed by them.  A driver must at all times, when acting in
accordance with a driver’s licence, wear their badge in a
position and manner such as to be plainly and distinctly
visible.
Section 75 of the Act allowed
the City Council, upon application, to specify either certain
occasions when the plate need not be displayed or issue a notice to
be carried in lieu of the plate being displayed.  In these circumstances the requirement that the
driver had to wear a badge was also waived.
Section 75 was often used in
relation to vehicles that provided ‘chauffeur services’
and ‘executive hire’.  The
Panel was informed that it was a matter for them to be satisfied
that the character of the business operation and the vehicle
warranted the issue of such exemptions.
The applicant attended the
meeting and confirmed that they had received a copy of the report
and had read and understood it. The report was outlined at the
meeting and the applicant was interviewed by the Panel.
topline: The Licensing and Registration Panel has decided to grant an exemption for a Private Hire Vehicle from displaying plates, signage, and door signs for public safety.

content:
Nick Edmonds attended to
provide Committee with an overview of the financial position of the
City Council as at the end of June 2025.

Emerging risks had been identified, primarily driven by increased
demand and inflationary pressures. Through targeted budget
management actions, the amount had reduced and further work was ongoing to further
mitigate the pressures.

The General Fund forecast outturn and variances for 2025/26 was
provided for each Directorate.

The Housing Revenue Account (HRA) was forecasting a balanced
position for 2025/26. Any surplus amounts generated through
underspends on the revenue budgets would be reinvested in the HRA
in future years.

The City Council had budgeted to invest in capital schemes during
2025/26 and the forecast outturn on investments was shared.

When questioned about the risk register, and the lack of amount
shown as red considering the position outlined, Nick Edmonds
confirmed that where there is significant pressure this is shown as
red however given the controls and measures in place there is less
risk given the confidence in mitigation measures.

When questioned regarding the savings which had not been achieved
from a previous year in relation to the Telecare and Community
Alarm Services, it was confirmed options were still being
considered with external partners. A draft response to this query
had been completed and Nick Edmonds agreed to follow this up and
share a response with Committee Members.
