content:
Emily Bagnall attended to
provide an update in respect of the Stoke-on-Trent libraries
volunteer model.

This was in response to a request from Committee earlier in the
year.

It was confirmed that following a successful appointment, a
permanent Volunteer Coordinator had been in post since the end of
July. This had been funded internally with existing budgets.

There were 27 current volunteers, with a further 10 to join at the
end of September. These would attend events and work would be done to deploy them to the
most appropriate areas.

The next step for the service was to expand the HomeLink service
with volunteers to support the demands, and this would be promoted
as an opportunity over the coming months. The aim was to have the
volunteers for this service in post by January to support the
demands over the winter months. This would be subject to the right
candidates coming forward and also required training, insurance and
the safeguarding of service users made a priority.

When questioned on the number of hours per week volunteers were
active, it was agreed this information could be provided to
Committee Members following the meeting.

Committee Members noted no online presence yet regarding
recruitment. It was confirmed the team were still assessing the
need in terms of attributes, such as if a volunteer would need to
be able to drive and if they would require a DBS check so these
adverts will follow.

Councillor Hill praised the work being done and was pleased to see
so much happening.

James Doble welcomed ideas from Committee Members in terms of where
to target adverts for these roles and welcomed contact from Members
with contact information.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to implement a volunteer model for Stoke-on-Trent libraries.

decision_maker: Strategy and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Lesli Good attended to provide
Committee with an update on the performance, activity, and future
priorities of the Apprenticeship Hub, highlighting key
achievements, trends, and upcoming changes to the national
apprenticeship landscape.

It was acknowledged that prior to its transfer into the Jobs,
Enterprise & Training (JET) Service in 2023, the Council had
not been maximising its levy allocation, leading to significant
underspend being returned to HM Treasury. Significant progress had
been made to improve on this.

Historically, the Council had shared up to 20% of its levy with
other local employers. This had been paused until October 2025 due
to full commitment of the allocation, although the Hub continued to
signpost organisations to alternative levy-share sources.

A priority focus was the development of tailored pathways into
apprenticeships for care-experienced young people. A steering group
had been formed with colleagues from Children’s and
Adult’s Social Care to design new approaches.

Apprenticeship delivery continued to perform strongly. In
2024–2025, the Council achieved 88 apprenticeship starts,
significantly exceeding the annual target of 50. This included a
wide range of occupational areas such as social work, civil
engineering, residential childcare, planning, ICT and
leadership.

As at September 2025, there had already
been 36 starts in the current financial year (against a full year
target of 50) with a healthy pipeline for the remainder of
2025–2026. Given current commitments, it is highly likely
that the annual target would again be met or exceeded.

Analysis had been carried out locally to understand the types of
apprenticeships required, such as within the communication
sector.

Committee Members asked about drop-out rates and also once an
apprenticeship had been completed, if officers tended to stay
within their current role or if there was a noted progression. It
was confirmed this level of analysis had not been done yet, but it
was felt that understanding this was important.

When questioned about those who paused apprenticeships, and if the
barriers to this were understood, it was confirmed the team
retained personal contact and had individual conversations to
understand what could be done to provide additional support. The
team were looking for trends within this data.

In addition to this work, Nick Edmonds spoke about the accountancy
training which was ran by the City Council. This was not included
within the figures reported as it was a separate piece of work, but
was another area of success.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to focus on improving apprenticeship opportunities and performance within the Council.

decision_maker: Strategy and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Angela Glithero attended to
provide a Quarter 1 update against the Council’s corporate
measures relevant to the committee.

When questioned why there were no areas shown as red, Angela
explained that whilst challenging and demanding, teams were working
hard to ensure targets were being achieved.

Nick Edmonds agreed that the position was positive, despite the
challenges, and also noted some elements would be seasonal and
therefore the next report may show some areas of red given the time
of year. It was acknowledged teams should not become
complacent.

When questioned about figures related to library visits, it was
confirmed there had been an issue with recording data due to a
broken device. This had since been addressed.

James Doble added his frustration at this, given the large number
of events which had taken place, so it would have been good to
showcase these figures.

When questioned regarding calls handled but the contact centre, it
was confirmed the measure covered all contact centres using the
platform. Work had been done to ensure calls were directed to the
correct area, such as revenues calls going to the correct teams,
for the best customer experience.

When questioned on abandonment figures, it was asked if these were
included in relation to all offices handling contact centre calls.
It was confirmed they were, and that a breakdown of the information
for each service had been included within the report. The figure
was aggregated and overall was showing as green. It was
acknowledged there was still room for improvement.

In terms of the length of time before an abandonment of a call, the
average was noted as 6 and a half minutes. These figures were
recorded down to service level. It was acknowledged further work
was needed to reduce this and of course the hope was for calls to
be answered as quickly as possible.

Committee asked if further details and breakdowns of these figures
could be shared, and whilst there was a discussion regarding where
the responsibility for scrutiny sat for the various areas, such as
calls going into either children’s or adult’s services,
it was felt that this Committee should have an oversight with a
holistic view, and the request was therefore accepted.

It was also acknowledged that some calls can be complex issues
which take a considerable time for an operator to respond to, so in
terms of context it was felt important to consider average call
duration times as well.

In terms of numbers related to library contacts, Committee Members
had previously requested a breakdown to understand the activity and
in particular those using the library for checking in/out books.
For example, Stoke Library also included a Local Centre, therefore
not everyone attending the site was a library user. It was
acknowledged this information was still to be provided, and would be sent to Committee
Members.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee has received a positive update on Council's corporate measures

decision_maker: Strategy and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
The Chair outlined a topic
suggestion which had been received in relation to officer salaries.
It was felt this was not an area for Committee to look at, given
salaries were considered via collective bargaining and this could also be considered as part
of budget considerations.

Committee Members also noted the upcoming Local Government
Reorganisation, with the potential for officer salaries to be
considered based upon these changes, and therefore did not feel it
would be appropriate or useful to consider at this time.

Committee Members were minded to look at Local Government
Reorganisation as a topic, and considered the possibility of
including this element within those discussions. It was agreed a
scope for this work was to be completed with the hope of a
discussion at the March 2026 meeting.

It was also requested that the item related to complaints and
compliments be brought to the November Committee
Meeting.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to focus on Local Government Reorganisation instead of looking into officer salaries.

content:
The Licensing Sub-Committee met
to consider an application for the variation of a premise licence
under section 51 of the Licensing Act 2003. Local residents had
submitted valid representations and therefore the Licensing
Authority were required to hold a hearing to determine the
application in respect of The
Jolly Potters, 296 Hartshill Road,
Stoke-on-Trent, ST4 7NH.
The proposed variation
application sought to:

·       
Extend the opening hours to permit the premises to
open from 08:00 hours daily for breakfast, coffee and tea
etc.

·       
Remove some existing Annex 2 and Annex 3
conditions.

·       
Add some new conditions including to
permit the performance of live music and recorded music outdoors
daily from opening until 22:00 hours.

·       
Amend the licensing plan in accordance
with the drawing which accompanied the application, and to permit
the sale of alcohol from an external bar servery.
On 11 August 2025,
Mr Lewis, from the City Council’s Public Protection team, had
contacted Licensing Services stating that whilst the premises had
utilised Temporary Event Notices (TENs) with few complaints, due to
the representations received, he would recommend that the premises
consider reducing the proposed hours for entertainment
outdoors.
On 19 August 2025,
Mr Domleo, acting on behalf of the
applicant, confirmed that this proposal would be acceptable to them
and amended the application as follows:

·       
The performance of live and recorded
music outdoors shall be permitted daily from opening until 20:00
hours. The sale of alcohol from the external bar servery shall be
permitted daily from opening until 22:00 hours.
On 20 August 2025,
those persons who had made representations were contacted and asked
if the new proposal was acceptable. Mr Morton replied that he
agreed that this was a compromise.  Mr
Steele and Councillor Pender both replied that the proposal was not
acceptable.
On 3 October 2025,
Mr Domleo, acting on behalf of the
applicant emailed Licensing Services and amended the offered
condition as follows:

·       
The performance of live and recorded
music outdoors shall be permitted daily from 12:00 hours until 20:00
hours. The sale of alcohol from the external bar servery shall be
permitted daily from 12:00 hours until 21:00 hours.
An additional
condition was also offered as follows:

·       
Customers shall not be permitted to use
the beer garden after 22:00 hours, except for smoking in the
designated smoking area.
The Sub-Committee
considered the written and verbal representations received on
behalf of the applicant and from those making
representations.
topline: The Licensing Sub-Committee has decided to permit live music outdoors and alcohol sales with restrictions at The Jolly Potters in Stoke-on-Trent.

decision_maker: Housing, Regeneration & Operations Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Councillor Robinson (Cabinet
Member), Tom Coates (Head of Planning and Building Control) and Tom
Lewis (Principal Planning Policy Officer) attended to present this
item, which provided an update on the progress of the
Stoke-on-Trent Draft Local Plan and public consultation.

Committee were reminded that it is a statutory requirement for
Local Planning Authorities to prepare a development plan for their
area, in consultation with a wide range of stakeholders; statutory
consultees and local people, with the development plan setting out
what the area would look like in the future, the aims and
objectives of the plan area, the level of development required,
where development should be located and the planning policies which
would be used to determine planning applications.

Cabinet had approved the Draft Local Plan for public consultation
at a meeting on 19 August 2025 and a six-week consultation period
subsequently began on 8 September 2025. This would conclude on 20
October 2025.

The Stoke-on-Trent Local Plan was being prepared in accordance with
the timetable as presented on the council’s website and this
was shared with Committee Members for clarity.

It was acknowledged that not all residents would wish to engage via
electronic methods, therefore a large number of drop-in sessions
had also been planned during the consultation period for residents
to attend in-person to speak with the relevant team members.

Committee raised questions about the inclusion of brownfield land
within the proposals, and in particular asked for a list of
brownfield sites which had not been included in the draft plan and
the reasons for their omission.

It was explained that sites were considered via a number of tests,
and that overall approximately 440 sites had been considered. All
sites which had been put forward had been considered however it was
acknowledged that for a variety of reasons not all sites were
viable to put into the draft plan.

Committee Members did not feel communication regarding the Draft
Local Plan had been enough, and requested further information be
put out to residents via social media, potentially with videos to
help with engagement, and potentially including information about
the brownfield sites in the City where work was already happening
to develop these.

Committee Members also asked for information to be shared
explaining to residents why some sites had not been included, the
reasons for them not being viable and also to confirm that just
because a site is included within the Draft Local Plan it does not
necessarily mean that it will ultimately be developed.

Committee Members also requested that there be further clarity for
residents on the newly defined grey belt, and what this means in
terms of comparison to green belt.

It was acknowledged some sites within the plan had not necessarily
been submitted as individual sites, but that they formed parts of
broader locations which were being looked at. Within this, it was
acknowledged that some land owners may not wish for their sites to
be included in the final version.

Within their considerations, Committee Members acknowledged the
changing landscape of the way in which people live their lives and
in particular shop, for example a greater use of online and
delivery, and asked that this be considered as part of
proposals.
topline: The Housing, Regeneration & Operations Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to progress the Stoke-on-Trent Draft Local Plan for public consultation.
